title: Keytips: full Excel sequential Alt table — 364 sequences, badges on every control, generated tests (fixes #33, #49)
author: jsymes21-byte
body: ## What does this PR do? Lands the full Excel sequential Alt access-key (keytip) table on top of the system refactor: **364 curated Excel sequences** (key combos) across every ribbon tab — 289 act today (219 live command sequences → 156 unique commands, 39 dialogs, 21 ribbon controls, 10 tab switches), 42 are bound to not-yet-built commands (silent no-ops until they land), and 33 are intermediate wait levels, keytip badges painted on every ribbon control, editable dropdown keytips, generated per-sequence regression tests, and the real-Excel corrections verified against a live copy of Excel. Sequences that have no matching GridCraft command yet are bound to their canonical future ids and resolve at runtime — silent no-ops today, live the moment the command lands (proven by a test that registers a fake command). title: CI: run cargo xtask ci on pull requests and pushes to main
author: neilcawse
body:

title: CLI: check subcommand - cached-value calc oracle and XLSX round-trip fidelity on any corpus
author: neilcawse
body:
## What changed
New `gridcraft-cli check <file-or-dir>... [--json] [--tolerance 1e-9] [--max-report 20]` (`apps/gridcraft-cli/src/check.rs`). It measures calculation correctness and file fidelity on any set of `.xlsx`/`.xlsm` files and writes nothing next to them.

- **Calc oracle.** Excel stores its own result next to every formula. `check` reads each file and keeps those cached values, recalculates every formula with GridCraft, and compares the two. Numbers must agree within a relative tolerance (absolute when the magnitude is below 1). Errors must be the same kind. Text and logicals must match exactly.
  - Cells with no cached value (including `fullCalcOnLoad` files from libraries that don't calculate, such as xlsxwriter) are counted as *no oracle*. Volatile formulas, and everything downstream of them in the dependency graph, are counted as *volatile*. Neither is compared.
  - Each mismatch lists the cell, formula, expected and actual values, and the functions it calls. Mismatches are also summed by function, where *primary* means none of the cell's precedents mismatch, so that function is the likely culprit. They are also summed by type signature (e.g. `number → #SPILL!`), which tends to group one root cause.
- **Round trip.** The recalculated workbook is saved with GridCraft's XLSX writer, then read back. The package is validated against the things Excel would "repair": missing content types, dangling relationship targets, duplicate relationship ids. Then sheets, values, formulas, per-cell number formats, merges, names, tables, conditional formats, validations, charts, comments, hyperlinks and pivots are compared with the original.
- `--json` gives a machine-readable report for CI or scripts. Usage is documented in `docs/cli.md`.

## Why
The parity docs count which functions exist, not whether they return what Excel returns. This gives a repeatable number from real Excel-saved files without needing Excel installed. It's clean-room: it only uses values Excel alr…

title: XLSX: legacy formulas (no dynamic-array `cm`) open with Excel's implicit `@` and calculate like Excel
author: neilcawse
body:
Follow-up to #64 / #267. #267 writes `@` as `_xlfn.SINGLE` in a dynamic-array formula, and its test notes that dropping the `@` instead "would need the reader to put it back on legacy formulas". This PR adds that reader side. The write side of #64 is already on main, so this PR does not close it.

## What changed
- **Read.** A cell formula saved without dynamic-array metadata (no `cm` attribute) and not entered as a Ctrl+Shift+Enter array is a legacy formula. Excel evaluates it with implicit intersection, and dynamic-array Excel shows it with `@` inserted at those places. GridCraft now does the same. After names and tables are read, `array_formula::apply_legacy` inserts `@` wherever a reference that may cover several cells meets a single-value parameter, an operator, or the cell result. Examples: `TANH(A1:A3)` → `TANH(@A1:A3)`, `MYUDF(A1:A3)` → `@MYUDF(A1:A3)`. `SUM(A1:A3)` and `SUMPRODUCT(A1:A3*B1:B3)` are left alone. The calc engine then gives the legacy result with no second evaluator. Dynamic-array formulas (`cm`) and CSE arrays are read as written.
- **Write.** `array_formula::export` replaces `needs_array` and has three outcomes:
  - unchanged;
  - dynamic (`cm` + single-cell array ref, as before);
  - legacy: every `@` in the formula is one legacy Excel would imply, or one of a single value. The implied ones are left out (the reader puts them back), and any other `@` of a single value is written as `_xlfn.SINGLE` inside the legacy formula, as Excel Online and EPPlus write it. The formula gets no `cm`.

  So a legacy formula read from a file saves back as a legacy formula, without `cm`, and with its text except for the known exceptions listed below. This holds also after an edit leaves an implied `@` on one cell: deleting rows 2:3 under the legacy `SQRT(A1:A3)` (read as `SQRT(@A1:A3)`) gives `SQRT(@A1:A1)`, saved as `SQRT(A1:A1)`, and so is `SQRT(@Rng)` after `Rng` is redefined to a one-cell range (`=Sheet1!$A$1:$A$1`). title: Numfmt: fraction literals and zero fractions, `?` pads thousands separator, TEXT booleans through text section
author: neilcawse
body:
## What changed
Fixes in `crates/numfmt`, shared by `TEXT()` and cell display, found by comparing against Excel-cached `TEXT()` results in number- and text-format test workbooks (352 TEXT cells: 226 mismatched before, 0 after).

- Fraction sections with literal text: `parse.rs` now treats a section as a fraction when literal text sits between the bar and the denominator (`#/ #`, `# ?=/=?`). `render.rs` splits a fraction section into `[whole] [sep] num [lit] / [lit] den` and keeps the literals between the parts (`|#\:#=/=#|` with 23.75 gives `|23:3=/=4|`).
- When the whole part shows no digit, its separator disappears, or becomes spaces when the whole part or the numerator has a `?` (`|#\:#/#|` with 0.75 gives `|3/4|`).
- Zero fractions: when the fractional part is zero and the numerator has no `0` placeholder, the separator, numerator, bar and denominator are hidden (spaces if any part has a `?`) and the whole part shows at least `0`. With a `0` in the numerator it shows `0/1` (`|#\:0=/=#|` with 0 gives `|0=/=1|`).
- Literal text before the bar keeps the improper fraction (`|#_#/#|` with 3.75 gives `|15 /4|`).
- `0` denominator placeholders zero pad on the left (`/000` gives `/004`).
- A blank `?` placeholder also pads the thousands separator it would have carried with a space (`?,?????????` with 1234567 gives `    1,234,567`).
- `TEXT()` with a boolean now runs `TRUE`/`FALSE` through the text section instead of returning it as is (`TEXT(TRUE,";;;\@@\@")` = `@TRUE@`). Number formats without a text section still return `TRUE`/`FALSE`.

## Tests
New tests in `crates/numfmt/src/tests.rs`:
- `fractions_with_literals`: 45 cases (literals around the bar, hidden whole part, zero fractions, `0` in the numerator, zero-padded denominators, literal before the bar).
- `question_mark_pads_thousands_separator`: 7 cases.
- `text_fn`: 9 boolean cases through the text section.

Expected values are Excel results as cached in the test workbooks.

title: Functions: MODE/VALUE/SUMPRODUCT text args, ADDRESS [Book]Sheet, Excel-style lookup bisection, SUBTOTAL skips filtered rows
author: neilcawse
body:
## What changed
Function fixes found by comparing GridCraft against Excel-cached formula results in test workbooks. One PR because they came out of the same comparison run; the parts are independent and grouped below.

### MODE / MODE.SNGL / MODE.MULT (`crates/functions/src/stat.rs`)
- New `mode_numbers`: inside multi-cell ranges and arrays only numbers count (as before), but direct text (even numeric text like `"1"`) and a single-cell reference to text or a blank cell give `#VALUE!`. Arguments are read left to right, so the first error wins (`MODE(1,1,#DIV/0!,"1")` is `#DIV/0!`, `MODE("1",1,#DIV/0!)` is `#VALUE!`).

### VALUE (`crates/functions/src/text.rs`)
- `VALUE("")` and whitespace-only text are now `#VALUE!` (they returned 0). A blank cell still reads as 0.

### SUMPRODUCT (`crates/functions/src/math.rs`)
- Text in a scalar argument (a literal or a single-cell reference) is `#VALUE!`. Text inside arrays and multi-cell ranges still counts as 0.

### ADDRESS (`crates/functions/src/lookup.rs`)
- A `[Book]Sheet` sheet_text is judged by its parts, so `ADDRESS(2,3,3,TRUE,"[Book1]Sheet1")` gives `[Book1]Sheet1!$C2` instead of `'[Book1]Sheet1'!$C2`. Names with spaces are still quoted (`'[My Book]Sheet1'!$A$1`, `'EXCEL SHEET'!R2C3`).

### Approximate match: VLOOKUP / HLOOKUP / LOOKUP / MATCH (`crates/functions/src/lookup.rs`)
- `bsearch_last` now bisects the whole vector the way Excel does, instead of first filtering to entries of the needle's type and searching those. A probe of a different type moves to the nearest same-type entry below it in the window (or the window moves up past it). An equal probe ends the search, then the run of equal entries after it is taken, so sorted duplicates give the last one. On unsorted, mixed-type data the answer now matches Excel's (e.g. `VLOOKUP(534, {"INTEGRAL";0;1;2;534;9999999999;-9999999999}, …)` finds 534). No allocation; linear work in the worst case, including long runs of trailing blanks.

title: Formulas: trim-reference operators (A1:.E10, A1.:E10, A1.:.E10); read unbracketed [[#This Row],Col]
author: neilcawse
body:
Follow-up to #297 (TRIMRANGE), which listed the trim-reference operators under "Not done".

## What changed
- **Trim references.** The lexer now produces a `Trim` token for `:.` (trailing), `.:` (leading) and `.:.` (both) when it sits between two range ends. That covers cells (`A1:.E10`), whole columns (`A:.A`, `$A.:.$C`), whole rows (`1:.5`, `$1.:$5`) and sheet-qualified ranges (`Sheet2!$A$1:.B9`, `'Q1 2026'!A1:.B2`). Decimals (`1.5+.5`), dotted names (`my.name`) and dotted sheet names (`Q1.2026!A1:B2`) keep their old meaning. Malformed forms (`A1.:`, `.:A1`, `A1:.:B2`) are parse errors.
- The parser builds `Expr::Unary(UnOp::Trim(TrimMode), range)`; `TrimMode` is exported from `gridcraft-formula`. The printer writes the operator back in A1 and R1C1 (`SUM(RC:.R[1]C[1])`). Insert/delete adjustment, relative shifting and `references()` go through the inner range, as for `:`.
- **Evaluation.** `crates/calc/src/trimrange.rs` gains `trim_ref`, which evaluates the range and runs it through the same trimming code as `TRIMRANGE(range, code, code)` (1 leading, 2 trailing, 3 both). The result spills and follows edits to the full range. An all-blank range gives `#CALC!`, as TRIMRANGE does.
- **XLSX.** On save, a trim reference is written as `_xlfn.TRIMRANGE(range,code,code)`. Public docs do not say how Excel spells the operator in files. On read, both that form and the `_xlfn._TRO_ALL` / `_TRO_LEADING` / `_TRO_TRAILING(range)` call forms parse back to the operator. A `_TRO_*` call on something other than a range prints as the equivalent `TRIMRANGE(x,n,n)`. `array_formula.rs` treats the operator as a reference operator, like `#`.
- **Unbracketed `[[#This Row],Col]`.** Some writers (xlsxwriter, for example) write `[@Units]` as `[[#This Row],Units]`, with the column name unbracketed. That form now parses, with or without a table name, and prints canonically as `[@Units]` / `Sales[@Units]`. title: Calc: iterative calculation for circular references (Maximum Iterations, Maximum Change)
author: neilcawse
body:
## What changed

Enable Iterative Calculation was already read from and written to XLSX (`<calcPr iterate iterateCount iterateDelta>`) and settable through `formulas.calculationOptions`, but the calc engine ignored it: circular references always gave `#CIRC!`. With it on, they now iterate.

- `crates/calc/src/recalc.rs`: with `wb.calc.iterative` on, a formula read while it is being evaluated gives its previous value (from the last iteration, else the value it shows; blank and a stale `#CIRC!` count as 0) instead of `#CIRC!`. The pass records which formulas sit on a loop and which results read a previous value, directly or through other formulas or spilled arrays. After the first pass, those formulas are evaluated again in the same order (each pass reads what it has already produced, Gauss-Seidel style) until no formula on a loop changes by Maximum Change or more, or Maximum Iterations passes are reached. Text, logical and error values count as changed unless equal. Total work is capped at 10,000,000 formula evaluations per recalculation, whatever Maximum Iterations says. With iteration off, behaviour is unchanged (`#CIRC!`).
- The `PassHost` struct literal, which was repeated in three places (recalc, `evaluate_expr`, the `visit_range` test probe), is now `PassHost::new`.
- `crates/model/src/workbook.rs`: `CalcSettings` gains `DEFAULT_ITERATIONS` (100), `DEFAULT_CHANGE` (0.001), `MAX_ITERATIONS` (32,767), `set_max_iterations` (clamps to 1..=32,767) and `set_max_change` (magnitude; ignores NaN/infinite). The XLSX reader and the command use them.
- `formulas.calculationOptions` (`crates/engine/src/cmd/formulas.rs`): changing `iterative`, `maxIterations` or `maxChange` outside manual mode now recalculates the workbook. The result returns all four settings, and the parameter description documents ranges and defaults.

title: File formats: CSV/TSV export writes displayed values; templates and .xlsm saved with their own content types
author: neilcawse
body:
## What changed
- Save As CSV/TSV now writes each cell as it is displayed: number formats applied (dates, currency, percent, fractions, thousands separators, `@` text), formula results, errors and booleans as shown. It never writes column-width `#####` and never applies the grid's General narrowing, so the field holds the whole value. This follows Microsoft's description of Save As CSV/Text ("the text and values as they are displayed in cells", all characters kept). Before this change the export wrote raw values (`46023` instead of `2026-01-01`).
  - `engine::display::value_text` is split out of `cell_text`: it formats the value without the show-formulas branch. A sheet with Show Formulas on still exports values.
  - `gridcraft_xlsx::write_csv(sheet, delimiter, cell_text)` takes a closure that supplies each field's text. Quoting, CRLF line ends and UTF-8 without BOM stay in the xlsx crate, and formatting stays in the engine (layering). The old raw `field_text` helper is removed.
- `.xltx`, `.xltm` and `.xlsm` are saved with their own `xl/workbook.xml` content type (template, macro-enabled template, macro-enabled workbook). Before, every one of them got the `.xlsx` workbook type, which Excel rejects for a template. The new `XlsxKind::from_path` picks the kind from the extension (case-insensitive; unknown or missing extensions give `.xlsx`). `write_xlsx_as(wb, kind)` writes it.
- The VBA project kept by #6 now follows the kind: the writer adds `xl/vbaProject.bin` only for `.xlsm` and `.xltm` (`XlsxKind::is_macro_enabled`), so `save_bytes` no longer clones the workbook to strip it, and a macro-enabled template keeps its macros. `write_xlsx(wb)` behaves as before: `.xlsm` when the workbook holds a VBA project, `.xlsx` otherwise. The `CT_WORKBOOK_MAIN`/`CT_WORKBOOK_MAIN_MACRO` constants are replaced by `XlsxKind::main_content_type`.

title: XLSX: strip _xlpm. from LET/LAMBDA parameters on read, keep line breaks in table columns, allow leading backslash in table names
author: neilcawse
body:
## What changed
Three XLSX round-trip losses, all in `crates/xlsx`:

- **`_xlpm.` LET/LAMBDA parameters.** Excel stores LET/LAMBDA parameter names as `_xlpm.name` in the file. The writer already adds the prefix, but `read_formula` (`sheet_read.rs`) used the raw `<f>` text, so a saved `LET(x,1,x+1)` came back as `_xlfn.LET(_xlpm.x,1,_xlpm.x+1)`. Cell, shared and array formulas now go through `fmla::from_file`, the conversion CF, data validation and names already use. When the formula parses, the stored text is the parser/printer form with `_xlfn.`/`_xlpm.` removed. When it doesn't parse, the text is kept as written. One side effect: cell formula text read from a file is now in printer form (for example, spacing may change) rather than byte-for-byte as stored.
- **Line breaks in table column names.** `table_columns` (`sheet_write.rs`) replaced `\r`/`\n` with spaces in column names. Excel allows a line break in a table header, and the header cell still had the break, so the column name and its header cell disagreed after a save. The name is now written unchanged (XML escaping already handles it).
- **Leading backslash in table names.** `table_name` turned a leading `\` into `_` (or fell back to `TableN`). Excel's rules for names in formulas allow a name to start with a letter, `_` or `\`, so `\_Prime.1` is now kept. Structured references such as `COUNTA(\_Prime.1[Name])` already parsed.

## Tests
- `tests::roundtrip::let_lambda_parameters_drop_xlpm_on_read`: LET, an immediately called LAMBDA and an array MAP/LAMBDA formula are written with `_xlpm.` in the sheet XML and read back with bare parameter names.
- `tests::roundtrip::table_newline_column_and_backslash_name_survive`: a table named `\_Prime.1` with a `Handle\nBars` column keeps both after a round trip, along with the header cell value and a structured reference formula to it.

title: Charts: read, write and draw trendlines
author: neilcawse
body:
## What changed

- **Model** (`crates/model/src/features.rs`): `Series.trendlines: Vec<Trendline>` (`#[serde(default)]`, so older saved state still loads). A `Trendline` holds the kind (linear, exponential, logarithmic, polynomial order 2–6, power, moving average period 2–255), an optional name, forward/backward forecast, an optional set intercept, show-equation and show-R² flags, and line colour, width and dash.
- **XLSX** (`crates/xlsx/src/chart.rs`): `<c:trendline>` is read and written with its children in `CT_Trendline` order (name, spPr, trendlineType, order, period, forward, backward, intercept, dispRSqr, dispEq, trendlineLbl). - **Drawing** (`crates/chart/src/trend.rs`, `render.rs`, `resolve.rs`): least-squares fits. Exponential, logarithmic and power fits are done on transformed values and skip non-positive points. A forecast widens the category or x axis, and the line is clipped to the plot area. Equation and R² labels are drawn in the plot, and the legend gets entries such as "Linear (Sales)". Degenerate data (too few points, constant x, singular system) draws no trendline and does not panic. Each series draws at most `MAX_TRENDLINES` trendlines.
- **Engine** (`crates/engine/src/cmd/extra.rs`): `chart.addElement` takes `element: "trendline"` with `series?`, `type?`, `order?`, `period?`, `forward?`, `backward?`, `displayEquation?` and `displayRSquared?`. `on: false` removes trendlines. title: Fix AutoFit width for table and AutoFilter dropdowns
author: derechopiano
body:
AutoFit currently measures column header text without accounting for the width of its filter dropdown button. As a result, longer headings such as `Quarterly Revenue` can be partially obscured by the dropdown, particularly when the cells below contain only short values (e.g. `1`).

Reserve dropdown space on visible filter header cells before comparing their widths with body cells. Share that geometry with header text layout and button hit-testing. This covers both tables and ordinary AutoFilters without double-counting overlapping buttons.

The allowance follows observations of Windows Excel 16.0 build 20326: 12.5 points at 100–200% zoom, 25 points at 50%, independent of header row height. Existing approximate font measurement remains unchanged.

Validation:
- Regression tests cover filter/header flags, ordinary and overlapping filters, longer body values, unaffected columns, zoom, row heights, and undo.
- UI tests exercise both the command and real header double-clicks at 50%, 100%, and 200% zoom.
- Native desktop launch and before/after renders were verified with a synthetic workbook.
- `cargo xtask ci`: all seven gates passed; 843 tests passed, 1 ignored. On Windows, the generated parity document was temporarily normalized to LF for its content check; the original checkout was restored without a content change.

title: Open password-encrypted workbooks (Agile and Standard encryption) (#11)
author: LloydNicholson
body:
Follows up #11 (closed by #17, which recognised encrypted workbooks and refused them). Requested by @LloydNicholson.

GridCraft now opens password-protected `.xlsx` workbooks: it asks for the password, decrypts the file and shows the workbook. This PR only opens them. Saving with a password is still to do.

## What changed
- **xlsx: new `crypto` module.** `decrypt(bytes, password)` reads Agile encryption (Excel 2010 onward: AES-128/192/256 in CBC mode, SHA-1/256/384/512) and Standard encryption (Excel 2007: AES with SHA-1) on top of the existing CFB reader. It is clean-room from the public [MS-OFFCRYPTO] spec. `check_encryption(bytes)` tells, without a password, whether any password could open the file. Files no password can open get their real message straight away: RC4, Extensible, certificate-only, rights-management (IRM) and damaged files.
- **Hostile input:**
  - The spin count is capped at 10,000,000.
  - The stated package size is checked against the ciphertext before anything is allocated.
  - Key, block and salt sizes are validated.
  - Every read goes through `get()`.
  - No new non-test code can panic.
- **New dependencies:** RustCrypto `aes` 0.9 and `sha1` 0.11 (pure Rust, MIT OR Apache-2.0, wasm-safe, default features off). xlsx also adds `sha2`, which was already in the workspace.
- **engine:**
  - `io::open_bytes_with_password`, plus the markers `PASSWORD_REQUIRED`, `WRONG_PASSWORD` and `DECRYPTED_NOTICE`.
  - `file.open` takes an optional `password`. Without one, an encrypted workbook returns an error and never opens a dialog.
  - A decrypted workbook gets **no save path**, so Save asks where to save it and never replaces the encrypted original with an unprotected copy.
  - The password stays out of the journal (it was already a secret param) and is never quoted in an error.
- **ui-egui:**
  - A new `openPassword` dialog, with a masked field and the existing Show password toggle.

title: Scatter charts of two unlabelled columns plot the first as X for one series (#428)
author: MarekSpodBiedry
body:
Fixes #428.

A scatter chart of two plain numeric columns came out as two series, each plotted against its point index, instead of one series with the first column as X and the second as Y.

`series_from_range` only treats the first column as categories when it holds text (or sits under a blank corner cell), which suits column/line charts but not scatter, where the first numeric column is the X values. The new `scatter_x_from_first` helper in `cmd/insert.rs` does what Excel does for scatter: when the block has no category labels, the first series becomes the X values (`categories`) of the remaining ones. Three columns give two series sharing the first column as X; a block laid out in rows uses its first row.

It runs on every path that builds a scatter chart's series from a range:
- `insert.chart` (and the Recommended Charts preview, which goes through `build_chart`),
- `chart.selectData` with a new `range`,
- `chart.switchRowColumn`.

Other chart kinds, and blocks that already have a text label column, are unchanged.

Test: `scatter_of_two_columns_is_one_series_with_the_first_as_x` inserts a scatter chart from `X`/`Y` columns and checks it gets one series, values `B2:B4` and X `A2:A4`. It then checks the same result after Select Data, and after Switch Row/Column on a block laid out in rows. Without the fix, `insert.chart` gives two series.

title: Rotated text follows the cell's alignment
author: itrycodinganditsbad
body:
Fixes #435

Rotated text (for example "up", 90°) was drawn at a fixed anchor: bottom-left for upward text, top-left for downward text. The cell's horizontal and vertical alignment were ignored, so upright text with Middle Align in a tall merged block stayed at the bottom.

The fix adds `rotated_text_pos` in `grid.rs`. It works out the bounding box of the rotated galley, places that box in the cell the same way flat text is placed (Left/Center/Right, Top/Center/Bottom, with pad and indent), and then derives the `TextShape` position from it, since egui rotates around the galley's top-left corner.

Default alignment (General, Bottom) keeps the old placement for ±90° text. Upward text sits at the bottom-left and downward text starts at the top-left, same as before. There is no separate "unset" vertical alignment, so for downward text Bottom still means top. Upward text at other angles (like 45°) with Bottom alignment now sits fully inside the cell. Before, the lower part hung below the bottom border and got clipped.

Tests: unit tests for 90°, -90°, 45° and -45° with every Top/Center/Bottom and Left/Center/Right combination. Each one rotates the galley corners around the returned position and checks the box is in the cell and lines up with the requested edge or the centre. A separate test pins the old default placement, and another covers the issue's case (90°, tall merged block, Middle and Center). The alignment tests failed against the old anchoring. I also checked offscreen snapshots of the issue repro before and after: the text is now centred in A1:A4, and default-aligned up and down text hasn't moved.

Not done or not verified:
- Underline and strikethrough on rotated text are still drawn as flat lines at the unrotated position. That was already wrong before this change and is still wrong.
- Print/PDF (`crates/engine/src/cmd/print.rs`) has its own copy of the old fixed anchor and still ignores alignment for rotated text. The helper can't be shared because the engin…

title: Release workflow: pass the Azure signing secrets
author: echelon
body:
Since this repo's `release.yml` moved to `storytold/craft-common-actions`, it has passed the Apple and `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE*` secrets to the shared workflow, but not the six `AZURE_*` secrets that Azure Trusted Signing uses.

The shared workflow's signing jobs run in this repo's `release` environment and read the values from there, but only for names the caller lists. So the next release would have built **unsigned** Windows MSIs and portable zips, with only a warning. craft-launcher 0.3.1 did exactly this, and storytold/craft-launcher#174 fixed it with this same change.

This adds the six names. All twelve secrets are already set in this repo's `release` environment. storytold/craft-common-actions#3 makes release builds fail outright if signing secrets are missing, and fixes the riscv64 `--formats` call. This PR should land first.

`actionlint` passes.

title: M12: formulas in German, Brazilian Portuguese, Russian and French, full Spanish table
author: quantmind-br
body:
Closes #367, closes #430. First of the focused PRs announced in #191: formula languages on top of main's `i18n.rs` and `FormulaLocale`, the way Spanish works now.

## What changes

With the interface language set to Deutsch, Português (Brasil), Русский or Français, the cell editor, formula bar, Show Formulas, autocomplete, argument hints, the Formulas ribbon and Insert Function use that language's formula syntax. Spanish gets its full table (main has 10 names). Stored formulas, XLSX, clipboard, engine commands, CLI and MCP keep canonical English, as with Spanish today.

| | Spanish | German | Portuguese (Brazil) | Russian | French |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Function names | 434 | 413 | 420 | 471 | 405 |
| Booleans | `VERDADERO`/`FALSO` | `WAHR`/`FALSCH` | `VERDADEIRO`/`FALSO` | `ИСТИНА`/`ЛОЖЬ` | `VRAI`/`FAUX` |

title: feat(python): add Python MCP client library for GridCraft automation
author: dronov-dmitry
body:
This PR introduces a new Python library (`libs/mcp-python`) that enables programmatic control of GridCraft via the MCP/TCP control channel. This allows users and AI agents to automate spreadsheet tasks using Python.

## Key Features
* **GridCraft MCP Client**: A native Python library for the GridCraft TCP control protocol.
    * Supports workbook creation (`new_workbook`), data manipulation (`set_cell`, `read_range`), formula evaluation, and charting.
* **CI/CD Pipeline**: Added GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/gridcraft-python-ci.yml`) to automatically test, lint, and format Python code.
* **Testing Infrastructure**: Comprehensive test suite with unit, integration, and example validation tests (89% code coverage).
* **Automation Scripts**: Added `run_tests.sh` and `run_ci.sh` for easy development and CI execution.
* **Documentation & Demos**: Includes installation guides, developer documentation, and interactive demonstration scripts.

## Demo
https://youtu.be/nV-wnZiPR-M

## Why this is useful
This library opens GridCraft to the Python data science and automation ecosystem (Pandas, NumPy, etc.), making it easier for users to perform complex data workflows and integrate GridCraft into their existing Python-based pipelines.

title: M12: regional formats (typed and displayed numbers, dates and times)
author: quantmind-br
body:
Closes #361. Second of the focused PRs announced in #191: a **Regional format** setting next to the interface language, the way Excel follows the Windows/macOS region. Typed numbers, dates and times, and how they are displayed, follow it (`1.234,56`, `25/09/2026`, `15.03.2026`). Stored values, formulas, number format codes and files stay en-US.

## What changes

- **15 regions** in `crates/core/src/region.rs`: en-US, en-GB, en-IN, es-ES, de-DE, fr-FR, it-IT, pt-BR, pt-PT, ru-RU, cs-CZ, ja-JP, ko-KR, zh-CN and zh-TW. author: neilcawse
body:
## What main still gets wrong

Main (84acf62) special-cases plain `General` in `io.rs::csv` with Rust's `f64::to_string()`, and leaves every other General through the 11-character cell display. Saving one row on main gives:

| Cell | Format | main writes | this PR writes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0.1+0.2` | General | `0.30000000000000004` | `0.3` |
| `1/3` | General | `0.3333333333333333` (16 digits) | `0.333333333333333` |
| `1/3*1E-6` | General | `0.0000003333333333333333` | `0.000000333333333333333` |
| `124412140710` | `[Blue]General` | `1.24412E+11` | `124412140710` |
| `-124412140710` | `General;[Red]-General` | `-1.24412E+11` | `-124412140710` |
| `124412140710` | `@` (Text) | `1.24412E+11` | `124412140710` |
| `124412140710` | `General" mm"` | `1.24412E+11 mm` | `124412140710 mm` |
| `1234567890123456`, `9007199254740994` | General | every digit | every digit (unchanged) |
| `12345678901234567`, `1E+20`, `1E15-0.5` | General | `12345678901234568`, `100000000000000000000`, `999999999999999.5` | unchanged |

Same for `.txt`/`.tsv`. Excel never shows binary noise like `0.30000000000000004`: its text conversion (`&`) stops at 15 significant digits. A CSV export never writes an exponent for a General number, though: reopening the file gives a number typed as `1.23456789012346E+16` a `0.00E+00` format, and the next save writes `1.23E+16`. title: io: remove the .sctmp temporary file when a save fails
author: SteamSmith
body:
## Summary

`crates/engine/src/io.rs` `write_file` writes `<path>.sctmp` and then renames it over the target. If either step fails — a full disk, or the workbook held open/locked by another app (Excel, a sync client) so the rename is refused — the `.sctmp` file is left next to the user's workbook.

title: perf: fill-handle double-click scans a dense neighbour column ~2.4x faster
author: Dejan-Port
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #210, which was correctly rejected: the stated cause (a sparse column with a stray distant value) doesn't hold, since the scan already stops at the first empty cell. This is a different, narrower fix that **doesn't change behaviour for any input** — it never truncates a long fill, unlike #210's cap — only how fast a genuinely long, densely-populated run is scanned.

`grid.rs`'s fill-handle double-click called `Sheet::value_ref` once per row to find where the neighbouring column's data ends. Each call does a band lookup + row lookup + column lookup (three `BTreeMap` probes) via `CellStore::get`. For a real dense run (e.g. a filled column near the 1,048,576-row sheet limit) that's a lot of point lookups on the UI thread in one frame: **~59ms for a 1,000,000-row run** in a release build (measured with the new `fill_handle_perf` example), likely worse under wasm, where GridCraft actually runs in the browser.

## Changes

- `crates/model/src/store.rs`: `CellStore::contiguous_value_run` walks each band's row `BTreeMap` with `range` (one in-order pass per band) instead of one `get` per row, so a dense run costs roughly one tree-traversal step per row instead of one binary search per row. Deliberately narrower than `has`/`get`: a stored cell always decides the row on its own (even with an empty value), matching what `value_ref`'s callers actually test for — not `has`'s "a formula counts regardless of its cached value" (used for Ctrl+arrow navigation).
- `crates/model/src/sheet.rs`: `Sheet::last_contiguous_nonempty` layers `spill` back in wherever `contiguous_value_run` finds no stored cell, exactly where plain `value_ref` would fall through to it.
- `crates/ui-egui/src/grid.rs`: the fill-handle double-click now calls this once instead of looping over `value_ref`.

## Result

999,999-row dense run: **59.2ms → 24.7ms (2.40x)**, same answer (asserted in the example).

## Test plan

- [x] Four new tests in `sheet.rs`, including a 300-trial property test…

title: Packaging: offer GridCraft for .xlsb and .ods files on macOS
author: neilcawse
body:
macOS counterpart of #321, which added `.xlsb` and `.ods` to the Linux desktop entry, MIME info and AppStream metadata, and to the Windows "Open with" list. GridCraft imports both formats (#101, #100), but `packaging/macos/Info.plist.in` still declared only `.xlsx`, `.xlsm`, `.csv` and `.tsv`. So Finder's Open With didn't offer GridCraft for `.xlsb` or `.ods`, although an `open -a GridCraft book.ods` already opened the file.

## What changed
- `packaging/macos/Info.plist.in`: two new `CFBundleDocumentTypes` entries in the existing style (role Editor, `LSHandlerRank` Alternate, extension and MIME type):

title: XLS: array formulas fill their range on recalculation
author: neilcawse
body:
A legacy array formula in a `.xls` file (`{=TREND(...)}`, `{=MMULT(...)}`, `{=A5:A6*2}`) is stored as one ARRAY record plus a FORMULA record in every cell of its range, each holding that cell's cached result. The importer attached the formula to the anchor cell but kept the cached results in the other cells as plain constants. When the workbook recalculated, the formula found its own range occupied and returned `#SPILL!`. Saving to `.xlsx` also wrote those constants into the array's range, so the file read back differently.

The `.xlsx` reader already drops the cached results of an array formula's other cells (#156). The `.xls` reader now does the same, but only after the formula has been attached to the anchor. If the formula couldn't be imported, the cells keep their values as before. Cell styles are kept.

## Evidence

Found with `gridcraft-cli check` over a new corpus of 4,224 real-world workbooks: Apache POI/NPOI/LibreOffice/calamine test data, XlsxWriter's Excel-made comparison files, and 1,000 Enron workbooks. Each file was checked in its own process with a 60 s timeout. Example: `poi/test-data/spreadsheet/MatrixFormulaEvalTestData.xls` had 30 mismatches, all `number -> #SPILL!` in `{=MMULT(...)}`/`{=MINVERSE(...)}` ranges. It has 0 now.

| corpus (4,224 files) | before (95c8776) | after |
|---|---|---|
| mismatching formulas | 69,682 | 69,603 (-79) |
| files with mismatches | 285 | 274 |
| files with round-trip differences | 57 | 41 |
| same, Excel-saved files only (3,170): mismatches / files / round trip | 54,825 / 180 / 33 | 54,750 / 172 / 21 |

15 files have fewer mismatches and none has more. 16 files no longer differ after a round trip. They include `Trend.xls` (64 -> 47), `testRVA.xls` (14 -> 9), `inline-array.xls`, `matrix.xls` and `testArraysAndTables.xls`.

## Verification

- `reads_values_formulas_formats_and_layout` in `crates/xlsx/src/tests/xls_tests.rs`: the array formula's other cell `C6` is now blank after import (it held `4`). This assertion …

title: UI: Paste button and menus paste the system clipboard; regression test for the Paste freeze (#273)
author: neilcawse
body:
The freeze in #273 is already fixed on main by #272. This PR adds the regression test that was missing. It also fixes the next thing a user hits once the freeze is gone: the Paste button ignored text copied in other apps. I didn't put `Fixes #273` on it because the freeze fix is #272's. #273 can be closed once a release includes #272.

## The freeze (#273)
In 0.5.0, clicking anywhere on the Home ribbon's Paste button (the label, the icon or the dropdown arrow) froze the app for good. Both reports use 0.5.0 or older: the macOS comment, and the Fedora RPM `gridcraft 0.5.0` in the Linux comment. #272 merged on 2026-10-11, after the v0.5.0 release on 2026-10-10. `git tag --contains e1939aa` lists no tag.

Cause: `ribbon::home` called `paste.secondary_clicked()` inside `ui.ctx().data_mut(|data| …)`. In egui 0.36, `Response::clicked_by` is `self.flags.contains(CLICKED) && self.ctx.input(…)`, so it only touches the context after a click. When it does, it tries to take the context lock that `data_mut` already holds, and the UI thread waits on itself. Which button was clicked and what is on the clipboard make no difference.

Reproduced on macOS (arm64) by building `v0.5.0` with `cargo build --release -p gridcraft` and running `--sample sales --control 7981`:
- `ui.inspect` answered. Then `ui.click {x:44,y:100}` (the Paste label) went through, and every `ui.inspect` after it timed out. I relaunched and repeated with `ui.click {x:61,y:125}` (the dropdown chevron): same freeze.
- `sample <pid> 3`, main thread (abridged):
  ```
  gridcraft_ui_egui::ribbon::home
    egui::context::Context::write  <data_mut<…ribbon::home…>>
      parking_lot::raw_rwlock::RawRwLock::lock_exclusive_slow
        __psynch_cvwait
  ```
  The control-connection thread was waiting in `RawRwLock::lock_shared_slow` behind it.

The Linux stack in the issue fits this: the main thread sits in a bare `syscall` (parking_lot's futex wait) and the other threads are idle. In release builds egui's lock just waits f…

title: File view: the recent list tells when each workbook was last changed
author: arcanii
body:
The follow-up invited in #337: the recent list's modified column, on top of the File view from #331.

## What it does

The recent workbooks on the File view's Home and Open pages gain a **Modified** column: "Just now", "5 min ago", "3 h ago", "Yesterday", "4 days ago", "3 weeks ago", "5 months ago", "2 years ago". A file that can't be reached (moved, deleted, on a drive that is away) says "Not available".

## How

- **The file system is never asked while drawing.** `RecentFiles`, a field of `Backstage`, starts a thread that reads each file's metadata; the list shows each answer as it comes back and asks for a repaint. A network drive that is asleep, or a share that is away, doesn't hold up the view: its rows fill in late, or say "Not available".
- **One thread asks at a time**, so a drive that never answers holds up one thread, not one for every time the view is opened. A view opened anew asks anew, so the times are current.
- **Only metadata is read.** No workbook is opened until the user picks one, as before. The module's opening comment said nothing on disk is touched; it now says what is.
- **Ages, not dates.** The UI crate has no time zone to tell a date by (`now_serial` is UTC), and a date could be a day out. "Yesterday" means 24 to 48 hours ago.
- **Translations.** From two days on a count is never one, so each language needs one form of "days", "weeks", "months" and "years". The ten strings are in all nine catalogs, with the count placed by `{n}`, the way `Page {page} of {pages}` places its numbers. Russian uses abbreviated units, which don't decline with the count. The translations are mine and unreviewed.
- **Layout.** A long name or folder now stops short of the column instead of running under it. The web build (no files to ask about) and a window too narrow for the column show the list as it was.

## Not in this pull request

- Dates and times instead of ages, which need the local time zone.
- Pinning a workbook, or removing one from the list.

title: XLSX: formulas into linked workbooks calculate from the values saved with the link
author: neilcawse
body:
A formula that reads another workbook (`=[1]Prices!B2`, `=SUM('[2]P&L Prices'!B1:B9)`, `=VLOOKUP(A7,Gas,4,FALSE)` where the name `Gas` is `[1]Bogey!$A$3:$B$33`) recalculated to `#REF!` in GridCraft. `#NAME?` showed up in a few cases too. Excel calculates these from the copy of the linked cells it saves in the file (`xl/externalLinks/externalLinkN.xml`, `sheetDataSet`), as it does whenever the source workbook is closed. The pass-through from #330 kept those parts on save, but nothing read them.

This was the largest root cause in a new corpus of 4,224 real-world workbooks. Over the Excel-saved files it accounted for about 21,500 mismatching cells directly (`[n]` in the formula) and most of another ~11,000 counted under VLOOKUP/MONTH, through names that point into linked workbooks.

## What changed

- **Model.** `Workbook::external_books: Arc<Vec<ExternalBook>>`, where `[n]` in a formula is `external_books[n-1]`. Each book holds its sheets with their cached cells, a `refresh_error` flag per sheet, and the linked workbook's defined names (`ExternalName`). The cache is behind an `Arc`, like sheets and preserved parts, so the workbook clone each edit makes and the undo history share it instead of copying it (the largest corpus file has 157,198 cached link cells). It is only set when a file is read, and it isn't saved in GridCraft JSON, which doesn't carry the link parts either: a JSON copy has no links, so a typed `[1]` is refused there rather than saved into an `.xlsx` with no link for it.
- **Read** (`crates/xlsx/src/external.rs`, new). Follows `<externalReferences>` in `workbook.xml` to each `externalLink` part and reads `sheetNames`, `sheetDataSet` (numbers, strings, booleans, errors) and `definedNames`. A link that isn't to a workbook (`ddeLink`, `oleLink`), or whose part is missing or unreadable, is an opaque book (`ExternalBook::opaque`) that keeps the later links at their indexes. A DDE link's items saved with values (`<ddeItem name="ENE"><values>…`) are read int…

title: OFFSET: huge offsets and sizes give #REF! instead of overflowing
author: webdevtodayjason
body:
`=OFFSET(B2,1E300,0)` and `=OFFSET(B2,0,0,1E300,1)` failed `cell.set` with `Internal("cell.set", "attempt to add with overflow")`. The row, column, height and width arguments are truncated to i64, which saturates for huge values, and the plain additions that place the result then overflow. Excel returns `#REF!` for these.

The additions now saturate, so any argument that would land outside the sheet returns `#REF!` like other out-of-range offsets. Normal offsets, negative heights and widths, fractional truncation and results at the last row or column are unchanged.

## How it was tested

- New tests: `offset_extreme_arguments_return_ref` (calc) and `crates/engine/tests/offset_overflow.rs` (`cell.set`) cover huge positive and negative rows, columns, heights and widths, combinations of them, and a full-height result at the sheet edge. They fail on current main with the overflow and pass with this change.
- `cargo test -p gridcraft-calc` passes. `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass. `cargo xtask` assets, layers, wasm and `parity --check` pass.
- `cargo test --workspace` has three failures that also happen on current main without this change (same as the main CI run): `csv_save_keeps_the_separator_it_was_opened_with` and `saving_an_opened_semicolon_csv_keeps_semicolons` (`1.24412E+11` instead of `124412140710`), and `translations_are_unique_and_preserve_unknown_text` (missing French for "Different First Page"). #449 addresses these.

body:
Typing `£5` now stores numeric `5` with pound formatting, so `=A1*2` produces `10`. The existing dollar parser also recognizes pounds in negative/grouped amounts and numeric-text arithmetic; apostrophe-prefixed input remains text.

A separate follow-up commit repairs the failures also present in [upstream main CI](https://github.com/storytold/gridcraft/actions/runs/38179244190):

Explicit currency, date and scientific formats still apply. title: Python in cells: engine, sandboxed worker processes, CPython and built-in backends
author: prxnvt
body:
## Summary

This pull request adds Python in cells to the engine, without any user interface. A Python cell holds Python code instead of a formula; its result is the cell's value, so formulas, display and files read it like any other cell. Cells run on the user's own CPython 3.11 or newer when one is installed, so pandas and numpy work, and otherwise on a built-in, sandboxed Python (Monty). Code never runs in the GridCraft process: every workbook has its own worker process, which is killed when a cell exceeds its time limit or its memory limit, and replaced when it crashes.

Everything is reachable through commands (`python.insert`, `python.set`, `python.clear`, `python.output`, `python.reset`, `python.diagnostics`, `python.initialization`, `python.options`, `python.enable`), and therefore through the CLI, MCP and the control channel. None of them opens a dialog. Workbooks opened from a file run no Python until `python.enable`. Python cells are saved to xlsx as `PY("…",0|1)` formulas with their cached values, so other applications show the results.

The editing interface (Python mode in the formula bar, the Diagnostics pane, the Enable bar, Python Options) is left for a later pull request, as are an application-managed Python environment with package installation, richer object output and import-aware time limits.

## Design

### Worker process

Python code runs in a separate process because no in-process harness can stop all hostile code: `'x' * 10**12` makes an interpreter allocate until the process aborts, and `10**10**8` never checks an interpreter's time limit; `catch_unwind` can stop neither. The worker is either

- the application binary started again with `--python-worker`, which runs Monty (the built-in Python), or
- the user's CPython, started as `<python> -P -X utf8 -u -c <shim>`, where the shim (`crates/python/src/shim.py`, embedded with `include_str!`) implements the same protocol.

The parent (`crates/python/src/client.rs`) reads the worker's output on…

title: Objects: one selection for every floating object, eight resize handles, and objects that follow edits
author: prxnvt
body: ## Summary The sheet tracked the selected floating object as a bare id in `selected_chart`. As a result, only charts and text boxes drew a selection frame, only the bottom-right corner resized an object (#190, fixed for charts in #218), and the kind of the selected object had to be inferred from its id. This pull request introduces a single selection model for charts, pictures, shapes and slicers, gives every kind a frame with eight working resize handles, and makes every kind follow structural edits in the same way. Depends on #456 (UI building blocks). The branch is stacked on it; the two commits listed below are the content of this pull request. ## Changes ### Selection, resizing and deletion - **Model.** `ObjKind` (chart, image, shape, slicer) and `ObjRef { kind, id }` name a floating object. `Sheet` gains helpers that find, move and remove an object by `ObjRef`, and `object_anchors` / `object_anchors_mut`, which visit every object's anchor in one fixed order. `Workbook::next_object_id` saturates instead of overflowing when a file contains an id at `u32::MAX`. - **Commands.** `object.delete`, `object.move` and `object.setAnchorMode` accept the four kinds through one parameter check. An unknown kind or id is now an error instead of a silent success, offsets are clamped, and `object.delete` replies with the deleted object. The `arrange.*` commands and the Selection Pane include slicers, which stack above the other objects. - **Sheet interaction.** The selected object, whatever its kind, draws a frame with eight handles above every other object. Each handle moves only its own edges, and the edges never cross; dragging the body moves the object. The first drag frame already applies the pointer's movement, so a quick drag is not lost. The pointer shows the handle's resize cursor or a move cursor. On a right-to-left sheet the frame moves with its object and the diagonal cursors are swapped.

title: control server: bound request lines and concurrent connections
author: SteamSmith
body:
## Summary

`apps/gridcraft/src/control_server.rs` (the opt-in `--control` loopback channel) read request lines with `BufRead::lines`, which buffers an entire line before anything checks its size, and spawned one thread per accepted connection with no limit.

- **Bounded line reads:** each line is read with `take(MAX_LINE + 1).read_until(b'\n', …)`. A line longer than `MAX_LINE` = 64 MiB (the existing `MAX_LINE`) gets an error reply and the connection is closed, without buffering the rest. Previously the whole line was buffered first and only then compared with `MAX_LINE`; an overlong line got an error reply and the connection stayed open.
- **Connection cap:** at most `MAX_CONNECTIONS` = 16 connections are served at once; further ones get `{"ok": false, "error": "too many control connections"}` and are closed. A slot is released when its connection ends, including if its thread can't start or panics (`Drop` guard).

Everything else in request handling is unchanged (blank lines skipped, same replies, same timeouts). The approach mirrors DesignCraft's control server.

## Tests

New tests in `control_server.rs`:
- `lines_are_read_up_to_the_limit`: line at the limit accepted, CRLF stripped, final line without newline read, then end of stream
- `an_overlong_line_is_refused_without_reading_the_rest`: at most limit+1 bytes buffered, remainder left unread
- `requests_are_answered_with_their_ids`: end to end over a loopback socket with a stand-in UI
- `extra_connections_are_refused`: the 17th concurrent connection gets the error line

## How this was verified

On my Windows machine, Smart App Control blocks a dependency's build script (`parking_lot_core`), so I couldn't build the full app locally. Instead I compiled **this exact file**, unmodified, as a module of a small harness crate with stand-ins for `egui::Context` and `ControlRequest`. title: INDEX: a huge area number gives #REF! instead of overflowing
author: webdevtodayjason
body:
`=INDEX(A1:B2,1,1,-1E300)` panicked in debug and test builds with "attempt to subtract with overflow" when taking one off the area number. The area number now goes through saturating unsigned math and a checked conversion to an index, so an area number that does not point into the reference returns `#REF!`, as the INDEX documentation describes.

One behaviour change: negative area numbers such as -1 or -5 used to select the first area; they now return `#REF!`. Area numbers 0 and 1 still select the first area, and area numbers past the last area still return `#REF!`. Some references say Excel returns `#VALUE!` for an area number of 0 or below; that is left for a separate change so this one stays a crash fix.

## How it was tested

- New test `index_area_number_overflow` uses a two-area reference: areas 1 and 2 pick the right cells, and 3, 1E300, -1 and -1E300 give `#REF!`. It fails on unchanged main and passes with this change.
- `cargo test -p gridcraft-calc`: 47 passed, 1 ignored.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.
- `cargo xtask assets`, `cargo xtask layers`, `cargo xtask wasm`, `cargo xtask parity --check`: pass.
- `cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast`: three failures, the same three that fail on current main: `io::tests::csv_save_keeps_the_separator_it_was_opened_with`, `tests::saving_an_opened_semicolon_csv_keeps_semicolons` and `i18n::tests::translations_are_unique_and_preserve_unknown_text`. #449 fixes them.

title: Python in cells: an application-managed environment, approved package installs and import-aware time limits
author: prxnvt
body:
Depends on #469 (Python in cells: engine), which depends on #462. Until #469 is merged, this pull request also shows its commits; the three commits listed under Changes are the ones to review.

## Summary

This pull request lets GridCraft install Python packages for Python cells, and keeps a slow first import of a newly installed package from looking like a failure. It is engine-side only: everything is reachable through commands, and therefore through the CLI, MCP and the control channel. There is no user interface; the approval dialog, the install progress and the related Python Options belong to a later pull request.

- GridCraft keeps one virtual environment of its own, made from the CPython it found. It never downloads or bundles an interpreter.
- `python.install` installs packages only when the call carries `approve: true`. Without it, the command fails with the question it would ask.
- Packages go into the person's own virtual environment when that is what runs cells, otherwise into GridCraft's environment, and never into a system or externally managed Python.
- On CPython, time spent importing modules that are not loaded yet does not count against a cell's time limit, up to an allowance. A cell stopped in the middle of an import runs once more on a fresh worker before the crash-loop guard refuses it.

New commands: `python.stop`, `python.install`, `python.installStatus`, `python.packages` and `python.environment`. `python.options` gains `environment` and `importSeconds`, and `python.diagnostics` gains `packages` and install rows. None of them opens a dialog.

## Design

### Where the environment lives

| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/GridCraft/python-env` |
| Linux and BSD | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/gridcraft/python-env` (by default `~/.local/share/gridcraft/python-env`) |

title: MCP: confine file access with --automation-read-root and --automation-write-root (#445)
author: isaac-levine
body:
`gridcraft-cli mcp` currently gives the agent on the other end the same file access as the user running it. VectorCraft already fixes this with two flags, so this adds the same ones here with the same names and behaviour. One client config then works for both apps:

    gridcraft-cli mcp --automation-read-root /work/project --automation-write-root /work/project/out

**How it works**

The engine only ever opens a user-named file through `io::read_file` and `io::write_file`, so the checks live there and every command picks them up for free. The new `crates/engine/src/file_access.rs` holds the roots and the path logic: make the path absolute, follow symlinks (for a file that doesn't exist yet, resolve its nearest existing ancestor and require the rest to be plain names), then compare with the root by whole path components. On Windows the comparison ignores case, handles `\\?\` and UNC prefixes, and refuses device names like `CON` and `NUL`.

`Headless::with_automation_roots` in gridcraft-mcp puts the roots in force for every call. The CLI accepts `--flag DIR` or `--flag=DIR`, refuses a flag given twice, and refuses a root that is missing or not a folder. A root left out grants none of its access, so `--automation-read-root` alone makes the server read-only. The flags only make sense for the in-process server, so combining them with `--connect` is an error.

**What is covered**

Reads: `open_workbook`, `file.open`, `data.fromTextCsv` and `insert.picture` with a path. Writes: `save_workbook`, `file.save`, `file.saveAs`, `file.exportCsv`, `file.exportHtml`, `file.exportPdf`, plus the `.sctmp` temp file the atomic save uses. Calls that return bytes instead of writing a path keep working with only a read root.

Not covered: `--in FILE` is the operator's own argument and is opened before the roots apply. The desktop app (`gridcraft --control`) doesn't take the flags yet, since VectorCraft's app-side version also has to leave the user's own file dialogs unconfined and handle …

title: AutoFill: times, quarters, ordinals and mixed sources continue as series
author: nihilist-narwhal
body:
AutoFill copied a single time and any source without a common pattern, counted `Qtr3` on to `Qtr5`, and turned `1st Period` into `2st Period`. Following Excel, `9:00` now continues `10:00`, `11:00`; `Qtr3` and `Quarter 3` wrap after 4 like `Q3`; `1st Period` continues `2nd Period`, `3rd Period`; and `Product 1`, `On backorder` continues `Product 2`, `On backorder` (plain drag only; Ctrl+drag keeps #264's alternate mode). Fill Series with a growth step below 1 and a stop value now stops in the direction the series runs, not only for rising series.

The Python-in-cells PRs (#469, #477, #482) touch the same line in `fill.rs`; whichever lands second keeps both conditions.

title: Formulas: long operator chains no longer hit the evaluator's depth limit
author: nihilist-narwhal
body: A formula such as `=A1+A2+…+A500` nests one level per operator, and the evaluator recursed once per level, so past its depth limit of 400 it returned `#CALC!`. Excel accepts such formulas up to its 8,192-character formula limit. Left-nested chains of arithmetic, comparison and `&` operators are now folded in a loop; range, union and intersection keep the recursive path.

title: Manage Rules: don't index past the list after a delete
author: nihilist-narwhal
body: `home.manageRules` read the rule count once, before deleting, so `{"delete":0,"moveUp":1}` with two rules swapped past the end of the shortened list and panicked with an index out of bounds (the session guard kept the workbook). The count is now taken again after each step.

title: Functions passed by name: GROUPBY(…,SUM), BYROW(…,SUM), MAP(…,ABS)
author: nihilist-narwhal
body:
Excel accepts a worksheet function by name where a function is expected. `GROUPBY(A2:A9,B2:B9,SUM)` and PIVOTBY, in their documented form, gave `#NAME?`, and BYROW, BYCOL, MAP, REDUCE, SCAN and MAKEARRAY gave `#VALUE!`. A name that is a worksheet function, and not a LET/LAMBDA variable or a defined name, now works as a function there.

Reading a file strips the `_xleta.` prefix Excel writes for these names. Writing it back on save is left for a follow-up, so such formulas still save with a bare `SUM`.

title: Merge Across: keep only the first value of each row
author: nihilist-narwhal
body: Merge & Center and Merge Cells keep only the upper-left value, but Merge Across left the other values of each row in place, hidden under the merge and still counted: with `1 2 / 3 4` in A1:B2, `SUM(A1:B2)` stayed 10. Each row's merged area now keeps only its first value, as the other merges do and as Excel does, where the sum is 4.

title: Build: the ui-egui build script reads CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR when it runs
author: prxnvt
body:
## Summary

`crates/ui-egui/build.rs` locates `contributors/` with `env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")`. The `env!` macro fixes the path when the build script itself is compiled, not when it runs. If a checkout is moved or copied after the first build, for example into another directory or a Git worktree that reuses a shared target directory, the compiled build script keeps reading the old location. Two effects follow:

1. The About window shows no contributors, because `contributors.json` and `people.toml` are not found.
2. The `rerun-if-changed` paths point at files that no longer exist, so Cargo reruns the build script, and therefore rebuilds `gridcraft-ui-egui`, on every build.

## Change

The build script now reads `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` from its environment with `std::env::var_os` when it runs. Cargo sets this variable for every build-script run, so the path always follows the current checkout. The behaviour is otherwise unchanged.

## Testing

- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p gridcraft-ui-egui --all-targets -D warnings` and `cargo xtask wasm` pass.
- The change is limited to how the path is obtained; the files read and the `rerun-if-changed` lines are the same as before.



---

**Generative AI use:** The code and descriptions in this pull request were written with the assistance of Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Code). I directed the work, chose its scope, and reviewed and tested the changes.

title: UI: an unsaved macro-editor draft counts as unsaved work when its workbook closes
author: prxnvt
body:
Depends on #478 (macro UI), which in turn depends on #456 and #465. Only the last commit belongs to this pull request.

## Summary

The macro step editor works on a draft that is saved into the workbook with `macro.save`. Before this change, closing the workbook (File > Close, Cmd+W, or Close in the Backstage view) took no account of that draft. A clean workbook closed at once and the draft was lost. A dirty workbook showed Save Changes?, and Save wrote the file without the macro. In both cases the editor could remain open after its workbook had closed, so a later Save would have written the draft into whichever workbook became active next.

With this change, a draft with unsaved changes counts as unsaved work in the existing Save Changes? prompt, in the same way as the cell that is still being edited:

- Closing asks even when the workbook itself has no unsaved changes.
- Save saves the macro into the workbook, then saves and closes the workbook. If the macro cannot be saved, the prompt stays open and the reason is shown.
- Don't Save closes the workbook and discards the draft.
- Cancel, or dismissing the prompt, keeps the workbook open and brings the macro editor back with its draft.
- A new macro that has not been edited does not count, so opening the editor and closing the workbook does not ask.

A workbook that closes now also closes the macro editor.

## Changes

- `macro_editor`: `Editor::has_unsaved_changes`. A new macro counts only once it differs from the empty macro the editor started with. The file also gains `has_unsaved_draft`, `save_draft`, `reopen` and `discard`, which the close prompt uses.
- `SheetApp::run`: `file.close` without `force` opens Save Changes? when the editor holds an unsaved draft. It returns `{"closed": false, "dirty": true}`, which is the result the engine gives for a dirty workbook. When the workbook does close, the editor closes with it.

title: UI: Save waits for running Python cells, so the file holds their results
author: prxnvt
body:
Depends on #482.

## Summary

Python cells run in the background, so a workbook saved directly after a Python edit could be written while the cell still showed `#BUSY!`, and the file then held `#VALUE!` in place of the computed result. With this change, a save requested while Python cells are running or waiting becomes a pending save. The pending save is checked every frame, never blocks the window, and runs as soon as the cells have finished.

The wait is bounded. A save waits at most one cell's time limit plus the import allowance plus one second, and the wait starts again whenever a cell finishes. If no cell finishes within that time, the workbook is saved with whatever the cells hold, and a warning is logged.

## Changes

- `Session::python_pending_cells` counts the Python cells, across all workbooks, that are running or queued. A package install on its own is not counted. A falling count is treated as progress.
- `SheetApp::run` defers `file.save`, and `file.saveAs` when it is given a path, while cells are pending. This covers Save, Save As, Cmd+S / Ctrl+S and the File menu and Backstage entries, which all go through `run`. A workbook with no file asks for a location first; only the save itself waits.
- When Save is chosen in the Save Changes? prompt, any uncommitted edit is committed first. The prompt then waits for the cells and closes the workbook once it has been saved.
- AutoSave does not run while a Python cell is pending or a save is waiting.
- Control channel: the reply to `app.save`, or to `engine.execute` (or a direct call) with `file.save` or `file.saveAs`, is held until the save has happened, and then reports how the save went. Each waiting save has its own number, so several such requests each receive their own outcome. `ui.inspect` reports `savePending`.
- `docs/control-protocol.md` describes the behaviour.

## Testing

- New `crates/ui-egui/tests/python_save.rs` covers these cases:
  - a save requested while a slow cell runs writes the computed v…

title: UI: closing the window or quitting asks to save unsaved workbooks
author: prxnvt
body:
## Summary

Closing the GridCraft window, or quitting the app, ended it at once and discarded every unsaved change. This pull request makes a close request with unsaved workbooks ask about each of them first, with Save, Don't Save and Cancel, on every desktop platform.

On macOS the app menu used the predefined Quit item, which ends the application without sending the window a close request, so no prompt could be shown. It is replaced by an ordinary menu item with the same label and shortcut (Cmd+Q) that requests the close.

The prompt is the existing Save Changes? dialog that File › Close, Cmd+W and the Backstage Close already show for one workbook; no new dialog or string is added. When several workbooks have unsaved changes, the app asks about each in turn, the active workbook first, as Excel does when it closes several workbooks:

- Save commits the cell being edited, saves the workbook (asking for a file name when it has none) and closes it.
- Don't Save closes the workbook without saving it.
- Cancel keeps the window open. A save that does not happen, such as a cancelled file picker, does the same.

The window closes once no workbook with unsaved changes remains. Choosing Don't Save for one workbook and then Cancel for the next leaves the window open, and the remaining workbook still has its unsaved changes, so the next close request asks about it again. A window whose workbooks are all saved closes without asking. `app.quit` on the control channel still closes the window without asking, so automation is never blocked by a dialog.

## Changes

- `crates/ui-egui/src/lib.rs`: `SheetApp::logic` handles the window's close request. With unsaved workbooks it cancels the close, makes the next unsaved workbook active and runs `file.close`, which opens the Save Changes? prompt. Once the prompt is answered, it moves to the next unsaved workbook, stops when the workbook it asked about is still open (Cancel, or a save that did not happen), or closes the window when none i…

title: Python in cells: dates and times in xl() and in results, in the 1900 and 1904 date systems
author: prxnvt
body:
Depends on #477 (which depends on #469 and #462). Only the last commit belongs to this pull request.

## Summary

Cells formatted as dates reached Python as bare serial numbers, so code had to convert them by hand, and dates that a cell returned were written back as plain numbers. With this change, on CPython, `xl()` gives cells formatted as dates or times as `datetime.date`, `datetime.datetime` and `datetime.time` values, and a DataFrame built by `xl()` has `datetime64` columns for its dates. Dates and times that a cell returns, pandas `Timestamp` values included, are written back as serials, and the cells that show them receive a date or time format when their format is General. The 1900 date system (with its fictitious 1900-02-29) and the 1904 date system are both handled. The built-in Python continues to receive serial numbers.

## Changes

- **Protocol** (`python/protocol.rs`). `XlReply::Dated { value, dates }` marks the numbers that are dates or times, with a `DateCell { at, kind }` for each (`date`, `time` or `dateTime`). `Output::dates` marks the same in a result. Serials cross the protocol in the 1900 date system. Both additions are optional on the wire, so earlier frames still parse.
- **Number formats** (`numfmt`). `NumberFormat::shows_date` and `shows_time` report whether a date or time format shows a calendar part, a clock part or both. The kind of a cell comes from these.
- **Engine** (`engine/python.rs`).
  - An `xl()` reply for one area (a cell, a range, or a name or table of one range; a reference past the used range reads its top-left part) marks numbers whose format is a date or time format. Negative numbers and numbers past 9999-12-31 are not marked.
  - In a 1904 workbook, the serials of dates are converted to and from the 1900 system (1,462 days). Times of day are unchanged.
  - Result positions outside the value, and repeated positions, are discarded. Cells in the General format that show a date or time result receive `m/d/yyyy`, `m/d/yyyy h:m…

title: INDIRECT: R1C1 offsets past the sheet give #REF! instead of overflowing
author: webdevtodayjason
body:
INDIRECT's R1C1 conversion now uses checked addition and checks each coordinate against `MAX_ROWS` and `MAX_COLS`. A huge relative offset such as `R[9223372036854775807]C` used to overflow (a panic in debug builds), `R[4294967291]C` overflowed when building the A1 text, and `R[4294967296]C` wrapped back to the formula's own row. All of these now return `#REF!`, as does an offset that fits in u32 but lands off the sheet, like `R[2000000]C`.

`r1c1_to_a1` now tells "not R1C1" apart from "R1C1 but past the sheet", so an off-sheet R1C1 reference gives `#REF!` instead of falling back to A1: `INDIRECT("RC16385",FALSE)` stays `#REF!` rather than reading cell RC16385. Text that isn't R1C1 still falls back as before, and references inside the sheet give the same results as before.

Thanks to quantmind-br for confirming the bugs and suggesting checked_add with sheet bounds in [the comment on #191](https://github.com/storytold/gridcraft/pull/191#issuecomment-6117263230).

## How it was tested

- `indirect_r1c1_out_of_bounds` fails on main (the i64::MAX offset panics) and passes with the change; each overflow case was also checked one by one against main. `indirect_r1c1_past_the_sheet_does_not_fall_back_to_a1` guards the A1 fallback, and `indirect_r1c1_valid_references` covers ordinary relative and absolute references.
- `cargo test -p gridcraft-calc`: 49 passed, 1 ignored (as on main).
- `cargo fmt --all --check` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.
- Merges cleanly with #466 and #476, which touch the same files.
- `cargo test --workspace` has the same three failures as main (two CSV separator tests and a translation uniqueness test); #449 fixes them.

title: Animation effects: Use system setting / On / Off in File › Options, following the system's animation setting
author: JeremyYao
body:
## Why

With Windows' Animation effects switched off (Settings ▸ Accessibility ▸ Visual effects), GridCraft still animated: wheel scrolling eased in over several frames, the Ctrl+wheel zoom glided to its next step, and the selection outline glided to the clicked cell. The only control was the View ▸ Animations checkbox, which ignored the system.

## What changes

File ▸ Options ▸ General gains **Animation effects**: **Use system setting** (default), **On**, **Off**.

Off, whether chosen or inherited from the system, stops the motion in the window:

- a wheel notch scrolls the whole distance in the frame it arrives (the sheet, the sheet tabs and egui's own scroll areas);
- a Ctrl/⌘+wheel notch puts the zoom on its next ladder step in that frame too;
- the selection outline is drawn on its cells instead of gliding;
- the dashes round a copied range stand still;
- menus, tooltips and dialogs appear without fading.

With animations on nothing changes. The View ▸ Animations checkbox stays as a quick on/off and shows what is in effect.

## How the system setting is read

A new host hook, `Services::animations_enabled`, is asked at the start of every frame and answers from memory. The desktop app supplies it in `apps/gridcraft/src/animations.rs`:

| Platform | Source |
|---|---|
| Windows | `UISettings.AnimationsEnabled` (WinRT), re-read at most once a second |
| macOS | `NSWorkspace.accessibilityDisplayShouldReduceMotion`, same cadence |
| Linux, BSDs | The XDG settings portal on a background thread, every 4 s: `reduced-motion`, GNOME's `enable-animations`, KDE's `AnimationDurationFactor`. Without a portal answer, KDE's `kdeglobals` and GTK's `settings.ini` |
| Web | The `prefers-reduced-motion` media query |

Where the system says nothing, animations stay on. A change made in the system's settings is followed while the app runs.

An idle window isn't woken to ask again: nothing moves until the next frame, and that frame asks before it draws. Only what an idle window show…

title: Data: live What-If data tables ({=TABLE()}) that recalculate, with XLSX round-trip
author: prxnvt
body:
## Summary

At present, `data.dataTable` computes every result of a What-If data table once, by substitution, and writes the results as static values. The command documents the result as "a snapshot, not a live {=TABLE()}" and returns `"static": true`. Consequently, the results do not change when an input value or a formula changes, and opening an XLSX file that contains a data table keeps only its cached values, with a warning.

This pull request makes data tables live, as they are in Excel. A data table is a multi-cell formula `{=TABLE(row_input, column_input)}` over its results. It is recalculated whenever one of its input values, one of its formulas or a precedent of those formulas changes. Edits of part of a table are refused, and tables round-trip through XLSX as `<f t="dataTable">`. The previous snapshot behaviour remains available through `static: true`.

## Changes

**Model** (`crates/model`)
- `DataTable` (range, row input cell, column input cell) and `Sheet::data_tables`. Helpers return the results area, the edge cells, the `TABLE(B1,B2)` text and the substitutions that fill the results. `MAX_DATA_TABLE_CELLS` (100,000 result cells, the limit the command already used) is shared by calc, the engine and XLSX.

**Calculation** (`crates/calc`)
- `Trial` moves from the engine to calc so that recalculation can use it; Goal Seek, Scenario Manager, Solver and static data tables use it unchanged.
- After the formulas have been recalculated, every table with an edge cell in the changed or dirty set is calculated again. Each result substitutes the edge value into the input cell on a copy of the workbook and reads the formula. The results are written as values, and their dependents are recalculated. A table whose formulas read another table's results is calculated after that table.
- F9 and opening a workbook calculate every table. In Automatic Except for Data Tables mode and in Manual mode, tables are calculated only on F9.

title: In-cell editing: the highlight stays on the cell while the text runs past it
author: arcanii
body:
**Stacked on #1921** (the selection's outline on the gridlines), split from this pull request at review. The first commit here is #1921's; this pull request is the two commits after it. Please merge #1921 first.

## What was wrong

Typing into a cell moved the highlight and then stretched it:

- The editor's border was drawn half a point further out than the selection's outline, and the editor was about three points taller than a default row, so the box left the gridlines the moment typing began.
- The border was then stretched round the text as the text grew past the cell.

Excel leaves the highlight on the cell, and text that runs past the cell clears the line it crosses.

## What it does now

The highlight of a cell being edited is the selection's own four sides (`outline_sides`, from #1921), and it neither moves nor grows:

- **While the text fits**, the editor is exactly its cell.
- **Text that needs more** is laid over the cells after it, a whole column at a time, so the editor always ends on a gridline. A cell it covers is covered entirely, and its contents come back when the editor closes.
- **The lines the text runs over are cleared**: the highlight's far side once the text reaches it, and the gridlines between the cells it covers. The other three sides stay.
- **Alt+Enter lines** go the same way downwards, in whole rows, with the highlight's bottom side left out. Two lines of the default font take two rows of the default height.
- **Frozen panes, merged cells and right-to-left sheets**: the editor grows only inside its own pane, a merged cell grows from its far edges, and a right-to-left sheet mirrors all of it.

## What is observed, what is a choice, and one difference

- **Observed in Excel on Windows** (black-box, from a capture at 150%): the highlight stays put while typing, and the line the text crosses is cleared.
- **Choices, not claimed as Excel's behaviour**:
  - Taking whole cells at a time, so a neighbour's contents are never cut off mid-word be…

author: vedran-dobos
body:
Fixes #506.

Excel's File › Options › Data › Automatic Data Conversion, for typing, pasting and opening CSV/text
files. **All on by default: nothing changes for anyone who doesn't opt out** (checked: converting the
reporter's 74-row file with defaults gives byte-identical output to `main`, 3926d21).

| Excel | GridCraft |
|---|---|
| Enable all default data conversions… | same (`all`) |
| Remove leading zeros and convert to a number | same: off keeps `0123`, `0042` as text |
| Keep first 15 digits of long numbers and display in scientific notation | same checkbox; **off means nothing is cut short or shown in scientific notation** (below) |
| Convert digits surrounding the letter "E"… | same: off keeps `1244121406E6`, `1e3` as text |

With "Keep first 15 digits…" unchecked, Excel still converts strings of up to 15 digits; General
