title: Expand chart formatting, editing, templates, and image export
author: bryanmenezes-qmc
body:
## Summary

This PR is updated against the current upstream `main` at `d8c5f58`, which is merged into the contribution branch. Relative to that base, it expands chart editing and formatting, plus chart-format persistence, without claiming full Excel feature parity.

## Features and improvements

- Select chart elements and open context-sensitive formatting controls for the chart/plot area, axes, series, markers, text, legend, and trendline.
- Format axes with bounds and units, logarithmic/reversed scales, tick marks, and gridline appearance.
- Configure fills, borders/lines, line width, markers, and chart text/fonts; Home font controls can also target selected chart text.

title: Delete separate rows or columns in one pass
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Fixes #2287

## Cause
`delete_lines` handled each selected area on its own. For every area it took that area's cells, moved every cell below or to the right of it, and rewrote every formula in the workbook. Each of those steps scans the whole sheet, so the time grew with the number of areas times the size of the sheet.

## Fix
A new `CellStore::delete_rows`/`delete_cols` removes all the deleted lines and moves each remaining cell once, by the number of deleted lines before it. Formulas, names and pivot sources are rewritten in one pass that applies the whole list of `Edit::Delete`s to each reference, through new `rewrite_many`/`rewrite_all_formulas_many` functions; the existing single-edit functions now call them. Verified: `tests::deleting_many_separate_rows_takes_about_as_long_as_one_block` fails on `main` (timing) and passes with this change. `tests::deleting_many_separate_columns_matches_per_area_result` checks the resulting values and formula directly. It is a correctness guard for the column path and does not reproduce the slowdown. Run both with `cargo test -p gridcraft-engine --lib deleting_many_separate`. `cargo xtask ci` passes except `too_wide_fill_number_shows_hashes_not_a_clipped_value`, which also fails on `main` without this change.

## Verified
- Regression tests `tests::deleting_many_separate_rows_takes_about_as_long_as_one_block`, `tests::deleting_many_separate_columns_matches_per_area_result`: fail on `main` without the fix and pass with it (`cargo test -p gridcraft-engine --lib deleting_many_separate`).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes.

## Not changed
`shift_sheet_features` still runs once per area, which keeps the existing per-area behaviour for anchors, merges, tables and other sheet features. Its cost depends on the number of features, not on the number of cells. Inserting rows or columns and the other callers of `rewrite` are unchanged.

title: PivotTables: Show Details, double-click a value cell to list its source records on a new sheet (#2364)
author: marcoarnulfo
body:
PivotTables: double-click a value cell to see the source records behind it (Show Details)

In Excel, double-clicking a cell in the values area of a PivotTable puts "the detail data that the value field is based on ... on a new worksheet" ([Expand, collapse, or show details](https://support.microsoft.com/en-au/excel/expand-collapse-or-show-details-in-a-pivottable-or-pivotchart)). A subtotal or grand total takes every record it adds up. Records that a report filter or hidden items leave out are left out here too. The new sheet goes before the current one, like a new PivotTable's sheet. It holds the source headers and the records in source order, as values with their column's number format, in columns wide enough for their text. One undo removes it. Double-clicking a label or header still edits the cell, as it does today. If Show Details fails on a value cell, for example in a workbook with a protected structure, the message is shown and the cell doesn't open for editing. Not included yet: the "Enable show details" option in PivotTable Options › Data ([PivotTable options](https://support.microsoft.com/en-US/Excel/pivottable-options)), which needs `enableDrill` read and written in XLSX, and the right-click "Show Details" menu item. Excel formats the detail block as a table, but I couldn't find that in Microsoft's docs, so this PR writes plain cells; happy to switch. The sheet gets the same name as any new sheet (`SheetN`). One difference from Excel: Excel reads the details from its PivotTable cache, but GridCraft has no cache and reads the current source. So when the source has changed since the last refresh, double-clicking anywhere in the report asks for a Refresh ("The PivotTable report is out of date. Refresh it first.") instead of listing records that no longer match the cell.

title: Fix MOD returning wrong sign and magnitude for tiny divisors
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/functions/src/math.rs:305-319` (no existing issue): MOD returns a result with the wrong sign and a magnitude above the divisor for a tiny divisor.

## Cause
`modulo` computed `x - d*q` with `q = floor(x/d)`. For a tiny divisor, `d*q` is rounded, so `r` is garbage. The sign correction then added `d`, which is far smaller than `r`, so the result kept the wrong sign and a magnitude far above `|d|`.

## Fix
`modulo` now takes `r = x % d`, an exact remainder with `|r| < |d|`. The existing sign correction and range guard then give a result with the divisor's sign inside the divisor's range.

## Verified
- Regression test `math::tests::mod_tiny_divisor_stays_in_range`: fails on `main` without the fix and passes with it (`cargo test -p gridcraft-functions mod_tiny_divisor_stays_in_range`).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes.

## Not changed
I did not change the Div0 handling, the `clean` rounding, or other functions such as QUOTIENT. I did not check what Excel returns for these inputs.

title: Conditional formatting: New Rule's formula box takes references clicked or dragged on the grid (#2348)
author: marcoarnulfo
body:
New Formatting Rule ▸ formula: clicking or dragging over cells on the grid now writes their reference into the formula box.

Excel's formula box in this dialog points like the formula bar, and Microsoft's conditional formatting page says "Selecting cells on the worksheet inserts absolute cell references". So with the box waiting for a reference (after `=`, `(`, an operator or a comma), a click on B2 writes `$B$2` at the caret, a drag writes `$B$2:$C$4`, and a second click replaces the reference just written. An empty box starts with `=`, so a click gives `=$B$2`. The selection the rule will apply to stays where it was, and the box keeps the keyboard, so you can carry on typing or press Enter. It reuses the formula bar's point-mode logic (`EditState::can_point` / `insert_ref`). After an operand (`=A1>5|`) a click does nothing instead of selecting the cell, because a new selection would change the range the rule is created for. Happy to switch that if you'd rather it did something else. Like Excel's "Applies to", the range is fixed when the dialog opens: pointing at a cell on another sheet writes `Sheet2!$A$1`, and the rule still goes on the original sheet's selection, found by name so that inserting or moving sheets meanwhile does not move it.

Not included: F4 in the box, column and row header clicks, Shift-click to extend and Ctrl-click to add a reference (both act as plain clicks for now), and the marquee around the pointed range.

#2184 replaces this dialog with `newFormattingRule`. The picking works for any `Field::Text` with `pick` set, so I'm happy to move it onto `newFormattingRule` if that lands first. #494's RefEdit fields could reuse the same mechanism.

Closes #2348

title: Accuracy: PMT to Excel's last bits via ln_1p/exp_m1
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
## What this fixes

`PMT` computed `(1 + rate)^nper` with `powf`. Rounding `1 + rate` first drops the low bits of a small rate, so PMT could sit up to about 1000 ULPs from Excel's value (59 of 400 synthetic probes bit-exact). Computing the power as `nper * ln_1p(rate)` and `p - 1` with `exp_m1` brings it within about 4 ULPs (244 of 400 bit-exact).

That matters for loan schedules guarded by `IF(p - SUM(principal) > 0, ...)`: in 3000 synthetic schedules, main disagreed with Excel on the number of live periods in 1382; with this change, 823.

Edge cases now follow Excel: a rate of -1 or less is `#NUM!`, a huge `nper` gives `-pv*rate` instead of `#NUM!`, a tiny rate no longer collapses, and a small negative rate keeps its payment. IPMT, PPMT, CUMIPMT and CUMPRINC pick this up through `pmt_calc`. FV and PV are unchanged.

## Overlap

Upstream PR #1462 also changes `pmt_calc` to `ln_1p`/`exp_m1`. This change goes further (avoids the cancellation in `p - 1`, handles the overflow edge and small negative rates), so the two will conflict in that function and one should be rebased on the other.

## How it was verified

- New tests: `pmt_matches_excel_within_a_few_ulps`, `pmt_edge_cases_follow_excel`, and `loan_schedule_residue_keeps_excels_sign` (a synthetic schedule whose 13th period exists only if PMT's last bits are right). The tests allow the one-ULP libm difference between platforms (the first run on Linux was 1 ULP off a bit-exact check).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes (fmt, clippy, tests, assets, layers, wasm, parity, keytips).
- CodeRabbit CLI review, gate `major`: passed.

## Minor review finding not fixed

- `PMT(1e-300, 10, 1e12)`: `(pv + fv) / m` can overflow before the multiplication by `rate`, giving a non-finite result for a huge balance with an extremely tiny rate.

title: Analysis ToolPak: value arguments reject multi-cell references, as Excel 365 does
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
## What this changes

The Analysis ToolPak functions now return `#VALUE!` when a value argument is a reference to more than one cell, as Excel 365 does. Before, GridCraft lifted the range and spilled an array.

Affected functions include EOMONTH, EDATE, WORKDAY and WORKDAY.INTL, NETWORKDAYS and NETWORKDAYS.INTL, YEARFRAC, WEEKNUM, the coupon, bond and T-bill functions, DISC, BIN2DEC and the other base conversions, the IM* functions (except IMSUM and IMPRODUCT, which aggregate), and the other functions in the same family.

Unchanged on purpose:
- Array constants and computed arrays still lift, so `EOMONTH({1;2},0)` and `EOMONTH(A1:A3+0,0)` still spill.
- Range parameters still take ranges: holidays, cash flows, schedules, and the WORKDAY.INTL / NETWORKDAYS.INTL weekend.
- A one-cell reference, an intersection, and `@` behave as before.

Example: `=EOMONTH(A1:A3,{1;2})` is now a 2x1 array of `#VALUE!`, with the rejected reference adding no shape, as in Excel.

## How it works

- `FnSpec` gains a `value_args` mask. It is filled at registration from one table in `crates/functions/src/lift.rs`, so the list of affected functions lives in one place.
- `call_lifted` turns a multi-cell reference at a value position into a scalar `#VALUE!` before lifting. Other arguments are untouched.
- Functions that don't take value arguments get an empty mask, so their behaviour does not change.

## Verification

- Regression tests in `crates/functions/src/lift.rs` cover the masks, the rejection, the unchanged cases above, and that every name in the table is a registered function with a matching mask.
- Regression tests in `crates/calc/src/tests.rs` cover the same behaviour through full formula evaluation, including defined names and dynamic-array and legacy formulas.

title: Read accounting negatives like $(1,234) in number text
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
## What this changes

Number text written in accounting style now reads as a negative number, as it does in Excel 365:

- `$(1,234)` and `$ (5)` give -1234 and -5 when typed, when passed to `VALUE`, and when coerced by arithmetic (`=--"$ (5)"`).
- `(5)%` gives -0.05 (and `*100` gives -5).

Before this, GridCraft returned `#VALUE!` for these.

Forms Excel does not read as numbers now stay text, so they also give `#VALUE!` where a number is expected:

- `(-5)`, `($-5)`, `$(-5)`, `((5))`, `(+5)`
- `$5%`, `$(5%)`, `$(5)%`
- dates and times in parentheses, such as `(3/4/2026)` and `(10:30)`, and a bare fraction `(1/2)`

Parentheses are read as a single pair. Previously `((100))` gave 100, and the change to text is deliberate: Excel reads one pair only. The stack-overflow guard from #2180 is kept. Nesting is now rejected in a single pass, with no recursion, and its regression test asserts the new result (text, no crash) at 100,000 levels deep.

## Where the code is

- `crates/core/src/parse.rs`: `parse_numeric` reads the accounting forms through a new `parenthesized` helper, then falls back to the existing unparenthesised parser.
- `crates/calc/src/tests.rs`, `crates/core/src/parse.rs` tests: coverage for accepted and rejected forms.
- `crates/functions/src/text.rs`: `VALUE` cases.
- `ROADMAP.md`, `docs/function-parity.md`: progress rows and timestamps.

## How it was verified

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` passes locally.
- The full suite (`cargo xtask ci`: clippy, tests, assets, layers, wasm) was not run on the machine this was prepared on, because of its memory limits. This PR's CI run on the fork is the gate.

title: XIRR and IRR follow Excel's solvers
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
## What this changes

XIRR and IRR now follow Excel's own solvers, so their answers match Excel's rather than an independent root-finder's.

- **XIRR** uses a sign-only bracketing and bisection search, reconstructed from observing Excel with synthetic inputs. Its answer is the same midpoint Excel returns, about 1e-8 from the exact root. XIRR's `#NUM!` cases follow Excel too. A date before the first cash flow is accepted, as Excel accepts it.
- **IRR** uses Newton's method on the discount factor `1/(1+rate)`, stopping at a step under 1e-8 and giving up after 100 steps. A guess at or below -100% is `#VALUE!`, as in Excel.
- The function reference (`docs/function-parity.md`) and the roadmap progress log record the change.

## Why

Before this change, the two functions gave the exact root, which differs from Excel in the last digits and in some `#NUM!` cases. Users who check a workbook against Excel saw mismatches. Financial functions with iterative solvers are the highest-risk area for these differences.

## How it was verified

- Against the observed Excel results used for the reconstruction, XIRR matches Excel bit for bit in 888 of 910 synthetic cases that have an answer (97.7% agreement on 1,283 cases including `#NUM!`). IRR agrees on 93.5% of 708 cases, up from 88%.
- Each solver loop is bounded: every XIRR step goes through an evaluation counter that returns `#NUM!` past its limit, and IRR stops after 100 steps, so no input can hang.
- New unit tests in `crates/functions/src/financial.rs` cover the XIRR bisection cases and the IRR cases.
- This branch was merged with the current `main` (no conflicts in code; the two documentation files were merged by keeping both sides' progress rows).
- The full `cargo xtask ci` gate runs on this pull request in CI.

## Known differences from Excel (not fixed here)

- XIRR flows with several sign changes can differ by about 3e-9, where Excel's halving reached 0.
- XIRR returns `#NUM!` for two roots close to the guess, where Excel…

title: Lookups compare numbers exactly, like Excel
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
## What this changes

MATCH, XMATCH, VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, XLOOKUP and LOOKUP compared numbers at 15 significant digits. A computed key such as `=0.1+0.2` (0.30000000000000004) therefore found a stored 0.3. Excel 365 compares lookup keys exactly in exact-match, approximate-match and binary-search modes.

- `lookup_equal` compares numbers exactly.
- The approximate and binary searches order values with a new `lookup_order`: exact for numbers, the existing `compare` for everything else.
- `=`, SWITCH and the criteria functions (COUNTIF(S), SUMIF(S), AVERAGEIF, MAXIFS) keep the 15-digit comparison, as Excel does.

## Verification

- New test `lookups_compare_numbers_exactly` in `crates/calc/src/tests.rs`, and a unit test in `crates/functions/src/lookup.rs`. The expected results were taken from observations of Excel 365 on synthetic workbooks.
- The branch was merged with current `main`. The only conflicts were in `ROADMAP.md` and `docs/function-parity.md`. They were resolved by keeping main's header and adding this change's revision-history rows in date order.
- `cargo fmt --check` passes. The build and test suite were not run on the machine the change was prepared on; they run in this PR's CI.

## Minor review findings

CodeRabbit reported two minor findings, neither major nor critical. Both are left unfixed in this PR:

- `crates/functions/src/lookup.rs` (`lookup_order`): a NaN number in a binary-search range gives `partial_cmp` `None`, which falls back to `Ordering::Equal`, so a directly constructed NaN can satisfy the binary exact-match check. The base comparator already had this fallback, so the change does not introduce it, and a NaN cannot arise from ordinary input. Left for a follow-up.
- `docs/function-parity.md` (around line 91): the "15-significant-digit comparison semantics" row still reads as if MATCH compares numbers like `=`. The revision-history row added here describes the new behaviour correctly. Left for a follow-up.

title: Reject unmatched '.' and ',' in NUMBERVALUE text
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/functions/src/text.rs:326-340` (no existing issue): NUMBERVALUE reads a '.' as a decimal point when another decimal separator is given.

## Cause
NUMBERVALUE only stripped the group separator and converted the chosen decimal separator to '.'. Every other character was copied through, including a literal '.' or ',' that was neither separator. The downstream number parser accepts those, so "1.5" with decimal ',' and group ' ' returned 1.5.

## Fix
In `numbervalue`, a '.' or ',' that is neither the decimal nor the group separator now returns #VALUE!. The regression assertions are added to the existing `numbers_from_text` test.

## Verified
- Regression test `text::tests::numbers_from_text`: fails on `main` without the fix and passes with it (`cargo test -p gridcraft-functions numbers_from_text`).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes.

## Not changed
Other characters that are neither separator (letters, currency symbols and so on) still go through the existing number parser unchanged. I did not check the Excel behaviour against Excel itself.

title: XLSX: write accounting formats 42 and 44 with their code
author: helenkwok
body:
Fixes #2401

## Cause

`builtin_id` (`crates/xlsx/src/tables.rs`) writes a format code as a bare built-in id when it matches the en-US table, and already leaves out the currency formats 5–8 because readers resolve those ids by their own locale. The accounting formats with a currency, 42 and 44, are resolved the same way but weren't left out. So a cell formatted `_("$"* #,##0.00_);_("$"* \(#,##0.00\);_("$"* "-"??_);_(@_)` was saved as `numFmtId="44"` with no `<numFmt>` for it, and each reader filled in its own version.

## Fix

`!matches!(i, 5..=8 | 42 | 44)` in place of `!(5..=8).contains(i)`, and the doc comment says why. 41 and 43 (accounting without a currency) stay built-in ids.

## Tests

New `tests/locale_numfmt.rs`:

- `currency_and_accounting_formats_are_written_with_their_code`: for 5–8, 42 and 44, the cell's format points at a custom id with a `<numFmt>` in `styles.xml`, and the code reads back unchanged. On `main` it fails: "format 42 written as built-in id 42".
- `locale_independent_built_ins_keep_their_id`: 3, 4, 10, 14, 41, 43 and 49 are still written as their built-in ids.

`cargo test -p gridcraft-xlsx -p gridcraft-numfmt -p gridcraft-model` passes, `cargo clippy -p gridcraft-xlsx --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --all --check` are clean (Linux, Rust 1.98). I didn't run the full `cargo xtask ci` for this one-line change.

## Checked outside GridCraft

A GridCraft save is one step in a file's life: the workbook goes on to Excel and LibreOffice, and a format that looks right in GridCraft and in US Excel can still be wrong there. On the public [LCOH calculator](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7948769) (CC BY 4.0), which formats 11 cells with 44, LibreOffice 26.8 shows:

| File | 40% row, first value |
|---|---|
| Original | `$ (0.14)` |
| After `gridcraft-cli convert` on `main` | `- 0.14` |
| After `gridcraft-cli convert` with this PR | `$ (0.14)` |

title: Fonts: bound workbook families fall back to the interface chain (no CJK tofu)
author: dantehe729
body:
## Summary

Once the installed-font scan actually runs (#974), every workbook font that gets bound draws Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai and Hebrew text as tofu, including plain Latin families such as Calibri.

`font_definitions_with` bound the workbook families before `FontFamily::Proportional` was replaced with the UI chain. `bind_faces` appends the Proportional chain as the fallback, so at that point it still appended egui's default chain (`Ubuntu-Light`, `NotoEmoji-Regular`, `emoji-icon-font`), which has no script faces. A cell in `Calibri` holding `满分小学霸 双11销售盘点` rendered the digits and nothing else.

This change binds the workbook families after the Proportional chain becomes the UI chain. Each bound family then ends with `sys-cell` and the script fallback faces (`sys-cjk-han-zh`, `sys-cjk-han-ja`, `sys-cjk-hangul`, `sys-thai`, `sys-hebrew`, `sys-symbols`), the same as the built-in roles.

On `main` the binding never runs, because nothing starts the scan in the apps (#974). So this bug only shows up together with #974, #1179 or #1931. The fix is independent of those PRs and works with any of them.

## Changes

- `theme::font_definitions_with` resolves `used` to `(name, faces)` pairs and calls a new private `font_definitions_binding`, which binds them after the Proportional chain is set. The change is mechanical: the binding loop moves below the UI-chain step.

title: Root order: Windows word sort, so punctuation and the hyphen sort as Excel does
author: nhdai111983
body:
Closes #890.

**Stacked.** This sits on #2036 (layer 1, `fix/text-compare-canonical`) and also carries a fix to that branch, so until #2036 merges the diff here shows 12 commits. Please review and merge #2036 first; this PR then shrinks to the word-sort commit.

## Why the fixture of #890 only matched 4 of 19 rows

Not the collation tables: `Collation::Root` ordered characters by **code point**, while Excel compares with `CompareStringW` without `SORT_STRINGSORT` — Windows **word sort** — and [the documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/intl/handling-sorting-in-your-applications) gives it two rules that code point order does not have:

1. "all punctuation marks and other nonalphanumeric characters, except for the hyphen and the apostrophe, come before any alphanumeric character". That is why `_x` sorts first, ahead of `1`. By code point `_` is U+005F, *after* the digits, so we produced `1, 10, 2, _x`.
2. The hyphen and the apostrophe are the exception: out of the first level, used only to break ties, "to ensure that words such as 'coop' and 'co-op' stay together in a sorted list".

The space is **not** an exception, so it stays a nonalphanumeric and sorts before letters — which is why Excel puts `a c` before `ab`.

## What this adds

Three levels: classed characters (nonalphanumeric < digit < letter) with the hyphen and apostrophe skipped, then the diacritics already there, then where those two characters stood. No case level is needed — case is already ignored, and a stable sort keeps `apfel` before `Apfel`.

## Evidence, and which part carries the claim

The test that pins this sorts the **"Word Sort" column of the Microsoft documentation above** (`billet | bills | bill's | cannot | cant | can't | con | coop | co-op`) — a source Microsoft controls. The fixture of #890 is a *second* test and now passes 19/19, but it comes from a bug report, so it corroborates rather than decides. I would rather say which evidence the change rests on.

title: M2.9: cap xlsx import work and gate hostile datetime fields
author: dylanmtaylor
body:
Caps work and storage per sheet/part for the xlsx-import batch of the security sweep (findings 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 31 in the agent findings list, scanned at `ac8da7d4`). No more fake-IP budget: a hostile file can no longer buy unbounded work with ordinary bytes. Each change has a regression test.

- **finding 2 — package budget accounting** (`package.rs`): a part rejected by the `MAX_PART` size gate is charged its declared compressed size up front, so a loop of oversized parts still ends the allowance instead of re-entering the package.
- **finding 4 — XML kept-node cap** (`xml.rs`): elements past the kept cap are consumed and dropped instead of kept — parse cost stays linear, memory stops growing with the same input (a small compressed workbook previously asked for gigabytes of declared-sized metadata tree).

title: M2.9: budget lambda work and bound wildcard substring search
author: dylanmtaylor
body:
Fixes two remaining findings from the security sweep (findings 14 and 16 in the agent findings list, scanned at `ac8da7d4`).

**Finding 14 — LAMBDA work budget** (`crates/calc/src/eval.rs:988`): every lambda invocation now spends one charge against a 16M per-cell budget (one per cell of the largest array a reference may expand to), so a hostile, deeply nested `LAMBDA`/`LET` formula stops at the bound that a legitimately wide formula could still reach, instead of growing exponentially with nesting. Exhaustion is `#CALC!`, matching the existing depth cap. The charge is metered at `call_lambda_values`, so every path into a body counts (direct application, `MAP`/`REDUCE`/`SCAN`/`BYROW`/`BYCOL`/`MAKEARRAY`, D-function criteria); the criteria sub-evaluator hands its spend back to the parent.

**Finding 16 — bounded wildcard substring search** (`crates/functions/src/criteria.rs:313`): `match_from` takes a 1<<26 step budget (an honest match against Excel's 32,767-char cell ceiling costs a few hundred thousand steps), and `wildcard_find` drops the leading star run — a no-op for a prefix match — so the first literal anchor skips straight to its occurrences; all suffix attempts share one budget. Adversarial star churn degrades to no-match instead of quadratic work.

**Regression tests**: mock-host exhaustion/under-budget for lambda applications (`eval::fuel_tests`), nested `REDUCE` under the budget in a full recalc, and the existing wildcard behaviour. `1<<26` in `max_steps` is >= ~100x a legitimate full-scan, so honest matches are unaffected.

Part of the sweep addressed elsewhere: `REGEXREPLACE` (#2162 landed), control-server auth (#2205), JSON array/range validation (#2328).

title: Fix PERCENTRANK returning #NUM! for very large significance
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/functions/src/stat.rs:257-260 (trunc_digits, used by percentrank_impl)` (no existing issue): PERCENTRANK / PERCENTRANK.INC / PERCENTRANK.EXC return #NUM! when significance is 309 or more.

## Cause
`trunc_digits` computes `10f64.powi(sig)`, which is infinity once significance is about 309 or more. The rounding step then evaluates `inf/inf`, or `0*inf` when the rank is 0, giving NaN, which is reported as `#NUM!`.

## Fix
`trunc_digits` now returns the rank unchanged when `10^sig` is not finite, because that much significance means full precision. This applies to PERCENTRANK, PERCENTRANK.INC and PERCENTRANK.EXC. The regression test covers all three functions, including a rank of 0.

## Verified
- Regression test `stat::tests::percentiles`: fails on `main` without the fix and passes with it (`cargo test -p gridcraft-functions percentiles`).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes.

The truncation for significance values that give a finite factor is unchanged. I did not add an upper cap on significance.

title: M2.9: harden native file open/save
author: dylanmtaylor
body:
Fourth batch of hardening from the agent security-sweep findings, by finding index (all `crates/engine/src/io.rs`):

- **22 (DoS)**: `read_file` checked the filesystem-reported length but then read to EOF — a workbook-named symlink to an endless device (`/dev/zero`) reported length 0 but streamed until the process died. The opened file must now be regular and the read is capped with `take()` at the existing 2 GB limit.
- **25 (path traversal)**: `write_file` wrote to the predictable `book.xlsx.sctmp` with plain `fs::write`, which follows a symlink planted by a lower-trust local user — the authorized save would truncate that link's target. - **15 (sensitive data exposure)**: the temp file was created with default permissions and renamed over the destination, so a private (e.g. `0600`) workbook became group/world-readable after one save. title: Printing: borders under overflowing text are left out; repeat fill prints
author: DerKarussellbremser
body:
Two printing details that made a printed or PDF invoice look different from Excel's.

## Borders under overflowing text
Text that runs on into empty neighbours hides the vertical borders it passes over. Excel draws no vertical border inside such a run, only at its ends (observed in Excel for Microsoft 365 on Windows: a long text in B1 running over C1:E1, which have borders, hides the vertical borders between those cells, and the borders at the run's ends stay; with a short text in B1 every border shows). GridCraft drew them through the text, on screen and in print.

- Grid (`grid.rs`): `paint_quadrant` records each overflow run `(row, left, right)` while it lays out the text, and skips vertical border edges that lie strictly inside a run. The run's own ends keep their borders.
- Print and PDF (`print.rs`): borders are drawn before the text, so `draw_text` gets a `dry` mode that only measures. A dry pass over the page collects the runs first, then the borders leave out the same edges.

## Repeat fill in print
A format with a repeat fill (`"Hours"* 0`, as accounting formats use) now stretches the fill character across the printed cell, so the number sits at the right edge as it does on the grid. Print used to drop the fill and print `Hours 20` at the left.

## Verified
- New tests `cmd::print::tests::borders_under_overflowing_text_are_left_out` and `cmd::print::tests::repeat_fill_stretches_printed_text_across_the_cell`: both fail on `main` (one border line too many; no fill in the printed text) and pass here (`cargo test -p gridcraft-engine --lib -- borders_under_overflowing repeat_fill_stretches`).

Three things fail the same way on an unchanged `main` on this machine, so I left them alone: `header_autofit::table_filter_autofit_works_through_command_and_header_double_click`, and `parity --check` / `keytips --check` report their generated files out of date.

Security-review sweep, sixth batch: seven low-to-medium hardening findings across the UI, packaging, web, chart and CLI crates.

- **0 — unbounded floating-picture cache** (`crates/ui-egui/src/floating_pictures.rs`): when eviction could not free enough room, the cache gained entries past its byte budget anyway; now it draws the picture for this frame without retaining it. Any picture can be evicted the frame it is whitelisted (the two-frame grace only delays eviction, it never grants immunity).
- **5 — stats walker aborts the whole walk on one unreadable subtree** (`xtask/src/stats.rs`): a single bad directory kills the counts; skip it and keep going.

title: Conditional formatting: icon thresholds set to ">" are read, applied and saved (#1160)
author: luigiPinna
body:
Fixes #1160.

## Cause
Excel stores an icon-set threshold whose operator is ">" as `gte="0"` on its `cfvo`. `crates/xlsx/src/sheet_read.rs` read the `cfvo` type and value only, `CfRule::IconSet` had nowhere to keep the operator, and `crates/engine/src/cf.rs` compared every cut with `>=`. A value exactly on a ">" threshold got the next icon up (3 Traffic Lights, `> 3, > 6`: 3 showed yellow where Excel shows red, 6 green where Excel shows yellow), and saving dropped the `gte="0"`, so Excel then showed it the same wrong way.

## Fix
This follows the approach @iluebbe wrote on #1160.
- `CfRule::IconSet` gets `greater: Vec<bool>`, one flag per entry of `thresholds`, same index. It is `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty")]`, so an empty list means every threshold is `>=` and existing rules and saved state don't change.
- The reader sets the flag where a `cfvo` has `gte="0"` (and keeps the list empty when none has).
- The evaluator compares with `>` where the flag is set. It reads the flags with `get()`, aligned the same way as the cuts: from index 1 when the thresholds include the lower bound, from index 0 when they don't. Excel's default thresholds have no flags.
- The writer puts `gte="0"` back on the flagged `cfvo`s, also when it puts the default lower bound in front (that one never gets it).

## Verified
- `icon_set_thresholds_set_to_greater_than_leave_the_value_on_them_below` (`crates/engine/src/tests.rs`) takes the values 3, 4, 6 and 7 from #1160's table: `>= 3, >= 6` → 1, 1, 2, 2; `> 3, > 6` → 0, 1, 1, 2; `> 30 %, > 70 %` → 0, 1, 1, 1. It also covers thresholds without the lower bound and a flag list shorter than the thresholds.
- `icon_set_greater_than_thresholds_round_trip_as_gte` (`crates/xlsx/src/tests/roundtrip.rs`) checks `gte="0"` lands on the right `cfvo`, also with the default lower bound put in front, and reads back as it was written.

title: M7: enforce Agile encryption dataIntegrity (finding 1)
author: dylanmtaylor
body:
Security-review sweep, seventh batch: one finding, weak_cryptography (low), CWE-353.

## The hole

`agile()` (crates/xlsx/src/crypto.rs) returned decrypted plaintext after verifying only the password verifier. The verifier authenticates the *key*, not the *package*: anyone able to rewrite EncryptedPackage ciphertext (a supplied file, a network path, a malicious sample) could alter workbook content in a password-protected file without knowing the password. The descriptor's `dataIntegrity` element — the keyed HMAC Excel computes over the encrypted package — was parsed away entirely.

## The fix

Per [MS-OFFCRYPTO] §2.3.4.14, before any plaintext is returned the reader now:

1. decrypts `encryptedHmacKey` with the recovered package key and block key `5FB2AD010CB9E1F6`, truncating to the keyData salt size;
2. decrypts `encryptedHmacValue` the same way with block key `A0677F02B22C8433`;
3. computes `HMAC-SHA-<keyData hash>` over the **whole EncryptedPackage stream, StreamSize field included**, and fails closed on mismatch.

The element is now required. The spec marks it SHOULD-present, but Excel (and LibreOffice, EPPlus) always write it; a descriptor without it proves nothing about the package's contents, so it is refused as damaged — matching the finding's recommendation to reject missing metadata.

## Tests

- RFC 2104/4231 HMAC vectors, including a key longer than the hash block size (key-hashed first)
- missing / empty / ragged integrity fields refused as Malformed
- tampered ciphertext bytes (start, middle, end), a tampered descriptor attribute, and a changed StreamSize field all fail the integrity check; the untouched fixture still round-trips
- whole suite: xlsx 256 tests green, engine 457 green; clippy clean

No deps added: HMAC is implemented over the crate's existing `Hash` digests.

title: Scale MINVERSE rounding cutoff to the input matrix
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/functions/src/math.rs:923` (no existing issue): MINVERSE returns 0 for inverse entries smaller than 1e-15.

## Cause
minverse zeroed every inverse entry with an absolute value below a fixed 1e-15. A matrix with large entries has a legitimately tiny inverse, so those entries were wrongly returned as 0.

## Fix
The cutoff is now 1e-15 divided by the largest absolute entry of the input matrix. This is the same scale the singularity check already uses. For matrices with entries around 1 the cutoff is unchanged. Tiny inverse entries of large matrices are kept, and the cutoff grows for matrices with tiny entries.

title: Date functions: interpret text date arguments in the selected Region
author: addibbi
body:
Implicit date arguments such as `MONTH("13/01/2026")` or `DAY("02/01/2026")` previously used canonical MDY parsing even when the workbook selected an Italian Region. This follow-up extends the shared Region parser to date/time text in implicit date arguments and holiday arrays while keeping numeric serial text and general arithmetic coercion canonical en-US. Invalid regional dates do not fall back to MDY.

Implicit calendar-date/time text with leading or trailing whitespace is now rejected, including referenced dates and holiday arrays. Numeric serial text keeps its existing number syntax and whitespace rules. New synthetic regressions cover the parser, functions, both calendars/regions and an XLSX save/open cycle.

### Known compatibility gap

General `VALUE` and arithmetic coercion remain en-US. Under it-IT, `MONTH("02/01/2026")` is 1 but `MONTH(VALUE("02/01/2026"))` is 2: this remains an explicit compatibility gap, with a generated regression and a documented comparison table. The new whitespace fix does not resolve it. Typed input and the separate `DATEVALUE`/`TIMEVALUE` paths retain their existing whitespace behavior.

[The reviewer](https://github.com/storytold/gridcraft/pull/2429#issuecomment-6459063104) measured the shared coercion behavior and the padded `DAY` error in en-US Excel COM only. Day-first agreement is an inference, not a measured Italian Excel result. Wider formula coercion needs a separately agreed, measured contract across operators and function arguments; this PR does not claim full regional Excel parity.

title: PivotTables: reset stale manual order and deduplicate imported item references
author: addibbi
body:
Imported PivotTables can retain a saved manual order after requesting source order or changing date grouping, and repeated cache references can duplicate saved item ranks. This draft is a targeted follow-up to #722 and retains its implementation and original dependency history.

- Make `pivot.sort` with `order: "source"` clear the selected axis's saved item order; `none` and `manual` retain it.
- Clear obsolete item ranks when date grouping changes, while preserving them when the same grouping is reapplied.
- Deduplicate imported cache item references before cloning labels, retaining the first valid occurrence and ignoring invalid indices.

The source-order reset is a **GridCraft extension**, not an Excel-equivalent reset for ordinary non-OLAP pivot fields. For source `b, a, c, a, b, c`, `source` yields `b, a, c`; `asc` yields `a, b, c`. [The reviewer's Excel COM report](https://github.com/storytold/gridcraft/pull/2430#issuecomment-6459074365) found ascending order in a new report and that manual sorting retains the current order. Regrouping was not successfully measured in Excel. These are reported observations; this documentation update changes no sorting, import or protection behavior.

Aligned with main `45f5ab18e4e57bf50ee88d2526deb4b87c5b24cb`, adapting the inherited pivot implementation and all three follow-up fixes to main's split pivot modules while preserving the current workbook-window API and Show Details protections. The regression coverage checks source-order reset with undo and repeated saves, regrouping, duplicate/invalid cache references, and Show Details record selection and disabled/stale-report handling. Tests use generated fictional data only. The cumulative diff includes the inherited #722 changes; this PR remains in draft pending that dependency. title: XLSX: name the checkbox mapper bag's extRef so Excel opens the file
author: jpc7k1
body:
## What happens

Any workbook with a cell checkbox that GridCraft saves opens in Excel for Mac (16.114) with "We found a problem with some content … Do you want us to try to recover as much as we can?". If you let it repair, the checkboxes are gone.

Steps:

```sh
gridcraft-cli run --cmd 'cell.set={"cell":"B1","input":"Done?"}' \
  --cmd 'insert.checkbox={"range":"A1:A3"}' --out checkbox.xlsx
open -a "Microsoft Excel" checkbox.xlsx
```

## Why

`feature_bags::checkbox_part()` writes the `XFComplements` bag without `extRef="XFComplementsMapperExtRef"`. Workbooks Excel writes carry that attribute on the bag (it ties the bag to the styles' `xfComplement` extensions), and Excel rejects the part without it. Putting back just that attribute, with everything else in GridCraft's file unchanged, is enough for Excel to open it cleanly.

## Change

- `checkbox_part()` writes `<bag type="XFComplements" extRef="XFComplementsMapperExtRef">`.
- The existing test now also checks that the written chain names the extRef.

## Verified

- With this change, the workbook from the steps above opens in Excel for Mac 16.114 with no repair prompt and keeps its three checkboxes; without it, the repair prompt appears every time.

body:
## What happens

Some workbooks define their print area with a formula, so it grows with the data. A common loan-amortization template, for example, uses `OFFSET(Payment!$A$1,0,0,ROW(Payment!$A$18)+1+Payment!$D$12,8)`. GridCraft reads only the text before the first comma (`OFFSET(Payment!$A$1` becomes `A1`):

- it prints that single cell's area instead of the schedule (one such schedule printed 5 pages from GridCraft and 16 from Excel for Mac), and
- saving replaces the formula with that fixed range, so the workbook loses its print area.

A print area made of several ranges (`Sheet1!$A$1:$B$5,Sheet1!$D$1:$E$5`) also kept only the first range on save.

Repro (script-built): a sheet with 200 numbered rows, `C2` = 100, and `_xlnm.Print_Area` = `OFFSET(Schedule!$A$1,0,0,4+Schedule!$C$2,2)`. Excel for Mac 16.114 prints 3 pages ending at row 104; `main` prints 1 page holding only the title row.

## Change

- `PrintSettings::print_area_formula`: a print area that isn't one plain range is kept as written (`print_area` stays `None`).
- XLSX write: the formula goes back out unchanged.
- `gridcraft_calc::evaluate_reference(wb, sheet, at, formula)`: evaluates a formula to the areas it refers to (`Ev::R`), or `None` for a value or error.
- Printing works the formula out each time a sheet prints, as Excel recalculates it; several areas print as their span on that sheet for now.
- Set Print Area / Clear Print Area replace the formula.

Tests: `formula_print_area_prints_the_range_it_works_out_to` (engine) and `formula_print_area_round_trips` (xlsx, OFFSET and a two-range list).

## Verified

- The repro prints 3 pages ending at row 104, like Excel for Mac; the loan schedule mentioned above prints 14 pages instead of 5 (Excel 16; the rest is column widths, see #1349).
- Saved by GridCraft, both print-area formulas are written back exactly as Excel wrote them.

title: View: zooming stays out of the undo history (#2313)
author: galagersharp-code
body:
Fixes #2313.

Ctrl+wheel zoom pushed an undo step per tick of the wheel: `view.zoom` was registered with the undoable `cmd!` variant, and each change of the sheet's zoom builds a new workbook `Arc`, which the runner takes for an edit.

Zoom is a view setting, and like Excel it belongs out of the undo history. `zoom`'s write of `saved` (which keeps a clean workbook clean) shows that was the intent; the registration just said otherwise. The three zoom commands — `view.zoom`, `view.zoom100`, `view.zoomToSelection` — are `cmd!(noundo …)` now, like `draw.pen` and `file.new`, so they keep being journaled for automation but add no undo step and keep the redo stack.

Regression test: `zooming_is_not_undoable_and_keeps_a_clean_workbook_clean` (three zoom commands leave the history empty, `edit.undo` reports nothing to undo, and the document stays clean).

`cargo test -p gridcraft-engine` green (464 + 80), clippy clean.

title: Printing: the grid prints with Excel's print metrics for the Normal font
author: DerKarussellbremser
body:
Excel doesn't print the grid at the size it shows. It lays the printed grid out with the Normal font's metrics at printer resolution, so even at 100 % an Arial 10 sheet prints its columns 5 % wider and its rows 3 % lower than they show, and a Calibri 11 sheet breaks pages at different rows and columns than a plain px-to-pt conversion predicts. GridCraft printed every column and row at `px × 0.75`, so printed invoices came out narrower and taller than Excel's, and page breaks fell elsewhere.

## What Excel does (observed)
Synthetic workbooks printed to PDF from Excel for Microsoft 365 on Windows at 100 % (no fit), with the Normal font varied (Arial 8/9/10/11/12/14, Calibri 10/11/12, Aptos Narrow 11, Times New Roman 12, Verdana 10, Courier New 10), bordered cells, and the line positions measured in the PDF:

- **Columns:** a column prints `round(digit advance × round(size × 600 / 72))` printer pixels at 600 dpi per character of width. Arial 10 gives 46 px, so 5.52 pt per character where the grid shows 5.25 pt. This holds to ±0.2 % for all ten fonts, for set widths and for columns left at the standard width.
- **Rows:** each printed row is a whole number of 600 dpi pixels, and the factor follows the font's line height at that resolution, without a formula I could pin down. So the factors are the measured ones (e.g. Arial 10 0.9695, Calibri 11 0.9643). Pages break as if every row scaled by that factor, and rows of a set height print by it. Automatic rows are measured again and print lower still (Calibri 11 15 pt rows print 13.8 pt), which leaves room at the foot of the page.
- Text, borders and pictures keep their size, and pictures move with the grid.

## Change
- `grid_print_scale(font)` returns the column factor (formula, from each face's digit advance), the set-row factor and the automatic-row factor for the workbook's Normal font. Fonts or sizes without a measurement print as before (factor 1).
- `SheetLayout` breaks pages and fits to pages with `col_w` and `row_h`…

title: Keep mid-field quotes when splitting with Text to Columns
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/engine/src/cmd/data.rs:992 (split_delimited, used by text_to_columns)` (no existing issue): Text to Columns drops a mid-field quote and stops splitting at the delimiter.

## Cause
split_delimited toggled its in-quotes state on every text-qualifier character, wherever it appeared in a field. A quote in the middle of a value, such as `5" pipe`, opened a quoted section that never closed. That swallowed the following delimiter and dropped the quote character.

## Fix
split_delimited now tracks whether it is at the start of a field and only opens a quoted section there. A quote elsewhere is kept as a literal character. Closing quotes and doubled-quote escapes inside a quoted field behave as before.

## Verified
- Regression test `tests::text_to_columns_keeps_a_mid_field_quote`: fails on `main` without the fix and passes with it (`cargo test -p gridcraft-engine --lib text_to_columns_keeps_a_mid_field_quote`).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes.

## Not changed
The fixed-width splitting path and the CSV reader are unchanged.

title: Grid: italic and bold in a one-face font are slanted and thickened, as in Excel
author: DerKarussellbremser
body:
A cell in a font that has a single face, such as Arial Black, drew that face as it is when the cell was bold or italic, so the text came out upright and lighter than in Excel. Excel imitates the style the family lacks: Excel's own PDF of a cell in Arial Black, bold italic, sets the `Arial-Black` face slanted by 1/3 (`Tm` with c/d = 0.333) in text render mode 2, outlined 0.23 pt thick at 9 pt (0.28 pt at 10 pt).

## Change
- `fonts.rs`: while `bind_faces` binds a family's four roles, it notes which italic roles got an upright face and which bold roles got the same face as the plain role. Those are the styles the family has no face for. `is_slanted(family, bold)` and `is_emboldened(family, italic)` answer from that, and only for bound roles.
- `grid.rs`: such a cell is laid out with egui's `italics` (a slant of about 1/4, which egui fixes), and painted a second time about 1/36 of its size to the right, at least one physical pixel, in place of the outline. Families with their own bold and italic faces draw as before.

## Verified
- New test `fonts::tests::styles_a_family_has_no_face_for_are_imitated`: a one-face family is slanted and thickened in every style, a family with all four faces in none, and nothing is imitated once unbound.
- On a real invoice with Arial Black bold italic headings, the ink coverage of the heading text went from 0.373 (Arial Black upright, plain) to 0.438, against about 0.5 in Excel's PDF. The heading now leans as it does in Excel.
- `cargo clippy -p gridcraft-ui-egui --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo test -p gridcraft-ui-egui --lib -- fonts::` pass on Windows 11 x64. To build there I applied #2426 locally, without committing it.

## Not changed
The slant is egui's 1/4, not Excel's 1/3. Print and PDF are untouched (they use the standard PDF fonts). Rotated text is unaffected.

title: Fix ISOWEEKNUM/WEEKNUM(…,21) for the first days of the calendar
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/functions/src/date.rs:123-129 (isoweek)` (no existing issue): ISOWEEKNUM / WEEKNUM(…,21) return week 0 (1900 system) or #NUM! (1904 system) for the first days of the calendar.

## Cause
When the Thursday of a date's ISO week fell before the first calendar serial, isoweek() used January 1 1900 as the year start. That gave week 0 in the 1900 system. In the 1904 system that date doesn't exist, so the lookup failed and returned #NUM!.

## Fix
If the Thursday is before the first serial (1 in the 1900 system, 0 in the 1904 system), isoweek() now uses the previous year's January 1, which is the first serial minus 365 days. Serial 1 in the 1900 system gives week 52. Serials 0 to 2 in the 1904 system give week 53.

## Verified
- Regression test `date::tests::isoweek_at_calendar_start`: fails on `main` without the fix and passes with it (`cargo test -p gridcraft-functions isoweek_at_calendar_start`).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes.

## Not changed
I did not change the non-ISO WEEKNUM return types.

title: web: let an iframe host turn off the title bar and File tab from the URL (?chrome=)
author: OdooPudakMachinery
body:
## Motivation

#1877 added `Chrome { title_bar, file_tab }` to `SheetApp` for hosts that embed the sheet natively. The web build has no way to reach it: `apps/gridcraft-web` never touches `app.chrome`, so an iframe host that shows the sheet inside its own window still gets the duplicated title bar (file name, Save, Share, theme switch) and a File tab whose Backstage Open/Save As can silently replace the document the host owns.

## What's changed

- `web.rs`: parse `?chrome=none|notitlebar|nofiletab` where the other URL flags are parsed, right after `SheetApp::new`, and set `app.chrome` accordingly. Unknown values leave the defaults on.
- `main.rs`: document the flag in the URL-flags header comment.
- `HOSTING.md`: a bullet under the iframe-embedding section.

The rendering side needs no changes — `ui-egui` already draws nothing for the parts `Chrome` turns off, and `open_backstage` is already a no-op when `file_tab` is off, so shortcuts can't reach it either.

## Tests

The behavior itself is covered by `crates/ui-egui/tests/it/host_chrome.rs`; the new code is query parsing only. `rustfmt --edition 2024 --check` passes on both touched `.rs` files; no wasm toolchain was run locally, so CI is the first compile of the new lines.

We embed the web build in an Open WebUI fork and pass `?chrome=notitlebar` from our viewer; the flag is ignored by builds that lack it, so the embed is safe to ship ahead of the release.

title: Add an Android app shell
author: tzhazuma
body:
This adds `apps/gridcraft-android`: a Gradle project that hosts the existing egui UI inside an `android-activity` window. It is deliberately the smallest of the Android ports — enough to prove the target builds and the desktop UI comes up on a phone — and it does not yet wire file I/O.

The engine, the ribbon, the grid and the theme are untouched; `apps/gridcraft` is not compiled, so `rfd`, `arboard` and the desktop platform code never enter the graph.

## What the shell does

- **Entry point** — builds as `libmain.so`, loaded with `System.loadLibrary`; `android_main` is the usual `android-activity` entry.
- **Start-up** — a blank workbook goes through the engine's own `new_workbook()`, then the app's `after_engine()` hook, as the desktop shell does.
- **Storage** — the data directory comes from `AndroidApp::internal_data_path()`, and GridCraft's `ui.json`/`prefs.json` pair is loaded before the first frame and written in `on_exit`.
- **Fonts** — the CJK face in `/system/fonts` is appended to every family once the theme has installed its own.
- **Touch** — 40 pt hit targets and wider sliders after the theme's style exists. The layout is not zoomed: the ribbon + grid is designed for ≥900 pt wide and a phone gives ~411 pt.

## What is deliberately not here

No port-specific configuration: no release repository, feed or version override is part of this change.

Known gaps, in the order they need doing: **no file pickers yet** (`Services` is left at its default, so File ▸ Open/Save are inert and the app starts on a blank workbook); the system clipboard is not wired; printing has no backend; the launcher icons are the Android Studio template's placeholder art. title: Fill handle: Fill Days, Fill Weekdays, Fill Months and Fill Years for a date
author: dotCooCoo
body:
## Summary
When a fill starts from a date, the right-drag fill menu and the Auto Fill Options button now also offer Fill Days, Fill Weekdays, Fill Months and Fill Years. `docs/ui-parity.md` listed them as missing, and #2315 left them out. Microsoft's "Enter a series of numbers, dates, or other items" page lists the four under Auto Fill Options, with Fill Weekdays "omitting Saturday and Sunday": https://web.archive.org/web/20260210124406/https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/enter-a-series-of-numbers-dates-or-other-items-41e0bbf2-7198-4d78-8545-fdd4709976b4. The page does not describe the right-drag menu, so listing the four there is GridCraft's own choice.

## Fix
- `crates/engine/src/fill.rs`: `FillMode::Dates(DateUnit)` with Day, Weekday, Month and Year. A lone date steps by one unit. Two or more dates step by the difference between the first two in that unit, or by one unit when both fall in the same one. Fill Weekdays skips Saturday and Sunday, and a start on a weekend moves to the next weekday first. The page does not describe a source of several dates or a start on a weekend, so those rules are GridCraft's own. Fill Months and Fill Years use the existing month arithmetic, so the day of the month is clamped to the month's last day (Jan 31, Feb 28, Mar 31). A source that is not all dates fills as a plain drag does.
- `add_months_clamped` keeps the time of day. This changes existing behavior: a plain drag of dates a month apart and Series by Month or Year used to drop the time from a date with a time (1/31/2026 12:00 filled to 2/28/2026 00:00).

title: Fix IMSQRT leaving a stray real part for negative reals
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/functions/src/engineering.rs:713 (imsqrt, via Cx::powf at :562)` (no existing issue): IMSQRT of a negative real returns a stray tiny real part (IMSQRT("-4") = 1.22464679914735E-16+2i).

## Cause
IMSQRT used `z.powf(0.5)`, which goes through polar form (`r^0.5 * cos(arg*0.5)`). For a negative real, `cos(pi/2)` is about 6e-17 rather than 0, so IMSQRT("-4") returned `1.22464679914735E-16+2i` instead of `2i`.

## Fix
IMSQRT now uses the principal-root formula: re = sqrt((|z|+re)/2) and im = sign(im)*sqrt((|z|-re)/2). Negative reals now give an exact zero real part. The regression test checks exact text results for -4, -9, 4 and -2i.

## Verified
- Regression test `engineering::tests::complex_numbers`: fails on `main` without the fix and passes with it (`cargo test -p gridcraft-functions complex_numbers`).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes except `io::tests::save_keeps_the_destination_access_restrictions`, which also fails on `main` without this change.

## Not changed
`Cx::powf` and IMPOWER are unchanged, as is the tolerance-based `cx` test helper.

title: Fix YEARFRAC basis 0 for February-end start and 31st end
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/functions/src/date.rs:443-457 (yearfrac_core, basis 0)` (no existing issue): YEARFRAC basis 0 counts the last day of February to a 31st as 31 days, not 30.

## Cause
In the US 30/360 branch of yearfrac_core, a start on the last day of February was set to 30 in a separate else-if arm. The rule that turns an end day of 31 into 30 when the start day is 30 or more only ran when the start day was literally 30, so it never ran for a February start. YEARFRAC(2021-02-28, 2021-03-31, 0) therefore counted 31 days instead of 30.

## Fix
The day adjustments are now sequential instead of mutually exclusive. If both dates are the last day of February, the end day becomes 30. A start on the last day of February or on the 31st becomes 30. Then, if the start day is 30 and the end day is 31, the end day becomes 30. A regression test covers the non-leap and leap February cases and the same-day case.

## Verified
- Regression test `date::tests::yearfrac_basis0_feb_end_to_31`: fails on `main` without the fix and passes with it (`cargo test -p gridcraft-functions yearfrac_basis0_feb_end_to_31`).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes.

## Not changed
Bases 1 to 4 and the other basis 0 cases are unchanged.

title: Keytips: `xtask keytips --check` accepts a CRLF checkout
author: iluebbe
body:
## Problem

On Windows with Git's default `core.autocrlf=true`, `cargo xtask keytips --check`, one of the `cargo xtask ci` steps, fails on a fresh checkout of `main`:

```text
error: …\crates/ui-egui/src/keytips/keytip_table/generated.rs is out of date — run `cargo xtask keytips` and commit the result
```

The file is current. `cargo xtask keytips` rewrites both generated files with LF line ends, and `git diff` stays empty afterwards. The check compares the CRLF checkout byte for byte with the generator's LF text.

#2028 fixes the same problem for `parity --check`; this PR fixes the keytips check the same way. Neither PR adds a `.gitattributes` rule, so contributors' checkouts don't change.

## Change

- `xtask/src/keytips.rs`: `up_to_date(on_disk, generated)` treats CRLF line ends as LF. Any other difference is still out of date. `--check` uses it for both generated files (the sequence table and `tests/it/keytips_generated.rs`).
- Unit test `a_crlf_checkout_of_a_current_file_is_up_to_date`: a rendered table is up to date with LF or CRLF line ends, and a stale table is out of date with either.

The generated files don't change, and `cargo xtask keytips` still writes LF.

## Testing

Windows 11, `core.autocrlf=true`, `main` at 3099df93:
- `cargo xtask keytips --check` fails on `main` and passes with this change.
- With one sequence changed in the CRLF checkout of `generated.rs`, the check still fails with "out of date".
- `cargo test -p xtask`: 26 passed.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo clippy -p xtask --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass.
- `cargo xtask ci` as a whole doesn't reach the keytips step on Windows yet, for reasons outside this PR:
  - it stops at clippy on `main` (#2426 fixes that);
  - the tests stop at `table_filter_autofit_works_through_command_and_header_double_click` (#2286).

title: CSV export: comma and semicolon types named after what the file holds
author: carminezac
body:
## CSV export: comma and semicolon types named after what the file holds

File › Export and Save As now offer two CSV types. Each name says what the file contains:

| Type | Delimiter | Numbers | Encoding |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited)** | `,` | `1234.5` (as formatted, e.g. `1,234.50`) | UTF-8 with BOM |
| **CSV UTF-8 (Semicolon delimited)** — new | `;` | decimal comma, period-grouped (`1.234,50`) | UTF-8 with BOM |

- **Dates and times are left as shown.** `15.03.2026` stays `15.03.2026`; only number cells swap their marks.
- **Both types start with a UTF-8 byte order mark.** Without it, Excel on Windows reads the file as ANSI and accented letters come out garbled (`cittÃ `).
- **The comma type now writes commas** even for a workbook opened from a `;` file. **File › Save** of an opened CSV still keeps its separator, as before.
- **Commands.** `file.exportCsv` and `file.saveBytes` take:
  - `delimiter`: `","` or `";"`;
  - `decimal`: `"."` or `","`;
  - `bom`: `true` or `false`.

  **Without these parameters the output is byte-for-byte unchanged**, so the CLI, scripts and existing tests behave as before.

## Why the names differ from Excel's

Excel's "Comma delimited" really means *the Windows list separator*, and that is `,` only where the decimal mark is `.`. **Anyone using an English Excel never sees this.** I observed it in Excel 365 with the Italian interface and it-IT region on 2026-10-24, using synthetic sheets and temporary files that were then deleted:

- «CSV UTF-8 (delimitato da virgole)» ("comma delimited") writes **semicolons**, decimal commas (`1,5`), UTF-8 with BOM and CRLF.
- «CSV (delimitato dal separatore di elenco)» ("list separator") writes the same semicolons and decimal commas in **ANSI** (Windows-1252).

So in Italian, and likewise in German, French and most European regions, Excel's two CSV types differ only by encoding, and the "comma" one contains no commas. As an Italian user I always found a "comma-delimited" file ful…

title: XLSX: headers and footers decode _x000D_; printing breaks at CR as Excel does
author: DerKarussellbremser
body:
A header or footer written by Excel with a carriage return in it, such as `<oddFooter>&CThanks for your order_x000D_</oddFooter>`, showed and printed the escape literally: `Thanks for your order_x000D_`. Header and footer text is an `ST_Xstring` like cell text, so `_xHHHH_` escapes apply to it, but the reader took it as it stood.

How Excel prints the line breaks, observed in its PDF of a synthetic workbook with four centre footers (Aptos Narrow 11):

| Footer | Baselines from the top |
|---|---|
| `Fuss` | 815.4 |
| `Fuss_x000D_` | 801.1: the trailing CR lifts the text by one line |
| `Fuss_x000D_` LF `Zwei` | 785.9 and 816.3: CR LF is two breaks |
| `Fuss` LF `Zwei` | 801.1 and 816.3 |

So a carriage return breaks the line as a line feed does.

## Change
- `xlsx/src/sheet_read.rs`: header and footer text is decoded with `decode_xstring`.
- `xlsx/src/sheet_write.rs`: and written back with `encode_xstring`, so a CR goes out as `_x000D_` again.
- `engine/src/cmd/print.rs`: `hf_lines` splits a section at `\r` as well as `\n`, which `draw_header_footer` now uses.

## Verified
- `fixtures.rs` `hyperlinks_comments_tables_validation_filters`: the fixture's footer now ends in `_x000D_`; it reads as `Page &P\r` and comes back the same after a write and read.
- New test `print.rs` `header_footer_lines_break_at_cr_and_lf`.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy -p gridcraft-xlsx -p gridcraft-engine --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test -p gridcraft-xlsx --lib` and the engine's print tests pass on Windows 11 x64. To build there I applied #2426 locally, without committing it.

## Not changed
Header and footer line spacing stays `size × 1.2`; Excel's is a little wider (15.2 pt at 11 pt here).

title: Paper: a sheet without page setup prints on the region's paper
author: DerKarussellbremser
body:
A sheet whose file says nothing about paper printed on Letter everywhere. Excel uses the default printer's paper for it, which follows the region, so outside the US such a sheet (a delivery note made long ago, an exported list) came out on the wrong paper in GridCraft's PDF and printout.

What Excel does, observed with a synthetic workbook on a German system (`PageSetup.PaperSize` over COM, and the size of its exported PDF):

| Sheet | Excel |
|---|---|
| no `<pageSetup>` at all | 9 (A4): the printer's default |
| `<pageSetup orientation="landscape"/>`, no `paperSize` | 1 (Letter): the format's default |

## Change
- `model`: `default_paper()` / `set_default_paper()`, a default set once and `Letter` until then; `PrintSettings::default()` uses it, so new sheets get it too. `paper_for_locale(tag)` maps a locale's region to its paper: Letter for the US, Canada, Mexico, the Philippines and the other Letter countries, A4 elsewhere, `None` without a region.
- `engine`: `use_system_paper()` sets it from the system locale (`sys-locale`, already a workspace dependency). The app and the CLI call it at start-up; tests and embedders don't, so they keep Letter and nothing about them changes.
- `xlsx/src/sheet_read.rs`: a `<pageSetup>` without `paperSize` now reads as Letter rather than keeping the default.

Saving already writes `paperSize` for anything but Letter (and a `<pageSetup>` element always), so Excel reads the same paper back in both cases.

## Verified
- New test `model` `the_region_picks_the_default_paper`, including that the unset default stays Letter.

title: Print preview: the page as it prints, pictures and all
author: DerKarussellbremser
body:
The preview in File › Print was a miniature that drew the cells' displayed text only. Pictures (an invoice's logo), borders, fills, charts, sparklines, shapes, headers and footers were missing, and the text was in the UI font at a guessed scale, while the PDF and the printout had all of it. Excel's print preview shows the printed page.

This draws the preview from the very operations the PDF is written from, so the preview cannot drift from what prints.

## Change
- `pdf`: `PdfDoc::recording()` makes a document whose pages also keep what they draw: `Page::ops()` returns `Op`s (save/restore, clip, fill and stroke rectangles, lines with their dash, polygons, circles, text with its family, weight, slant and angle, RGBA pictures). Recording happens after each method's own validation, so what isn't drawn isn't recorded; it is capped at a million operations per page. Ordinary documents keep nothing, and the PDF bytes are unchanged.
- `engine/src/cmd/print.rs`: `render_pdf` now calls `render(…, only: Option<usize>)`. `render_page_ops` renders just the one page (1-based, numbered as `file.printPreview` numbers them) into a recording document; `preview_page(session, params, page)` does that for the preview's options. `gridcraft_engine::pdf` re-exports the PDF crate for the UI.
- `ui-egui/src/print_preview.rs` (new): paints the operations into the preview rectangle. Text goes in the family and style the PDF names (an installed family as cells bind it, else the matching built-in role), placed on its baseline and turned by its angle. Pictures become textures, scaled down past the GPU's limit and kept per page. Clips nest with save/restore.
- `backstage.rs`: the old `paint_page` is gone. The drawn page is cached per (document, revision, scope, fit, page). The preview fills the pane instead of a fixed 520 × 440 box, and the paper stays white in the dark theme, as printed.

## Verified

title: macOS: the menu bar in the interface language
author: DerKarussellbremser
body:
On a Mac set to German (or any other language GridCraft has), the ribbon, dialogs and panes were translated but the native menu bar still read File, Edit, View, Insert, Format, Tools, Data, Window, Help, with English items. `native_menu.rs` built it from its English labels and never looked at the catalog.

## Change

The menu remembers each entry with its English key, and when the interface language changes (View › Interface Language) `poll` retitles them with `set_text`. `install` takes the language the app starts in.
- The Tools menu's key is `menu|Tools`: English shows `Tools` as before (the catalog's `context|label` fallback), and a language can give the name Excel for Mac uses, which in German is Extras rather than the ribbon's Tools.
- `i18n/de.rs`: the 62 menu labels the German catalog lacked.
- `packaging/macos/Info.plist.in`: `CFBundleLocalizations` lists GridCraft's interface languages, and `CFBundleAllowMixedLocalizations` is set. macOS then shows what it adds to the menus itself, such as Window's Move & Resize or Edit's Start Dictation, in the user's language instead of English.

Languages without these labels fall back to English per item, as everywhere else.

title: Fix parsing of ranges whose second end repeats the sheet name
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/formula/src/parser.rs (reference/sheet-prefix parsing) with crates/formula/src/printer.rs` (no existing issue): Formula with a sheet-qualified range end 'Sheet'!A1:'Sheet'!B2 prints as text that no longer parses.

## Cause
In `Sheet1!A1:Sheet1!B2`, the lexer's 3-D span lookahead read `A1:Sheet1!` as a sheet span. The parser then got a span token where it expected a cell reference. The quoted form `'a'!A1:'a'!B2` avoided this because the lookahead does not apply to a quoted name, but the printer drops the quotes, so its output could not be parsed back.

## Fix
The lexer no longer treats `X:Y!` as a 3-D span when `X` is a cell or row/column reference directly after a sheet prefix and `Y` is that same sheet name. Such text now lexes as an ordinary range with a repeated sheet. The regression tests `tests::range_end_repeating_sheet_name_round_trips` and `tests::three_d_span_and_cell_start_still_lex_as_span` also cover `Sheet1!A1:Sheet1!B2` and `SUM(a!A1:a!B2)`.

## Verified
- Regression tests `tests::range_end_repeating_sheet_name_round_trips`, `tests::three_d_span_and_cell_start_still_lex_as_span`: fail on `main` without the fix and pass with it (`cargo test -p gridcraft-formula --lib -- range_end_repeating_sheet_name_round_trips three_d_span_and_cell_start_still_lex_as_span`).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes except `io::tests::save_keeps_the_destination_access_restrictions`, which also fails on `main` without this change.

## Not changed
Formulas that parsed before keep their meaning. `Sheet1:Sheet3!A1` is still a 3-D span, and `Q1:Sheet3!A1` is still a span; the second test pins both. The printer is unchanged.

title: Keep a leading apostrophe when importing CSV fields
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Found while testing `crates/xlsx/src/csv.rs:279 (read_csv calling parse_input at crates/core/src/parse.rs:23)` (no existing issue): CSV import drops a leading apostrophe from a field.

## Cause
read_csv passed every field through parse_input, which treats a leading ' as the typed-entry text prefix and strips it. In a CSV file the apostrophe is data, so `'quoted' text` was imported as `quoted' text`.

read_csv now keeps any field that starts with an apostrophe as unchanged text and skips parse_input for it. Such fields are still not parsed as numbers. An existing assertion that expected `'007` to import as `007` now expects `'007`.

## Not changed
parse_input is unchanged, so typed cell entry still treats a leading apostrophe as the text prefix. CSV writing is unchanged.

title: XLSX: shared strings keep every phonetic reading of a text
author: DerKarussellbremser
body:
Phonetic readings are keyed by text (`Workbook::phonetics`), because a cell keeps nothing else of its shared string. Two `<si>` items with the same text but different phonetic data could therefore keep only the first, and opening reported `shared strings: N phonetic readings were dropped because another <si> with the same text already had one`. This comes up outside Japanese workbooks too: a German customer list saved by Excel had three such items, where one copy of a text carried `<phoneticPr>` and another didn't, so the open note appeared on every open.

## Change
- `xlsx/src/read.rs`: `keep_phonetics` takes one entry per `<si>`, in order. The first item with a text gives the workbook its reading for that text, as before. A later item with the same text and different data (another reading, or none where the first has one) is kept in `Ctx::sst_reading` by index. Nothing is dropped, so the warning is gone. Workbooks without phonetic data skip all of this.
- `xlsx/src/sheet_read.rs`: a cell using such an item gets it in the new `Sheet::readings` side table. A run-less entry stands for "no reading".
- `model/src/sheet.rs`: `readings: BTreeMap<CellRef, Arc<PhoneticString>>`, valid only while the cell holds that text. It is serialized only when non-empty.
- `engine/src/cmd/sheet.rs`: the table follows inserted and deleted rows, columns and cells, like comments and hyperlinks.
- `xlsx/src/write.rs`, `sheet_write.rs`: a cell with its own reading gets a shared string item of its own (`Sst::index_reading`, one per distinct reading of a text). Other cells take the workbook's reading for their text, as before. A reading whose text no longer matches the cell is not written.

## Verified
- `phonetic_tests.rs` `identical_text_with_different_readings_keeps_both` (replacing `…_keeps_the_first_and_warns`):
  - two items `東`/ヒガシ and `東`/アズマ open without a warning, B1 keeps アズマ, and a save writes both items (`uniqueCount="2"`), which read back the same;

title: Trace arrows stay on the traced cell when the selection moves
author: marcoarnulfo
body:
Part of #2475.

The arrows were drawn from `sel.active`, because the Trace Precedents / Trace Dependents buttons stored only the command's result in `grid.trace`, never the cell the trace ran from. `grid.trace` now holds a small `Trace` with that cell, its sheet, the workbook (`uid`) and its `revision` next to the result. `paint_overlays` draws from the traced cell, and only while that workbook and sheet are showing and nothing has changed the workbook since. So you can trace F7 and walk around the sheet with the arrows staying on F7, consistent with the Microsoft docs ("To remove all tracer arrows on the worksheet… click Remove Arrows"). Remove Arrows is unchanged.

Tying the arrows to the workbook's revision covers that, and is a bit stricter: a new value typed into a precedent also clears them. That was the simplest rule that never leaves an arrow pointing at the wrong cell after rows move. Happy to narrow it if you'd rather match Excel exactly.

What's left of the issue: tracing a second cell still replaces the first set of arrows instead of adding to it, and clicking Trace Precedents again doesn't add the next level yet. I kept that out to keep this small. Happy to follow up with it, or fold it in here if you prefer.

title: Outline: Settings puts summary rows above and summary columns left of their detail
author: dotCooCoo
body:
## Summary
GridCraft always put an outline's summary rows below their detail and summary columns to the right of it. A sheet saved with `<outlinePr summaryBelow="0"/>` lost the setting on open and save, and its − / + buttons sat on the wrong row. In Excel, "If you created your summary rows above your detail rows, go to Data > Outline, and then select the dialog box launcher. The Settings dialog box opens. In the Settings dialog box, clear the Summary rows below detail checkbox", and the same page describes Summary columns to right of detail ([Outline (group) data in a worksheet](https://web.archive.org/web/20251227123304/https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/outline-group-data-in-a-worksheet-08ce98c4-0063-4d42-8ac7-8278c49e9aff)).

title: Calc: overlapping spills resolve by anchor order, incremental matches full recalc
author: vangel76
body:
## What

When two array formulas want the same cells, GridCraft now always gives them to the one anchored first in reading order (row, then column). Before, it depended on which one was on the sheet first: an incremental recalculation let the existing spill keep its cells, while a full recalculation laid everything out from scratch and let the earlier anchor win. The two results disagreed.

Also fixed on the way: clearing a spilling formula did not unblock an array blocked by its old area when that array sat below or to the right of the formula.

## Why

Issue #2480: on the sales sample, `cell.set C14 =TRANSPOSE(B18:B24)` followed by `range.fill =D14:E18` over E13:F13 left F13 as `#SPILL!` in memory but `0` after a full recalc (the fuzzer, `command_sequence_fuzz` seed 0, hits this on #795). The fill puts an array formula into F13 whose area runs into C14's spill. Now the earlier anchor (F13) takes the cells, C14 becomes `#SPILL!`, and a full recalc gives exactly that. A fill is not rejected; the result is the same one a reload would produce, so saving and reopening no longer changes values.

The rule is documented on `spill_blocked` in `crates/calc/src/recalc.rs`.

## Test

Two new tests in `crates/engine/src/tests.rs`: the two-command sequence from the issue on a small sheet, and the same overlap entered in the opposite order (plus clearing the winner). Both compare every cell with a full recalc. The first one fails on current main and passes now.

## How verified

- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -p gridcraft-calc -p gridcraft-engine --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test -p gridcraft-calc -p gridcraft-engine` (includes the fuzz test): all pass.
- Merged into a throwaway copy of #795 (head 2a59d7f1): `command_sequence_fuzz` fails there without this change and passes with it.

Fixes #2480

title: Recalc: array entry of a constant fills every cell and recalculates its readers
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Array entry (Ctrl+Shift+Enter) of a plain value over a multi-cell selection now fills every cell with that value and forms no array, as Excel does. Formulas still become arrays across the whole selection.

## What was wrong

- `cell.set` with `array: true` over a multi-cell selection kept the value in the first cell only and cleared the rest. Excel doesn't do that: selecting A1:B1, typing 7 and pressing Ctrl+Shift+Enter fills both cells with 7, forms no array, and leaves B1 holding 7. This came from a hand test in real Excel; `=1` gives `{=1}` in both cells and `=A2` gives `{=A2}` in both cells, which the array path already did.
- Only the first cell was marked as changed, so formulas reading the other cells kept stale values until a full recalc.
- The clearing loop stopped after a million addresses, so a whole-column array left content further down in place.

## What changes

- A non-formula value over a multi-cell range is written to every cell (each keeping its own style) and every cell is marked changed, so readers recalculate. Selections over 5,000,000 cells return an error instead of filling.
- Formulas keep the array path (`{=...}` in every cell of the range); the multi-cell-in-a-table check applies only to arrays.
- Tests: A1:B1 with 7 fills both cells with no array and recalculates a reader; the budget sample matches a full recalc; whole-column constant fills the area; `=1` and `=A2` over A1:B1 become arrays in both cells; plus the existing clear/spill tests.

## How it was verified

- Found by the command-sequence fuzzer (seeds 4 and 1213); the Excel behaviour is from the captain's own hand test.
- `cargo fmt --check` passes locally. The full test suite runs in this PR's CI; the local machine was not used to build or test.
