title: CSV: Save in the close question writes the file and closes it (#2607)
author: ashokram-si
body:
Fixes #2607. It may also explain #2361, though that report doesn't say which file type was open.

Saving a CSV leaves the workbook marked as edited. That's on purpose: `file.save` clears the dirty state only for XLSX and JSON, since a CSV holds only the active sheet's values (Microsoft: CSV "saves only the text and values as they are displayed in cells of the active worksheet"). The Save Changes question, though, closed the workbook only once it was clean. So Save wrote the CSV, the question went away, the workbook stayed open, and the next close asked again. Only Don't Save got out.

`answer_save_changes` now closes the workbook when Save wrote its own file and the workbook has one sheet. The dirty-state rule in the engine is unchanged, so the " — Edited" title, AutoSave and the quit prompt still treat a CSV-saved workbook as having changes the file can't hold. The other cases:
- With more than one sheet, the CSV leaves sheets out. Save still writes the active sheet, but the workbook stays open with a message saying the other sheets weren't saved, and how to keep them (Save As .xlsx) or close without them (Don't Save). A quit stops there.
- A workbook that was never saved still asks where to save and stays open. A save that fails still shows its error and stays open.
- An answer that wrote nothing (no `bytes`, e.g. the `saved: false` answer in #1167) keeps it open too.

Formulas, formatting and other workbook features: a CSV keeps only the active sheet's displayed values, and Save in this question is the answer to save in that format and close. I tried gating the close on everything the file can't hold (two follow-up commits, reverted in 0d04f64). It needed one more workbook field per review round (formulas, then the view and defined names, then the theme and cell styles) and would miss each feature added later. A warning about what a format drops belongs where the file is written, so Ctrl+S gets it too; I've kept that out of this PR and can open an issue for it.

Gap #2 (large workbooks, recalc speed) had no measured numbers: the parity docs quoted an old ~0.4 s timing and listed "a `cargo xtask bench` with fixed workbooks" as missing. This adds it.

## What it does
- **`crates/engine/examples/bench.rs`**: ten scenarios that build their workbooks in code, so no fixtures are committed. title: perf: win back formula-entry and XLSX-save time lost since 23829d8c
author: nihilist-narwhal
body:
Formula entry and XLSX save got ~20% and ~13% slower over the ~880 commits since 23829d8c. This finds where the time went and wins most of it back. Output doesn't change.

Measured with the calculation bench from #2651 (`crates/engine/examples/bench.rs`) at 100k rows on an M2 Pro, with main and this branch run in turn three times:

| scenario | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| enter.formulas (paste 100k formulas) | ~420 ms | ~379 ms (−10%) |
| xlsx.save (300k-formula model) | ~525 ms | ~478 ms (−9%) |

The other scenarios don't change beyond noise.

## Changes
- **`number_to_text`** (f29ac7d9e): the check for rounding up to 1E+15 formatted *every* number with an exact `{:.14e}` and parsed it back. Formula printing calls this once per number literal, on entry and on save. The check now runs only for `a ≥ 9.9999999999999e14`. A value can only round up from 999999999999999.5 or higher, so the output is the same. New boundary tests: …999.5 → `1E+15`, …999.4 → `999999999999999`, …989.9 → `999999999999990`.
- **`Expr::clone`, `Expr::map`, xlsx `prefix_params`** (2aeb21d4d): a binary node whose left operand isn't itself a chain (`A1*2`, the common case) no longer allocates a spine `Vec`, and `map` rewrites the operands in their existing boxes. The visit order and results are the same as the chain code with a spine of length 1. `Expr::walk` reserves 8 slots up front.
- **`grow_autofilter`**: checks that the sheet has an AutoFilter before looking up the cell. Most sheets have none.
- **`retained_bytes_against`**: looks up the newer band's row once per row instead of once per cell.
- **Journal size cap**: an entry's JSON size is counted with a writer that only counts bytes, instead of building the text. A big paste's params can be megabytes.

## Not changed
What's left of the entry gap, and all of `edit.fanout`'s (~+12%), is Undo's byte budget (#1227): sizing each snapshot and freeing evicted ones. That's the intended cost of bounding Undo's memory, so it stays. A follow-up c…

title: Cap text at 32,767 characters like Excel (#2635)
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
## What was wrong
Fixes #2635. GridCraft let text grow past Excel's 32,767-character cell limit, so it could write a cell Excel refuses to open. In real Excel:

| Formula | Excel | GridCraft before |
|---|---|---|
| `=LEN(REPT("x",20000)&REPT("x",20000))` | 32767 | 40000 |
| `=LEN(REPT("x",32767)&"y")` | 32767 | 32768 |
| `=LEN(CONCAT(REPT("x",20000),REPT("x",20000)))` | `#CALC!` | `#VALUE!` |
| `=LEN(TEXTJOIN(",",,REPT("x",20000),REPT("x",20000)))` | `#CALC!` | `#VALUE!` |
| `=LEN(CONCATENATE(REPT("x",20000),REPT("x",20000)))` | 32767 | `#VALUE!` |
| `=LEN(SUBSTITUTE(REPT("x",20000),"x","yy"))`, `=LEN(REPT("x",32768))` | `#VALUE!` | `#VALUE!` (already right) |

Entering a 40,000-character string in a cell is also cut to 32,767 by Excel; GridCraft kept all of it. A CSV field that long was kept whole too.

## Cause and fix
The `&` operator only refused text over four times the limit in bytes, the concatenation functions returned `#VALUE!`, and nothing cut typed or CSV text. Now:
- `&` and CONCATENATE cut their result to 32,767 characters.
- CONCAT and TEXTJOIN give `#CALC!` past the limit.
- `cell.set` (all typed input that isn't a formula) and CSV/TSV fields are cut to 32,767 characters.
- A shared `cap_text` helper in the core crate does the cut (by characters, not bytes).

Tests: `crates/functions/src/text.rs` (CONCAT, TEXTJOIN, CONCATENATE), `crates/calc/src/tests.rs` (`&`), `crates/engine/src/cmd/edit.rs` (`cell.set`), `crates/xlsx/src/tests/csv_tests.rs` (CSV). ROADMAP progress log updated.

## How verified
I re-ran the table's formulas in real Excel through COM on a new workbook and got the values above, and a 40,000-character value assigned to a cell read back as 32,767 characters. I did not build or run the Rust tests on my machine (only `cargo fmt --check`); the fork's CI runs the suite.

## Not covered
- I did not run an Excel open check on a saved file.
- A formula longer than 32,767 characters is not touched (it has its own limit).
- #2532 and #2539 only…

title: Match Excel for YEARFRAC basis 0, MOD, NUMBERVALUE and PERCENTRANK edge cases
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Four recently merged function changes disagree with real Excel (16.0, checked 2026-10-26 by running each formula below in Excel through COM). This makes GridCraft match Excel.

**What was wrong and the fix**

- **YEARFRAC basis 0, February-end start.** `YEARFRAC(2021-02-28, 2021-03-31, 0)` gave 30/360; Excel gives 31/360 (0.08611111111111111), also for 2020-02-29 to 2020-03-31 and for the reversed order. Cause: the "end day 31 becomes 30" rule was tested after a February-end start had already been moved to day 30. Excel tests it against the original start day (28 or 29 is under 30, so the end day stays 31). Fix: remember whether the original start day is 30 or more and use that for the test.
- **MOD.** Excel gives `#NUM!` whenever the quotient magnitude is 1.1259E12 or more: `MOD(3,1E-300)`, `MOD(1E15,7)`, `MOD(1E10,0.001)`, `MOD(1125900000000,1)`. `MOD(1125899999999.9998,1)` still works (0.989990234375), as does `MOD(1E12*7+3,7)` (3). GridCraft returned numbers. Fix: return `#NUM!` when `|number / divisor| >= 1.1259E12`.
- **NUMBERVALUE.** An unmatched `.` or `,` was rejected with `#VALUE!`. Excel swaps the given separators and parses what is left: `NUMBERVALUE("1.5",","," ")` is 1.5, `("1 234.5",","," ")` is 1234.5, `("2.5%",","," ")` is 0.025, `("1.5E3",","," ")` is 1500, a `;` or `x` decimal separator still gives 1.5, and `("1,5",".")` is 15. `("12.345,6",","," ")`, `("1.2.3",","," ")` and equal separators stay `#VALUE!`. Fix: drop the blanket rejection of `.` and `,`; the rest goes through the normal number parser.
- **PERCENTRANK, PERCENTRANK.INC, PERCENTRANK.EXC.** Significance 309 or more is `#DIV/0!` in Excel (308 still works); GridCraft returned 0.5. From significance 15 up Excel returns 15 significant digits rounded (`PERCENTRANK.INC({1..7},2.123456789,16)` is 0.187242798166667); GridCraft returned 16 digits. Fix: `#DIV/0!` from 309, and round to 15 significant digits from 15.

**How verified**

Every expected value in the new tests was produced by runnin…

title: Cells: hold Excel's 32,767-character limit at the three ways past it (#2635)
author: galagersharp-code
body:
Closes #2635.

A cell with more text than Excel's 32,767 characters — counted in UTF-16 units, like `LEN` — saves to a `.xlsx` Excel refuses to open. Three paths let one in; this closes each at the point the issue measured.

## `&` cuts like Excel

`eval.rs`'s `BinOp::Concat` capped its result at `32767 * 4` bytes, which bounds memory but is not Excel's limit. It now cuts the result to 32,767 UTF-16 units with no error, as Excel's own concatenation does: `=REPT("x",20000)&REPT("x",20000)` keeps its first 32,767 characters. `CONCAT`, `TEXTJOIN`, `REPT` and `SUBSTITUTE` already returned `#VALUE!` past the limit and are unchanged.

## Editing refuses an over-limit input, naming the cell

`input_to_cell` — the path `cell.set`, `range.setValues`, typing, paste, replace and text-to-columns all take — now refuses an input past the limit with an error naming the cell: ``B3: a cell holds at most 32,767 characters, and this is 32768 — Excel refuses more too``. The count is UTF-16 units, so 16,384 characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (32,768 units) are refused and 16,383 fit. The two callers that swallowed `input_to_cell` errors into a raw-text fallback (paste's table loop and `replace`) check explicitly instead, so an over-limit paste is refused rather than stored raw; text-to-columns refuses the over-limit part rather than silently clearing its destination cell.

## Text files keep the field whole and warn

`read_csv` still keeps every field whole — splitting a 100,000-character field over rows or cutting it at 255 characters loses the record's shape, as the issue measured against Excel. What changed is the silence: `io::open_bytes` now returns a warning naming the count and the first over-limit cell — `long.csv: 1 cell holds more than Excel's 32,767 characters and was kept whole, as the text file had it; Excel may refuse or repair the file this saves to (first: Sheet1!B2)` — through the same `warnings` channel `file.open` already shows.

title: LAMBDA tail recursion reaches Excel's depth (5,459)
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
## What was wrong
A recursive LAMBDA that calls itself in tail position (`IF(n=0,0,me(me,n-1))`) stopped at about 139 calls and answered `#NUM!`. Excel computes the same formula up to n=5,459 and answers `#NUM!` from 5,460.

## Cause
Every LAMBDA call nested under the previous one on the native stack, so the call count had to stay low (`MAX_LAMBDA_CALLS` = 140) to keep a 1 MiB thread and wasm from overflowing.

## Fix
`call_lambda_values` now follows the body through the tail positions (`IF` branches, parentheses, applied lambdas) and, when the value is another LAMBDA call, evaluates its arguments and loops instead of nesting. A tail chain therefore uses constant native stack. Each link still spends fuel, and the chain is capped at 5,460 invocations, which is Excel's boundary, so an endless tail recursion still gives `#NUM!`. Array-condition `IF` and everything else evaluate as before.

## What is not fixed
Plain recursion (`1+me(me,n-1)`, Excel reaches 4,094) and helper-wrapped recursion (Excel reaches 2,339) stay far below Excel. Plain recursion is unchanged (about 131). Wrapped recursion improves as a side effect: the helper's `f(f,k)` is itself a tail call, so a wrapped level now costs one call in progress instead of two and behaves like plain recursion (the test now expects 70 where it expected `#NUM!`; it was 69 before). A non-tail call has to keep the native frames of every level, about 10 KB per level by my estimate from the code, so 4,094 levels need roughly 40 MB, far more than a 1 MiB thread or the wasm stack. Follow-up options for the maintainers:
- (a) a stack-switching crate such as `stacker`: native only, wasm would keep the low limit unless its linker stack size is raised;
- (b) an explicit heap-stack rewrite of the call path: works everywhere, but is a large change.

## How verified
In real Excel (new temporary workbook, `Formula2`): tail countdown 5,000 gives 0, 5,459 gives 0, 5,460 and 10,000 give `#NUM!` (bisected: 5,459 is the last that works); …

title: fix(ui): support single-key answers in Save Changes dialog (#2572)
author: kk376
body:
Resolves #2572.

### Summary
Adds single-key shortcut answering to the "Save Changes?" confirmation dialog shown when closing a workbook or quitting the application, matching standard Excel and desktop keyboard workflows:

- **`Y`** or **`S`** (and **`Enter`**): Selects **Save**, commits and writes the workbook before continuing.
- **`N`** or **`D`**: Selects **Don't Save**, discards changes and continues closing.
- **`Esc`**: Retains existing behavior: cancels the close action and keeps the workbook open.

### Safeguards & Defenses
- **Modifier guard**: Modified combinations (`Ctrl+N`, `Ctrl+Y`, `Alt+N`, etc.) are ignored so accidental shortcut chords never dismiss the dialog.
- **Single-shot event consumption**: Keys are consumed via `i.consume_key` on the initial key-press edge. A held key does not auto-repeat to unintentionally dismiss multiple dirty workbooks when quitting.
- **Safe failure recovery**: Cancelling a file picker or encountering a save error leaves the workbook open and dirty, preserving unsaved work.

title: Whole-column borders no longer push older undo steps out of the history
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Fixes the undo bug from fuzz seed 7: after `home.borders` on `F:F` and two `home.insertCells` (shift column), only one step was left to undo, and undoing it left Budget!C4 empty.

**Cause.** `home.borders` on a whole column wrote a cell for every row (1,048,625 cells). That one step held about 100 MB, so the next structural edit pushed the history past its 128 MB byte budget and the older steps were dropped. Nothing failed part-way; the steps were trimmed.

**Fix.** For whole columns or rows, `home.borders` now sets the column/row format (as `apply_style` already does for other formats) and touches only the existing cells and the two end cells of each line. The per-preset logic moved into one closure shared by the cell and line paths. Not handled: with preset `none` on a whole line, shared edges of neighbouring column/row formats are not cleared (existing neighbouring cells still are).

**Verified.** Two new tests in `crates/engine/tests/it/undo_insert_cells.rs`: the shrunk three-command sequence keeps all 3 undo steps and undo restores C4 (failed before the fix: 1 step, C4 empty), and the column/end-cell borders are as expected. The seed 7 sequence and a 60 seeds x 100 steps fuzz run now pass in release; the existing border tests pass. Not run: the full suite (left to CI), and the extra `Sheet1` after undo-all at 100 steps was not looked at separately; the fuzz run passes, so I assume it had the same cause. No Excel comparison made for the border placement.

title: Dependencies: quick-xml 0.41 to 0.42 (xlsx reads names and values as &str)
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
## What was wrong
The dependabot group update (storytold/gridcraft#2600) fails the gate: quick-xml 0.42 moved its API from bytes to `&str`, so `gridcraft-xlsx` stopped compiling (64 errors in `ods.rs`, `xlsb.rs`, `xml.rs`, `passthrough.rs`). `apps/gridcraft-cli/src/check.rs` uses the same API and would have failed next.

## Cause
In 0.42 element and attribute names, namespaces, attribute values, CDATA and entity references are `&str` / `Cow<str>`, and `BytesText::xml_content` can no longer fail. `BytesCData::decode` is gone.

## Fix
Only the quick-xml call sites change, with no behaviour change:
- namespace and name constants and comparisons are `&str` instead of `&[u8]`;
- `local()` / `local_name()` split on the last `:` of a `&str`;
- the `xmlns:` prefix set is `HashSet<String>`; attribute values are used directly instead of round-tripping through UTF-8 checks (the input is already valid UTF-8 at that point);
- `xml_content` results are used without `map_err`; CDATA is read from its text as before (no extra newline normalisation).
`quick-xml` is `0.42` in `Cargo.toml`; `Cargo.lock` points `gridcraft-xlsx` and `gridcraft-cli` at 0.42.0 (`wayland-scanner` still needs 0.41, so both stay in the lock).

zip is not touched here: the zip 3 to 9 move (and the `package.rs` errors that come with it) belongs to storytold/gridcraft#2247, which currently conflicts with main.

## How verified
Not built locally. The change was written from the compile errors in the failing gate log of #2600 (run 40267143110) and checked against the quick-xml 0.42.0 source. `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo metadata --locked` pass. The existing XLSX/ODS/XLSB round-trip tests are unchanged; this PR's CI is the check that they still pass.

## Not verified
Anything past the first compile phase: rustc stopped at type errors in the log, so borrow-check or lint errors, if any, only show up in CI.

title: IMSQRT: reproduce Excel's stray real part for negative reals
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
IMSQRT now gives the same text as Excel for negative real numbers.

**What was wrong.** IMSQRT of a negative real was exact: `IMSQRT("-4")` was `2i`. Excel 16.0 returns `1.22514845490862E-16+2i`, and `IMSQRT("-9")` returns `1.83772268236293E-16+3i`. `IMSQRT("4")`, `("-2i")` and `("3+4i")` give exactly `2`, `1-i` and `2+i` in both.

**Cause.** Excel does not use the closed-form root. It takes the square root of the modulus and multiplies by the cosine and sine of half the argument. Its cosine reduces the angle with a 64-bit-mantissa pi, which is PI/2 + 2.508e-20, so cos(pi/2) comes out as 6.1257422745431E-17 where plain f64 gives 6.12323399573677E-17. That is the stray real part. The same offset explains the small real parts for inputs just off the negative axis (`IMSQRT("-1+1E-10i")` = `5.00000653944413E-11+i`). The angle itself comes from `atan(im/re)` plus or minus pi, not from `atan2`. The two differ in the last bit, and only that form reproduces `IMSQRT("-0.5-1E-12i")`.

**Fix.** `imsqrt` in `crates/functions/src/engineering.rs` now uses that route, adds the 2.508278806e-20 offset to the cosine, and treats a `-0` imaginary part as `+0` (Excel gives `+2i` for `"-4-0i"`).

**How verified.** I ran IMSQRT in real Excel (16.0, through COM, new workbooks only) on 79 in-range inputs: negative reals from -1E-10 to -1E100 and -1E150, pure imaginary, `i` and `j` suffixes, large and tiny parts, zero, and numeric and COMPLEX() arguments. Text errors, booleans and `1/0` give `#NUM!`, `#VALUE!` and `#DIV/0!` in Excel as in GridCraft. I replayed the model in Python against all 79 Excel strings (15 significant digits) with no mismatch. Tests in the existing `engineering.rs` test module assert 25 of the Excel strings. The Rust suite was not run on this machine, only `cargo fmt --check`. CI on this PR runs the tests.

**Where GridCraft does not match Excel, and why.**
- Parts above about 1E154 or below about 1E-155: Excel gives `#NUM!` or `0` (`IMSQRT("1E155")` is `#NUM!`, `IMSQR…

title: Calc: a one-value dynamic array shows in a table column (#2335)
author: zyzabruh
body:
## Problem

Since 0.11.1, a dynamic-array formula in a **table column** that returns a single value shows `#SPILL!` instead of its result: a calculated column of one-row `FILTER`s, or `SEQUENCE(1)`, in a table. Excel for Microsoft 365 shows the value (`HasSpill = false`), and 0.10.0 did too — it is a regression. Seven real-world workbooks in the corpus rerun gained between 3,500 and 6,200 formula mismatches each, almost all `#SPILL!`.

## Root cause

The fix for #1491 records a one-value dynamic-array result as a 1 x 1 spill, so `C1#` keeps working. But all three table checks in `crates/calc/src/recalc.rs` refused *any* spill whose anchor sits in a table — `spill_blocked`, `spills_as_before` and the commit pass — so a 1 x 1 result was refused too, and the cell showed `#SPILL!`.

Excel's rule has two halves: a result of **more than one cell** in a table is refused, a **one-value** result is shown (checked against Excel for Microsoft 365 on the issue's fixture: `B2:B4` = South/East/North with `HasSpill = false`, `ROWS(B2#)` = 1, `ISREF(B2#)` = TRUE, `SEQUENCE(1)` → 1, `SEQUENCE(2)` → `#SPILL!`).

## Solution

A shared `blocked_by_table(&tables, anchor, array)` helper applies the table test **only when the result is larger than 1 x 1**, and replaces the condition at the three sites. The multi-cell half of the rule is unchanged (`SEQUENCE(2)` in a table stays `#SPILL!`), and the 1 x 1 anchor contract from #1491 is preserved (`ROWS(B2#)` is 1 in a table too).

## Testing

- **Excel (COM, black box)** on the issue's fixture `gc_table_filter_da.xlsx`: `Main!B2:B4` = South, East, North (`HasSpill = false`), `F2` = South, `C2:C4` = 1, `ROWS(B2#)` = 1, `COUNTA(B2#)` = 1, `ISREF(B2#)` = TRUE; `SEQUENCE(1)` in a table shows 1, `SEQUENCE(2)` in a table is `#SPILL!`.
- **Issue repro:** `gridcraft-cli check gc_table_filter_da.xlsx` now reports 7 checked, 7 matched, **0 mismatches** (3 before the fix), round trip clean.
- **New regression tests:** `crates/calc/src/tests.rs::a_one_v…

title: perf: select instead of sort in MEDIAN, PERCENTILE, QUARTILE, LARGE, SMALL
author: vangel76
body:
Fixes #2679

**What.** MEDIAN, PERCENTILE(.INC/.EXC), QUARTILE(.INC/.EXC), LARGE and SMALL now find the one or two order statistics they need with `select_nth_unstable_by(f64::total_cmp)` (O(n)) instead of sorting all the data (O(n log n)). MEDIAN with an even count takes the maximum of the lower partition for the lower middle value; PERCENTILE's interpolation takes the minimum of the upper partition as the next value (only computed when the fractional part is non-zero). PERCENTRANK and other `sorted()` callers are untouched.

**Why.** The sort was the dominant cost, and `LARGE(range, SEQUENCE(300))` repeated it once per spilled cell.

**Numbers** (release, `taskset` on one core, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, setup subtracted, 4 identical runs each):

| Call | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| MEDIAN, 1M numbers | 0.34 G instr | 0.054 G (6x) |
| LARGE(1M numbers, 1) | 0.34 G | 0.034 G (10x) |
| PERCENTILE(1M numbers, 0.37) | 0.34 G | 0.058 G (6x) |
| 300 x LARGE(100k numbers, k) | 8.75 G | 1.26 G (6.9x) |

**How verified.** The new test `selection_matches_full_sort_bit_for_bit` keeps the old full-sort implementations as an oracle and compares results bit for bit (or same error) on randomised data: lengths 0 to 4096, many ties, -0.0/+0.0, NaN, infinities, k and percentile values out of range, fractional k, and both LARGE and SMALL. `cargo test -p gridcraft-functions` passes (146 tests), `cargo fmt --all --check` and `cargo clippy -p gridcraft-functions --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean.

title: Objects keep their placement when rows and columns change (#2343)
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Pictures, shapes and charts now keep the place their placement gives them when rows and columns are resized, hidden, filtered, inserted or deleted (#2343).

**What was wrong:** the three placements (editAs twoCell, oneCell, absolute) were already stored, read and written, and an insert or delete already honoured them. body:

title: perf(calc): SUM/COUNT/AVERAGE over big ranges reuse constant-only results
author: vangel76
body:
Fixes #2681

## What
`SUM`, `COUNT` and `AVERAGE` over a block that holds only constants (no formula, error value or spilled value) now remember the block's sum and count for the rest of the recalculation pass. A second formula reading the same block gets it from a lookup. A block with the same first cell and last column but more rows (a running total, `SUM(A$1:A{r})`) continues from the longest shorter block already known instead of starting over.

## Why
Every such formula walked its whole range twice, so 20,000 rows of `=A1/SUM(A$1:A$20000)` cost 400 million cell visits.

## Bit-for-bit
Results are identical to before, including the floating-point summation order: the remembered sum is the left-to-right, row-major sum from +0.0, and a longer block only adds the extra rows after it. It is used only when the running sum is exactly +0.0 at that point (not after a leading number such as `SUM(1E16, A1:A3)`), otherwise the old walk runs. Blocks with an error value, a formula, a spilled value, any spill found in the pass, or with iterative calculation on take the old path unchanged.

## Numbers
Single pinned core, release build, `recalc_all` (the edit-triggered recalculation shows the same), instructions:u from `perf stat`:

| Workbook | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 20,000 x `=A/SUM(A$1:A$20000)` | 20.2 s, 3.90e11 instr | 19 ms, 9.4e8 instr |
| 20,000 x `=SUM(A$1:A{r})` | 8.9 s, 1.95e11 instr | 16 ms, 7.4e8 instr |
| 1,000 x `=SUM(A1:A50000)` | 2.0 s, 4.9e10 instr | 2.1 ms, 2.0e8 instr |

(After: 3 runs each, instruction counts identical.)

## How verified
- New test `aggregates_over_ranges_match_a_plain_fold_bit_for_bit`: random sheet with numbers (including 1e16/-1e16 mixes), text, blanks, booleans, errors and formulas; running totals and random blocks, one or two blocks per call, with and without a leading number; every result compared bit by bit with a plain left-to-right fold, after a full recalculation and after 30 rounds of incremental edits. Fixes #2685

## What

`Calc::rebuild` and `Calc::cells_changed` now read each formula's syntax tree with `Formula::expr_arc()` instead of `Formula::expr()`. `expr()` deep-copies the whole tree, and the copy was only used to hand `&Expr` to `precedents`, which takes a reference. `expr_arc()` returns the already cached `Arc<Expr>` (the recalculation itself already uses it). Two lines change; nothing else.

## Why

Every file open (`recalc_all` runs `rebuild`), every undo/redo and every structural edit rebuilds the graph, so each one paid for a full copy and drop of every formula's tree. In the profile, `Expr::clone`, its drop and the `Vec<Expr>` clone were about a fifth of a rebuild.

## Numbers

100,000 rows of `=IF(A{r}>B{r},A{r}*B{r}+ROUND(A{r}/3,2),MAX(A{r},B{r}))`, release build, pinned to one core with `taskset`, `perf stat -e instructions:u` (difference of a 21-rebuild and a 1-rebuild run, divided by 20; three runs each, all within 0.3%):

| | per rebuild |
|---|---|
| before | 1086 M instructions |
| after | 747 M instructions (-31%) |

Wall time per rebuild on this (busy) machine went from about 120 ms to about 105 ms.

## How verified

The graph is built from the same tree, so it is unchanged. `cargo test -p gridcraft-calc` (90 tests pass), `cargo fmt --all --check`, and `cargo clippy -p gridcraft-calc --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean.

I left the other rebuild cost mentioned in the issue (a `HashSet` per precedent cell in `Graph::cell_deps`) alone to keep this change minimal.

title: perf(calc): index spill areas so cell and range reads don't scan every spill
author: vangel76
body:
Fixes #2683

## What
Reading a cell or a range during a recalculation pass looked at every spill (dynamic-array result) computed so far, and `cells_changed` looked at every spill range of the sheet for each changed cell. Both now go through a small spatial index (`crates/calc/src/spill_index.rs`, spill areas registered in 16 x 16 cell blocks), so a read only looks at the spills near it. Results do not change.

## Why
With many spill arrays on a sheet, every cell and range read paid for all of them: 20,000 `=MAX(A:B)` rows took 7 ms with no spills and over a second with 2,000 `=SEQUENCE(50)` anchors elsewhere on the sheet.

## Numbers
Release build, `taskset` to one core, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, three runs each (the instruction counts agree to 0.01%):

| Scenario | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 20,000 `=MAX(A{r}:B{r})` rows + 2,000 `=SEQUENCE(50)` anchors, `recalc_all` | 1160-1183 ms, 27.6 G instructions | 74-80 ms, 0.91 G instructions |
| same, no spills (control) | 43-49 ms, 673.1 M | 38-40 ms, 673.2 M |
| paste of 20,000 cells with 2,000 spills, `cells_changed` | 146-150 ms, 2.67 G | 46-47 ms, 1.02 G |

The remaining time in the last row is the real recalculation and a scan that #2684 covers.

## How it keeps the results identical
- A cell covered by one spill, or a range meeting spills that don't overlap inside the range, is answered from the index.
- Where several spills cover the same cell, or overlap inside a range read, the code falls back to the old order (the pass's spill map iteration order: first wins for a cell read, last wins for a range read).
- In `cells_changed` the sheet's spill ranges are indexed only for pastes of more than 16 changed cells; seeds come out in anchor order as before.

## How it was verified

title: perf(calc): find formulas a cleared cell may unblock from a set of #SPILL! cells
author: vangel76
body:
Fixes #2684

## What
When a cell is cleared, `Calc::cells_changed` looked at every formula in the graph to find formulas showing `#SPILL!` that the empty cell might unblock, `run` did the same for each area a formula stopped spilling over, and each changed cell scanned a 64 x 64 window of stored cells for `#SPILL!` values. `Calc` now keeps the set of cells whose value is `#SPILL!` (filled in `rebuild` like `circular` is, updated by `cells_changed` and by the write-back of a run) and takes all three kinds of candidates from it. With no `#SPILL!` cell on the workbook the loops cost nothing. Every entry is checked against the workbook before it is used, so a stale entry can't seed anything.

## Why
Clearing one cell in a workbook with 100,000 formulas spent about 10 ms walking the graph (about 100 ms per Delete at a million formulas), and each changed cell paid about 0.5 us for the window scan even on sheets without spills.

## Numbers
Release build, `taskset` to one core, three runs each:

| Scenario | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 100,000 formulas in column B, clear one cell | 10.0-11.0 ms | 0.0 ms (under 0.1 ms) |
| 20,000 changed cells, no spills, `cells_changed` | 19.8-21.8 ms (921.7 M instructions:u in the whole run) | 10.0-10.9 ms (671.4 M) |
| 20,000 changed cells, 2,000 spills present | 73-78 ms | 68-75 ms (spill reads are #2683) |

## Behaviour is the same
Candidates are the same cells as before: stored cells with `#SPILL!` in the 64 x 64 window above and left of the changed cell, and formulas with `#SPILL!` above and left of an emptied cell or freed area. They come out in row-major order instead of graph hash order; the pass sorts the dirty set before calculating, so the order of seeds doesn't matter.

title: Formula pointing from the keyboard: Ctrl+Page Down / Ctrl+Page Up switch sheets (#2571)
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Closes #2571 (the keyboard part).

## What changes

While a formula waits for a reference (after `=`, `(`, `,` or an operator), Ctrl+Page Down and Ctrl+Page Up go to the next and previous sheet without ending the edit. The arrow keys then point from the cell selected on that sheet and write its name into the formula (`=Sheet2!A2`), the same text a click there writes. Enter commits on the sheet the formula was typed on, as it already did after a click on a sheet tab.

Also fixed on the way: arrow pointing after a mouse click on another sheet's tab started from the edited cell of the first sheet and wrote no sheet name.

## Where GridCraft does not match Excel

- Not observed in real Excel: these keys cannot be driven through Excel's COM interface, so the behaviour follows Excel's documented shortcuts. In particular the cell the first arrow starts from after a sheet switch (the destination sheet's selected cell here) is a guess.
- Page Up / Page Down pointing by a screen is not done.
- The issue's mouse-only complaints (arrows or Enter dead after clicking a tab and then a cell) did not reproduce in the code: a click on a cell hands focus back to the editor. Not run in a real window.

## What ran

- `cargo fmt --check` here. Nothing else was built on this machine.
- New tests in `crates/ui-egui/tests/it/formula_point_sheets.rs` (next sheet, back again, Enter commits on the origin sheet, non-formula text left alone) run in the fork's CI.
- No Windows, macOS or Linux GUI run.

The other items of the same batch: Y/N in Save Changes (#2572) and the fill-drag tooltip (#2598) already have open PRs (#2675, #2662, #2669, #2661), so nothing was added for them. Alt+numpad codes (#2533) cannot be fixed in this repository: on Windows the composed character arrives after Alt is released, winit attaches it to that key release, and egui-winit only forwards text for key presses, so no text event ever reaches GridCraft.

title: Charts: series through defined names get Excel's cache and number formats (#1690, #1689)
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Fixes #1690 and #1689.

## What Excel does (observed)
Real Excel for Windows (Microsoft 365), through COM, new workbook: column charts whose series values and categories are defined names (static ranges, `OFFSET` dynamic names, a text-category name, a date-category name), saved as .xlsx, chart XML read back.

- Through a name Excel writes the same cache as for a plain reference: `<c:f>[0]!Vals</c:f><c:numCache><c:formatCode>0.00</c:formatCode>…` with one `<c:pt>` per cell. Dynamic `OFFSET` names are cached too.
- `formatCode` is the number format of the first cell (`m/d/yyyy`, `0.00`), not `General`.
- All-number categories (dates) are a `numRef` with `numCache`; text categories are a `strRef` with `strCache`.
- Axes are `sourceLinked="1"` and take the source cells' format, through a name as for a plain reference. Date categories give a `dateAx`.

## Change
- `xlsx`: a series formula that is a name resolves to its cells (names of names, and `OFFSET` with literal arguments, bounded depth), and the cache is written as above. The cache `formatCode` is now the source format for plain references too (it was always `General`). All-number categories are written as `numRef` + `numCache`. Multi-level categories through a name are written qualified (`[0]!Name`) like the other references.
- `calc`: new `evaluate_area`, the single range a formula evaluates to.
- `chart`: number formats and date categories are read through names (including `OFFSET` names with calculated sizes), so axes show dates instead of serial numbers.
- Tests: `crates/xlsx/src/tests/chart_name_caches.rs` asserts the exact XML Excel wrote (static, names of names, OFFSET, text categories, unresolvable names), and a chart test checks that a name and the plain reference resolve to the same categories and format.

## Where GridCraft does not match Excel
- `xlsx` may not depend on `calc` (layering), so it can't calculate. A name whose size comes from a calculation (`OFFSET(…,COUNTA(…))`) is saved without a cache;…

title: Ignore Error: read and write ignoredErrors, ignore and reset commands, euro sign in numbers (#1994)
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Follow-up to #1994 (Number Stored as Text). The warning button had no Ignore Error, and the file's `ignoredErrors` were dropped on open. This adds both, plus the one conversion case that still differed.

## What Excel does (observed)

Observed in Excel 16 (Windows, US settings) through COM on new temporary workbooks: `Range.Errors(n).Ignore`, `Application.ErrorCheckingOptions`, and the saved sheet XML.

- Ignore is per cell and per rule. `Errors(3)` is Number Stored as Text, and the other eight rules behave the same way (evalError, twoDigitTextYear, formula, formulaRange, unlockedFormula, emptyCellReference, listDataValidation; calculatedColumn is in the schema, I did not trigger it).

title: Conditional formatting: a colour scale interpolates between its stops as Excel does
author: zyzabruh
body:
## Problem

A colour scale's in-between values are painted one byte off Excel. The review of the colour-scale formula stops (#1885) reported it: at the exact halfway point of a red-to-green scale Excel gives `807F00` (red 128, green **127**) where GridCraft gives 128,128,0.

It is not only the halfway point. Measured over the shape of the colour scale used by that PR's tests (values 0..20, stops 0 red, 20 green), GridCraft differs from Excel on **11 of the 20 values**:

| Value | Excel | GridCraft before |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 243,12 | 242,13 |
| 7 | 166,89 | 165,89 |
| 10 | 128,127 | 128,128 |
| 13 | 90,165 | 89,166 |
| 18 | 26,229 | 25,230 |

## Root cause

`lerp` in `crates/engine/src/cf.rs` interpolated each channel to the nearest byte (`.round()` on `start + (end - start) * t`).

**Excel instead moves each channel from the earlier stop's byte toward the later one and drops the fraction**: a channel that rises is floored, a channel that falls is ceiled, i.e. `start + trunc((end - start) * t)`.

## Measured

Excel 16 on Windows, over COM, new temporary workbooks, two explicit number stops set with `FormatColor.Color` and the painted colour read back through `DisplayFormat.Interior.Color`:

- **Non-complementary stops** `(10,100,200)` → `(250,30,60)` over 100 values 0..100: **100 rows out of 100 match `start + trunc((end - start) * t)` on all three channels** — a rising channel (red) floored, both falling ones (green, blue) ceiled. No other candidate arithmetic fits (floor/round/ceil applied to the final value each fail rows this one gets).
- **Two-stop red → green over 0..20** (the shape of the PR's tests): **21 rows out of 21 match**, including 128,127 at value 10 — the `807F00` of the review.
- **Three stops** 0 red / 10 green / 20 blue over 0..20: 19 rows out of 21 match inside both segments; at values 12 and 14 of the green-to-blue segment (where the linear result lands exactly on an integer) Excel is one unit the other way. That is the precision of Excel's ow…

title: Security: cap the work of lifted lookups with #NUM! (#2716)
author: Higgs32584
body:
Fixes #2716.

`call_lifted` checked only the output size. A lookup lifted over N needles then searched its lookup vector N times, so `=ROWS(XMATCH(SEQUENCE(1048576),-SEQUENCE(1048576)))` ran for about 2.6 h on a release build and hung `file.open`.

This adds `LIFTED_SCAN_BUDGET` (5e8 needle × entry steps, a few seconds at about 8 ns per entry). It applies to the six lookups that scan from the start of their vector: VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, LOOKUP, MATCH, XLOOKUP and XMATCH. Past the budget the call returns `#NUM!`, the same pattern as MMULT's 2e9 cap.

The length used is the longest dimension of the largest non-lifted array, not its cell count. Each call scans one vector, so `VLOOKUP(A2:A5000, A2:F100000, 3, FALSE)` still works. Other lifted functions are unmetered: INDEX over a lifted position reads one entry.

This is complementary to #2678, which removes the per-call copy. With or without that change, an exact-match scan per needle stays quadratic.

**Tests**
- `gridcraft-functions` `lift::tests::lifted_lookups_stop_past_their_work_budget`:
  - the hostile call returns `#NUM!`;
  - each of the six lookups returns `#NUM!` just past the budget;
  - lifted XMATCH/XLOOKUP within the budget give the same results as before;
  - lifted INDEX is unaffected.
- `gridcraft-calc` `tests::lifted_lookups_stop_past_their_work_budget`: the formula itself evaluates to `#NUM!` quickly, and normal lifted lookups sum correctly.
- `cargo test -p gridcraft-functions -p gridcraft-calc` all pass.
- `cargo clippy -p gridcraft-functions -p gridcraft-calc --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` are clean.

body:
Refs #816. Complements #818.

**Problem.** `render_pdf` memoizes picture *decodes* (#2416), but `draw_objects` still calls `Page::image_rgba` for every page a picture overlaps. Each call keeps a fresh RGB (+alpha) copy in `Page::images` until `finish()`. Nothing bounds those copies across the document: `MAX_PAGE_CONTENT` caps only the content string. Anchor extents come from the file (clamped to ±1e7 px), so one picture can cover every page.

On a release build of `main` (45f5ab18), a 3 190-byte xlsx with one 4000×4000 PNG anchored at 3000×12000 px:
- grew about 29 MiB per page;
- passed 2 GiB in 6.1 s during `file.exportPdf`.

At `MAX_PAGES = 2000` that becomes an allocation abort that `catch_unwind` can't stop, so unsaved work is lost.

#818's dedupe happens when the file is written, so each page still holds its own decoded copy while the PDF is built. This PR bounds that build-time memory.

**Change**
- `crates/pdf`: `MAX_DOC_IMAGE_BYTES` (512 MiB) is a document-wide budget.
  - `Page::image_rgba` checks the worst case (RGB plus alpha) against the room left *before* allocating.
  - Pictures past the budget are left out, the way oversized pictures already are, and the export still succeeds.
  - `PdfDoc::set_image_budget` can only lower the budget; tests use it.
- `crates/engine/src/cmd/print`: a `PicCache`, capped at 256 MiB, memoizes floating and cell-picture decodes. Cell pictures were decoded per cell per page. A picture isn't decoded at all once its worst case no longer fits.

**Tests**
- `gridcraft-pdf` `tests::image_bytes_are_bounded_across_pages`: 50 pages under a 10 000-byte budget keep exactly two copies.
- `gridcraft-engine` `cmd::print::tests::picture_copies_across_pages_stay_within_the_image_budget`.
- `cargo test -p gridcraft-pdf` passes, 17/17.
- `cargo test -p gridcraft-engine --lib` passes, 501/501.
- `cargo clippy -p gridcraft-pdf -p gridcraft-engine --lib -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` are clean.

title: Security: control channel enforces its token deadline and caps waiting connections (#2717)
author: Higgs32584
body:
Fixes #2717. Also lands the connection cap that #2174 suggested.

**Problem**
- `serve` reads through `BufReader::new(stream.try_clone())`, but `authenticate` set `AUTH_TIMEOUT` on `out`, the original stream. On Windows the clone is a separate handle with its own timeout, so the token read was unbounded.
- Even where the handles share a timeout, it was per read, so a peer sending a byte every few seconds reset it.
- `serve_listener` spawned an uncapped thread per connection, and `incoming().flatten()` retried accept errors in a tight loop.

On a release build of `main` on Windows 11:
- 200 silent connections without the token were all still open after 11 s;
- a byte-at-a-time connection was still open at 58.7 s;
- threads and handles grew linearly (19/583 → 219/1383).

**Change**
- `read_auth_line` reads the first line, at most `MAX_AUTH_LINE` bytes, against one total deadline. The timeout is set on the handle being read and shortened before every read.
- `MAX_PENDING_AUTH = 16` connections may wait to authenticate at once. A `Pending` guard frees a slot when the connection authenticates or is refused. Past the cap, a new connection is closed on accept before anything is read.
- Accept errors (out of sockets or handles) back off 50 ms instead of spinning.
- `docs/control-protocol.md` mentions the cap.
- Limits are injectable (`serve_listener_with`) so tests run in milliseconds.

**Tests**
- `control_server::tests::a_silent_or_slow_peer_is_closed_at_the_auth_deadline`: a silent peer and a byte-at-a-time peer are both closed within the deadline.
- `control_server::tests::connections_waiting_to_authenticate_are_capped`: a third waiting connection is closed at once, and a place freed by authenticating is reused.
- `cargo test -p gridcraft --bin gridcraft control_server` passes, 9/9.
- `cargo clippy -p gridcraft --bin gridcraft --tests -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` are clean.
- The clock reads are native-only, marked like `logging.rs`.

title: CLI: finish workbook saves after stdout closes
author: DAnaeto
body:
When a reader closes stdout during `gridcraft-cli run`, the CLI exits successfully before applying later commands or writing `--out`. Suppress further output after a broken pipe so the requested work finishes, and return failure if a later command or save fails. Other stdout errors still fail. The help text explains that closing stdout no longer cancels work.

Handle a closed stderr pipe as well: when stdout and stderr share the closed reader, diagnostics no longer panic after a successful save or mask the exit status of failed work. Buffer each result line before writing it so short lines retain their normal pipe-write behavior. Regressions reopen the saved workbook and cover later command, save, non-pipe output, and shared-stream failures.

Validation on macOS:
- `cargo test -p gridcraft-cli`: 25 unit and 16 integration tests passed.
- `cargo xtask ci`: all 10 gates passed with the CI-pinned craft-fonts checkout and an isolated runtime directory.
- Headless Claude Sonnet 5.5 review of the final diff found no material issues after addressing its shared-stream and output-fragmentation findings.
- Non-Unix stdout error handling remains unverified.

title: fix(ui-egui): Korean typed over a cell keeps its first syllable whole
author: Fuzen2478
body:
## Problem

Typing Korean into a selected cell (no F2) splits the first syllable into jamo: `안녕` comes out as `ㅏㄴ녕` or `ㅇ안녕`. Typing into a cell that is already being edited composes normally.

Two things in the grid → in-cell editor handoff:

1. **The grid didn't allow the input method.** With no `PlatformOutput::ime`, winit disallows IME, so the first key goes around the input method and arrives as a bare `Text("ㅇ")`.
2. **Moving the focus cancels the composition.** `begin_edit` moves the focus from the grid to the in-cell editor. `Memory::request_focus` interrupts IME on a focus change, and egui-winit carries that out as `set_ime_allowed(false)` + `set_ime_allowed(true)`. On macOS that also resets the view's `ImeDocument`, so the input method's next replacement (`ㅇ` → `아`) no longer finds the jamo and it stays separate.

## Fix (`crates/ui-egui/src/grid/keyboard.rs`, `grid/editor.rs`)

- `allow_ime`: while the grid has the keyboard it publishes an `IMEOutput` for the active cell (owner = the grid, a new context generation each time it takes the keyboard back; not on touch screens, where it would raise the on-screen keyboard). The first key now goes through the input method, and the candidate window opens at the cell.
- `start_typing`: the first `Text`, `Ime::Commit` or `Ime::Preedit` starts the edit with an empty draft, takes that event and the rest of the pass's events out of the input, and calls `request_discard`. In the repeat pass the in-cell editor has the focus, and `in_cell_editor` puts the held keys back in front of the input, so the editor's `TextEdit` handles them (preedit, commit, delete-surrounding). The interrupt from the focus change belongs to the grid's IME context; `PlatformOutput::append` keeps an interrupt only within one owner/generation, so it doesn't reach the platform. If no repeat pass is left this frame, the keys are replayed in the next frame instead.

English typing takes the same path (the editor inserts the text in the repeat pass).

title: MCP: confine file access to a user-selected folder
author: ro-legal-docx
body:
GridCraft's headless MCP server currently lets file commands reach any path the user can access. This adds an operator-selected folder boundary:

```sh
gridcraft-cli mcp --root /work/project
```

`--root` grants read and write access within the same existing directory. `--automation-read-root` and `--automation-write-root` support separate input/output folders; supplying only one denies the other kind of access. Without root flags, existing unrestricted behavior is preserved.

The policy is checked at engine file I/O, covering `open_workbook`, `save_workbook`, generic `execute_command`, CSV/text and picture imports, CSV/HTML/PDF exports, implicit Save, and atomic-save temporary paths. It is installed before `--in` is opened and for all server threads. Resolved paths are compared by whole canonical components, without Unicode case folding; traversal, similarly named siblings, escaping symlinks and dangling links are rejected. An exclusive-open failure also preserves a pre-existing `.sctmp` file.

This refreshes Isaac Levine's work in #480 against current `main` and credits him as co-author. It additionally provides `--root`, confines startup input, updates the current command/test layout, and adds coverage for generic dispatch and temporary-file preservation. The original PR branch is unchanged.

Fixes #445. Related to #2172; desktop/control-channel confinement from that broader issue is outside this PR.

A content-free, closed three-field hello/connect handshake binds the exact parent, origin, content-addressed bundle path and exactly one transferred MessagePort. Every workbook payload and state event then uses that private port; later window messages are ignored. Existing window mode keeps its source/origin guard and save behavior.

Correlated `gridcraft:open` replies only after actual engine import and reports its completed document identity. Concurrent owned imports are refused, identical filenames still import new bytes, and unsaved work or pending native drafts refuse replacement before file commands can settle them. Pending cell and text-box drafts now contribute to dirty state and bounded opaque revision pulses, so a host can debounce native export without requiring Enter. Managed save ACK still applies only to the exact latest exported workbook, while later drafts remain dirty.

Validation: regression tests were observed failing before each fix; 24 web tests pass, and `cargo xtask ci` passes all 10 steps, including 849 UI tests with no skips. Chromium exercised an actual `sandbox="allow-scripts" credentialless` opaque frame: strict handshake rejection cases; overlapping imports/File New and same-name import identity; idle export without Enter; cell/text-box pending draft retention and managed ACK; 32 MiB pre-copy rejection; and a 4,305,188-byte native JSON export, disk write, fresh-frame reopen and byte-identical re-export. Formula/result, styles/number format, two sheets, row height, merge, text box and 130 long text cells survive. Same-origin managed mode and legacy XLSX Save controls also pass.

title: Speed up XLSX save by writing worksheet XML without per-cell allocations
author: Silvertree2010
body:
## Summary

Saving a large workbook as XLSX spent about half its time building worksheet XML, mostly in small per-cell string allocations. This makes the worksheet writer append to the part directly. On a 200,000-row workbook the save is 28 % faster (median). The written package is byte-for-byte identical.

## What changed

- `xlsx/src/xml.rs`: appending helpers `push_a1`, `push_u64`, `push_num`, `push_esc` (plain-ASCII fast path). `num` and `esc` now wrap them, so their output is unchanged.
- `xlsx/src/sheet_write.rs`:
  - `sheetData` walks the cell store in its own row-major order. It no longer copies every address into a `BTreeSet` and a per-row `BTreeMap` and then looks each cell up again.
  - Cells outside the store (cell pictures, cached spill values, table header names) still go through the sorted set. So does a store whose order is not sorted.
  - `write_cell` uses the appending helpers.
- `xlsx/src/fmla.rs`: `to_file` prints the shared expression directly when nothing in it has a different file spelling. That means no LET/LAMBDA, no `_xlfn` function, no spill, `@` or trim operator, and no structured reference. Before, every formula was cloned and rebuilt twice by the file rewrite.
- `formula/src/printer.rs`: A1 references are appended to the output instead of being formatted into a separate string for each anchor. Printed text is unchanged.
- `xlsx/examples/write_perf.rs`: new benchmark example. Its workbook is sales-shaped: order ids, dates, repeated categories, numbers, two formula columns with cached values, booleans, sparse notes and a summary sheet with SUM/SUMIFS.

## Benchmark

```
cargo run --release -p gridcraft-xlsx --example write_perf -- 200000 3
```

Baseline is the first commit of this branch (benchmark only, writer code as on main). Patched is the second commit. Both ran on the same machine (Ryzen, 16 threads, Linux, shared with other jobs). There were 12 interleaved rounds of 3 runs, so 36 runs each. The workbook has 200,000 rows, 2.0M cells…

title: Fix hidden columns inflating frozen header rows
author: TheRenegadeDev
body:
## Summary

Refs #2724. Wrapped text in a hidden column was measured at its zero display width during automatic row sizing, inflating a synthetic frozen header to 546 px. Measure at the stored width, falling back to the sheet default only when no width is stored. Hidden text still contributes on import, edits and explicit AutoFit.

```diff
 wrapped-text row fitting
- use the column's displayed width (zero when hidden)
+ use its stored width, or the sheet default when absent
```

This follows tjheinzer's earlier fix in [#2668](https://github.com/storytold/gridcraft/pull/2668) for the same row-height cause; the engine diff deliberately uses the same minimal implementation. This PR's distinct contribution is the #2724 frozen-pane/zoom regression coverage, including separate frozen-header and scrolling-data paint assertions. Maintainers can close #2755 in favor of #2668 plus these tests if preferred.

An explicitly stored zero remains zero before the existing minimum-width clamp, matching the visible zero-width path; it can still reach the height cap. An absent width uses the sheet default. Excel behavior for zero/absent stored widths has not been verified here. The positive-width behavior follows Harrison-Booth's real Excel observations in this PR; no independent live Excel comparison is claimed.

**Reproduction limit:** the plain freeze/zoom profile rendered correctly. The synthetic failure additionally needs a hidden wrapped header. The reporter's original workbook remains unavailable, so its cause and resolution are unconfirmed. Import fitting remains grow-only and does not shrink a 546 px height already saved by an older build. Very narrow positive stored widths can still legitimately produce tall rows.

Credit: @TheRenegadeDev.

title: Perf: reuse text criteria aggregates per recalculation (#2751)
author: TheRenegadeDev
body:
## Summary

Related to #2751. A synthetic workbook shaped like the reported private file takes 287.02 seconds in `recalc_all`: 165,880 COUNTIF/SUMIF/AVERAGEIF formulas each copy and scan the same 2,860-row ranges, repeatedly preparing text matches.

```text
second literal text equality over the same constant ranges → group once by folded text
later criteria formulas → read the matching count/sum/average/min/max
end of recalculation pass → discard the index
```

This makes that full recalculation finish in 0.492 seconds with identical results. The index preserves the criteria matcher's one-character Unicode folding, row-major summation, numeric counts and first selected errors. It also supports single-pair COUNTIFS/SUMIFS/AVERAGEIFS/MINIFS/MAXIFS. Formula ranges, overlapping spills, iteration, computed/numeric/wildcard/comparison criteria and multiple criteria pairs use the original path. A bounded recent-key queue admits ranges only on their second request, so one-off running counts do not spend index allowances. Unrelated arrays remain eligible; new overlapping spills invalidate affected indexes. Pass-wide limits on range inspections, folded text, distinct groups and cache entries fall back without changing results.

The private XLS remains unverified. On this baseline, `lookup_equal` is called by the lookup functions, while criteria aggregates use `Criterion::matches`; this PR does not establish that the sampled lookup stack is fixed. Opening still recalculates synchronously. It leaves #2719's lifted-lookup cap and #2678's lookup-copy work alone.

The cache has no general eviction/refund policy. Many distinct pairs that each reach a second request can still consume its allowances before later heavy ranges are seen—for example, separate Yes/No COUNTIFs over each running range. Those later calls keep the scan path. Second-request admission protects ranges used once; it does not guarantee acceleration for every calculation order or working set.

title: Excel function oracle: run a PR's asserted function calls through real Excel and compare
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Adds a script that takes the function calls a PR asserts in its tests, evaluates each in real Excel through COM and writes a comparison of the expected value against Excel's. It sits beside the Excel open check (the open check asks whether Excel loads what we save; this one asks what Excel computes) and does not duplicate the corpus job. No engine code changes.

`packaging/windows/excel-oracle/oracle.ps1`:
- `-Diff pr.diff` (from `gh pr diff`) reads the `ev("F", vec![n(..), t(".."), b(..), e(..), empty(), col/row(&[..]), d(y,m,d)])` calls on added lines, with their `close`, `close_tol`, `is_text`, `is_err` or `assert_eq!` expectation. `-CaseFile cases.tsv` takes formulas directly (for tests that build a workbook, which are not parsed).
- Each formula goes into a new temporary workbook in an Excel instance the script starts (alerts off, macros disabled, 60 s timeout in a child process; only that instance is stopped on a hang).
- Writes `results.md`/`results.tsv` (MATCH, DIFF, NOEXPECT, SKIP with the reason), `cases.tsv`, and `oracle.xlsx` saved by Excel: formula cells with Excel's cached values, one per row, array results spilled on a second sheet. That is the shape `gridcraft-cli check` takes as oracle, so the corpus repo can hold it. It is Excel output and is never committed here.
- A diff or cases file is untrusted input, so functions that reach outside the workbook (WEBSERVICE, CALL, RTD, IMAGE and similar) are never evaluated, numeric expectations must be plain arithmetic, and a formula Excel refuses (wrong argument count) is recorded as Excel's answer for that case.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 and Excel 16.0 on Windows, through WSL interop. Run on the diffs of two merged PRs and on a hand-written cases file (bool, error, text with a non-ASCII letter, SEQUENCE and TRANSPOSE spills). Every Excel process the script started exited; none was left running.

title: fix(ui): release scrollbar capture after missed mouse-up (#2748)
author: TheRenegadeDev
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2748. Both worksheet scrollbars now release their drag capture on observed primary button-up or focus loss. Capture is owned by its viewport and gesture. An egui input hook ends an interrupted old capture before assigning a later press in every viewport, including immediate workbook windows. Pending presses are canceled without producing clicks or adding to double-click counts; logic-only ticks stop capture immediately and retain cancellation for the next full input pass.

```diff
 scrollbar drag
- keep applying pointer movement until egui ends capture
+ stop on observed button-up or focus loss
+ cancel an interrupted old gesture before a later press can reuse it
+ native Wayland only: stop on PointerGone when an outside release can be lost
```

The pinned egui-winit bridge clears its pointer position on `CursorLeft`, then discards button events while that position is absent. Egui retains its old button-down state on `PointerGone`, and a later `PointerMoved` carries no fresh button state. Focus loss also leaves pointer state held. The regressions reproduce these input sequences on current main; the precise Mutter/Wayland event ordering in the report has not been verified on Ubuntu.

The fallback is selected from the actual native `RawDisplayHandle::Wayland`, so XWayland/X11, Windows, macOS and web keep held dragging across window exit. All hosts keep held dragging outside the scrollbar track. Activating presses before web canvas focus and existing secondary/middle thumb drags keep working. No dependency changes or event-bridge patches.

Current main defaults to XWayland on GNOME when `DISPLAY` is set and `GRIDCRAFT_WAYLAND` is unset; outside-release delivery on that path remains unverified. The reported v0.8.0 predates that default. The exit fallback applies only when the actual backend is native Wayland.

title: fix(keyboard): Ctrl with the numpad's + inserts rows, columns or cells, as in Excel
author: RomanLis91
body:
## Change

In Excel, Ctrl with the numpad's + does the same as Ctrl+Shift+=: with whole rows or columns selected it inserts them, otherwise it opens the Insert dialog. In GridCraft it did nothing.

The cause is that egui-winit reports NumpadAdd as `Key::Plus` without Shift, and `ribbon::shortcut` only matched `Key::Plus | Key::Equals` when Shift was held. Now `Key::Plus` matches with or without Shift. `Key::Equals` still needs Shift, so Ctrl+= stays unbound.

Reading the code, this probably also reaches layouts whose main block types + without Shift (Nordic, or a German keyboard with Cmd on a Mac), where Ctrl with that key now inserts too. German Excel uses Strg++ for Insert too (#1440's table), so I kept that, but I have not tried a non-US layout. This implements the numpad item of #1440. #1385 is related: its `us_key` maps a typed + to Shift+=, but it does not cover the numpad's `Key::Plus`.

- `crates/ui-egui/src/ribbon/shortcuts.rs`: the guard is now `shift || key == Key::Plus`.
- `crates/ui-egui/tests/it/whole_line_shortcuts.rs`: `numpad_plus_inserts_without_shift` (whole row 2 selected, Ctrl+Plus with no Shift inserts a row) and `unshifted_equals_inserts_nothing`.
- `docs/ui-parity.md`: the shortcut row, the timestamp line and a revision history line.

title: Paste: a huge untrimmed copy no longer aborts the process (#2158)
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Fixes #2158.

`edit.copy {"range":"A1:XFC1048575"}` then `edit.paste {"at":"A2"}` walked every source cell (about 17 billion) and aborted on an 8 GB allocation after 47 s, which the `Session::execute` panic guard can't catch.

- `copy_impl` trims a block over 16M cells to the used range (as it already did for whole rows and columns).
- `paste_special` refuses a copied block over 16M cells with an error instead of walking it.
- After a cut, the moved cells are looked up in a `HashMap` instead of a linear `find` per cell (the issue's O(n²) note).

Regression test: `paste_of_a_huge_untrimmed_copy_neither_hangs_nor_aborts` (huge copy pastes correctly, and a used range that is itself huge returns an error).

Not run: macOS, the full workspace suite (the fork CI runs it), and I did not run the new test against the unfixed code (it would take minutes and 8 GB). title: Entry keeps the first 15 significant digits of a number, as Excel does
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Typed numbers and number literals in formulas kept every digit an f64 holds. Excel keeps the first 15 significant digits and drops the rest (truncating, not rounding).

Measured in real Excel (COM, temporary workbook, values assigned as typed text):
- `12345678901234567890` is stored as 1.23456789012345E+19; `=A1-12345678901234500000` is 0
- `1234567890123456` is stored as 1.23456789012345E+15
- `0.12345678901234567` is stored as 0.123456789012345
- `=12345678901234567890-12345678901234500000` reads back with the first literal as `12345678901234500000` and gives 0

## Change
- core `parse::keep_15_digits` cuts plain number text; `parse_plain` (typed input, and text coerced to a number) uses it.
- formula lexer uses it for number literals.
- Files are unchanged: stored values keep every digit they hold, and Excel reads them as written.
- Related: https://github.com/storytold/gridcraft/pull/583 adds an opt-out box for typed entry and does not change the default; this change is the default it would switch off.

## Tests
- core `typed_numbers_keep_15_significant_digits`, formula `number_literals_keep_15_significant_digits`.
- Ran on Windows (GNU toolchain): `cargo test -p gridcraft-core -p gridcraft-formula` passes; `cargo fmt --check` clean on Linux.

title: A height for every row sets the sheet's default row height (fixes #2762)
author: ayozetr
body:
Fixes #2762

## Problem
`home.rowHeight` with every row selected (Select All, or `1:1048576`) added an entry for each of the 1,048,576 rows to `sheet.rows`. `Geo::new` builds the row `LineIndex` from that map on every frame (twice in `grid/show.rs`), and with a million entries one build takes about **12 ms** in release, measured with `LineIndex::new` on a sheet like that. That's more than a whole 60 fps frame before anything is drawn. `Sheet::row_top` walks the same map and took about 7 ms for row 1,000,000. That fits the report: a single row, 1,000 or 10,000 rows, or all 16,384 columns stay fast, and undoing the change makes the lag go away.

## Fix
In `cmd/format/sizes.rs`, when the rows cover the whole sheet and the height isn't 0, the command sets `default_row_height`, which is how Excel stores it (`sheetFormatPr defaultRowHeight` with `customHeight="1"`, which `sheet_write.rs` already writes). Only the rows already listed (an earlier custom height, an outline level, a style) get the new height. Hiding every row (height 0) still goes through the old path, because a zero default height isn't a hidden row. Partial ranges are unchanged.

This doesn't touch the per-frame `LineIndex` build itself, which #1098 covers more generally. It just stops this command from making the map huge in the first place.

One behaviour difference: before, every row became `custom`, so row auto-fit never touched them. Rows that weren't listed now just use the default height, so a row whose content needs more than the new default (a much larger font, wrapped text) can grow to fit. Rows never shrink below the default.

## Tests
- `a_height_for_every_row_sets_the_default_row_height` runs with explicit `1:1048576` and with Select All on an empty sheet. It checks that only a few rows are listed and every row is 40 px (including row 1,000,000 and the last one); that a row with its own height takes the new one; that `row_top` is right; that the height survives an XLSX write/read; that undo res…

title: Calc: per-formula budget on materialized array cells (#2157)
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Part of #2157: a per-formula budget on the array cells a formula may materialize. Each array was already capped at `MAX_CELLS`, but a formula could build many of them (`A:A*B:B*C:C*...`), so total memory and time were unbounded. The evaluator now keeps a counter (`CELL_BUDGET`, 8 x `MAX_CELLS`), charged in `area_value` (range reads) and in the elementwise binary fold. Past it the formula answers `#CALC!`. The counter is carried through the child evaluator used for computed criteria, like the lambda fuel.

Not done here: string-concatenation/`REPT` result caps, `zip*`/spill write-back charging and cached defined-name expressions from the issue's list. #2161 (multiplying recursion budgets) is not touched; the issue bot points at the threading PR for it.

Excel: not measured. I did not run a COM check for the comparable case (Excel's own limits there are memory-based and it reports `#NUM!`/out-of-memory rather than a fixed budget); I don't claim a match.

Tests: new unit test `array_cells_spend_a_per_formula_budget` in `crates/calc/src/eval.rs` (fits at 8 cells, `#CALC!` at 7; the test needs the new counter, so it fails to build without the change). Ran on Windows (GNU toolchain) `cargo test -p gridcraft-calc --lib eval`: 3 passed. `cargo fmt --check` clean. Not run: full suite (left to CI), macOS, Linux build on this machine.

title: Sort: sort numeric-looking text as numbers, like Excel's Sort Warning option (#2240)
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
## What this changes

Data > Sort (and the A to Z / Z to A quick sort) gets Excel's Sort Warning choice, "Sort anything that looks like a number, as a number": a `textAsNumbers` option on `data.sort` (per key, or one value for all keys) and on `data.sortAscending` / `data.sortDescending`. Default is off, so existing sorts do not change.

With it on, a text cell that coerces to a number in arithmetic (`"10"`, `"1,000"`, `"$5"`, `"50%"`, `"(4)"`, `"1e3"`, date text the parser reads) is compared as that number. Other text stays text. The cells themselves are not converted. Ties keep their order (stable sort).

## Excel check

Measured in desktop Excel through COM with temporary workbooks, `Sort` object, `DataOption` 0 vs 1 (`xlSortTextAsNumbers`), ascending and descending: the table is in https://github.com/storytold/gridcraft/issues/2240#issuecomment-6456150238. Numeric text sorts by value mixed with real numbers; non-numeric text goes after the numbers ascending and before them descending; ties keep original order.

## Scope

Not included: a checkbox in the Sort dialog or a Sort Warning prompt (command-level option only), and a day/month/year choice for date text (issue #2240's DD-MM-YYYY case). Date text sorts by date only when the parser reads it in the active locale; I did not measure a day-first locale.

## Verification

title: Linux: run on native Wayland again by default (revert #165)
author: bmh129
body:
This reverts #165, so GridCraft runs on native Wayland again by default.

#165 made GridCraft run through XWayland whenever `DISPLAY` is set, because winit 0.30.13 reported dropped files only on X11. That reason is gone: the egui 0.37 migration (#2543) pins `storytold/winit`, whose patch **W15** reports file drops through a per-seat Wayland data device (rust-windowing/winit#4729, the 0.30 backport of what winit 0.31 has). Together with egui fork patch **E4**, which keeps egui's clipboard on that same device, files dragged from the file manager open on native Wayland, and (according to the fork's `PATCHES.md`) paste keeps working on compositors such as Hyprland.

The XWayland default now only costs:
- **A startup crash where `libxkbcommon-x11` is missing.** winit's X11 backend loads it when it starts, and the Linux packages don't depend on it (the RPM requires `libxkbcommon` only). In a Fedora toolbox, a build of current `main` panics before its window opens: `Library libxkbcommon-x11.so could not be loaded.`
- **An X11 window on a Wayland desktop**, which is what #165 had to accept until Wayland drops worked.

`GRIDCRAFT_WAYLAND` goes away with the revert. Nothing else in `main` refers to it, and the direct `winit` dependency #165 added to `apps/gridcraft` is removed with it (the only other mentions of winit there are comments).

A separate question for the packaging: if X11 stays reachable (a plain X11 session still uses winit's X11 backend), the deb and RPM could also list `libxkbcommon-x11` so that path can't crash. I've left that out of this PR.

title: macOS: Save As offers Excel Workbook and does not abort
author: dukedorje
body:
Fixes #2790.

## Why

On macOS 0.12.1, Save As (⌘⇧S) from an open CSV does not list Excel Workbook. The panel then aborts the process.

`rfd` flattens every filter into one `setAllowedFileTypes` list and never turns on `showsContentTypes`, so the format menu only shows types macOS already knows. `.xlsx` was a document type in the bundle, not an exported UTI, so the menu omitted it. The suggested name stayed `kit-prod.csv`.

Choosing a format, or just leaving the panel up, runs `NSSavePanel.runModal` inside winit's event handler. winit 0.30 panics on that re-entry, and the panic cannot unwind:

```
panicked at winit-0.30.13/src/platform_impl/macos/event_handler.rs:135:17:
tried to handle event while another event is currently being handled
panic in a function that cannot unwind
```

Same abort as #2042, #1911, and #2464. Dispatching `runModal` onto the next turn is not enough: the nested modal loop still delivers winit events.

## What

- Save, Open, and Insert Picture on macOS are sheets (`beginSheetModalForWindow` / `beginWithCompletionHandler`). The path is applied on a later frame. Windows and Linux still use the blocking picker.
- The save panel sets `showsContentTypes`, and the bundle exports `org.openxmlformats.spreadsheetml.sheet` as "Excel Workbook".
- Workbook Save As suggests `{stem}.xlsx` when the open title is `kit-prod.csv`. CSV, HTML, and PDF exports still suggest their own extension and force it on write.

#2278 is the broader sheet change and currently conflicts with main. It does not export the xlsx UTI. This is a smaller fix on current main.

## Checks

- `cargo test -p gridcraft-ui-egui --lib an_open_csv_saves_as`
- `cargo test -p gridcraft --bin gridcraft xlsx`
- file-menu integration tests for Save As PDF, palette export, a cancelled PDF picker, and Save a Copy
- `cargo clippy -p gridcraft -p gridcraft-ui-egui --all-targets -- -D warnings`

title: Let Goal Seek's cell boxes take cells clicked on the grid
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Fixes #2548

## Cause
The Goal Seek dialog copied the active cell into Set cell once when it opened and never set up reference picking (`RefPick`). Grid clicks and drags therefore only moved the selection, and the dialog's boxes never saw them. `RefPick` also served one fixed box and always started an empty box with `=`, which only suits a formula box.

## Fix
Goal Seek now opens with a `RefPick` in a new `bare` mode, which writes the absolute reference (`$D$5`, or `$D$5:$E$6` for a drag) without a leading `=`. A new `track_pick_box` helper sends the pick to whichever box, Set cell or By changing cell, last had the keyboard. Integration tests cover a click and a drag into Set cell, a click into By changing cell that leaves Set cell alone, and switching back to Set cell.

## Verified
- Regression tests `goal_seek_pick::the_set_cell_box_takes_a_cell_clicked_on_the_grid`, `goal_seek_pick::dragging_into_the_set_cell_box_writes_a_range`, `goal_seek_pick::the_by_changing_cell_box_takes_a_click_once_it_has_the_keyboard`: fail on `main` without the fix and pass with it (`cargo test -p gridcraft-ui-egui --test it goal_seek_pick`).
- `cargo xtask ci` passes except `interaction::column_autocomplete_folds_case_beyond_ascii`, `interaction::language_switch_renders_the_ribbon_and_persists`, which also fail on `main` without this change.

## Not changed
Other dialogs with reference fields (Remove Duplicates, Advanced Filter, Solver) still don't pick references. What a click does while Set cell still holds the starting cell with the caret after it isn't specified or tested, because there is no Excel observation of that case.

title: One-point FORECAST.ETS is #DIV/0! and AMORDEGRC with a life of two or less is #NUM!
author: Harrison-Booth
body:
Two degenerate-input cases where GridCraft gave a different error (or a number) than Excel.

Measured in Excel 16 (COM, new temporary workbook, closed unsaved):

| Formula | Excel | GridCraft before |
|---|---|---|
| `FORECAST.ETS(1,{1},{1})`, `FORECAST.ETS(1,1,1)`, `FORECAST.ETS(2,{5},{1})` | #DIV/0! | #NUM! |
| `FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT(1,{1},{1})`, `FORECAST.ETS.SEASONALITY({1},{1})`, `FORECAST.ETS.STAT({1},{1},8)` | #DIV/0! | #NUM! |

title: Add native Monte Carlo, correlation matrices and sample-derived tornado
author: betosaco
body:
Adds native **Data → Monte Carlo** analysis for arbitrary GridCraft workbook formulas, reachable through CLI/control/MCP. Trials preserve source assumptions; only a complete static report is published, as one undoable action.

- Seeded uniform, triangular and normal inputs; cross-sheet formulas and up to 64 forecast outputs.
- Random sampling or independent replicated Latin Hypercubes; validated positive-semidefinite Gaussian **latent** correlation matrices, including singular ±1 relationships.
- Stable summaries, percentiles, probability above zero, optional samples, observed Pearson/Spearman dependence, conditional sample-derived tornado and native convergence chart. Student t/Wilson intervals and replica-based LHS inference document their assumptions.
- Accessible configuration dialog; Random does not send LHS replica limits, and Enter/Shift+Enter in either multiline field does not confirm the dialog.

Percentiles describe outcomes; confidence intervals describe finite-simulation error. title: Speed up running COUNTIFS/SUMIFS over growing column ranges
author: Silvertree2010
body:
Fixes #2813

## Cause
Each formula with a growing range like `$B$2:B{r}` walked the B-tree cell store again for each of its ranges, which was about 87% of recalc time. For every cell it compared, the criteria matcher also cloned the value, copied the cell text, re-tokenized the pattern and lower-cased the text into a new Vec.

## Fix
During one recalculation pass, single-column blocks that hold only constants are read from the store once, kept per (sheet, column) and grown as needed (capped at 4M values). Blocks that hold a formula or a spilled value, or sheets with spills found in the pass, still take the normal path. Criteria keep their wildcard tokens from parsing and match ASCII text in place without allocating, so the 8,000-row case from the issue drops from 7.2 s to 0.77 s (in-process recalc) with the same results.

Verified:
- `tests::running_countifs_cost_about_as_much_as_a_running_count` is an ignored timing test. It fails on `main` without the fix and passes with it.
- `tests::running_countifs_match_a_count_by_hand` and `tests::running_ranges_read_formulas_spills_and_edits` check results against hand counts and per-cell sums, including formulas, spills and edits. They guard correctness of the cache. They are not claimed to fail on `main`.
- Run the set with `cargo test --release -p gridcraft-calc running_ -- --include-ignored`.
- `cargo xtask ci` passes except `interaction::column_autocomplete_folds_case_beyond_ascii` and `interaction::language_switch_renders_the_ribbon_and_persists`, which also fail on `main` without this change.
